- **The kit ships a runnable, independent deck checker.** `review/check.mjs` is the *same* reviewer AND the *same* linter the Lattice Studio runs on decks its own model writes, bundled as one self-contained file. `node check.mjs deck.md` names what is wrong — an invented `_class`, a card written flat where the layout needs nested bullets, placeholder titles, headings that are labels rather than takeaways, a missing ask, elements past their word budget — each with the fix, in about a tenth of a second, **offline and at zero token cost**. `--json` emits one envelope carrying a `partial` flag, `--strict` exits non-zero. It reads the kit's own `reference/components.json` for per-element word budgets, and says plainly when that is absent rather than reporting a partial check as clean.
- **Why it is there:** a model reviewing its own draft against a rubric it just read will declare the draft fine. The checker is code, so it cannot be talked into approving. It catches the falsifiable half; `review/rubric.md` lists the same checks in plain form for a human pass, and taste is still the reader's.
- **Every folder is now its own entry point.** `README.md` in each of `authoring/`, `components/`, `skills/`, `review/` and `reference/` says what is inside and in what order to read it — and GitHub renders them on open, so a human browsing lands oriented. The root `README.md` is the single front door, costed by task — one door, so a reader is never choosing between two.
- **`components/README.md` carries what to use a component FOR, what it is NOT for, and what to use instead.** All 61 components, derived from their manifests' `antiPatterns` and the 244 `related` edges. The pick list truncates to a first sentence and says the when-not-to-use half is deliberately off that surface; choosing between two plausible components is exactly where an agent goes wrong, and the deciding fact is the anti-pattern.
- **`skills/README.md` resolves the rules the skills cite.** The seven skills still ship byte-identical to `design/skills/`, so their "HARD RULE #N" citations and repo paths remain — a generated glossary now says what each cited rule means, and the index states plainly that repo paths and `npm run` commands assume a clone.

- **Avatars can wear earrings, head coverings and a choice of top.** Four new traits, all opt-in, so a
  face you already drew does not change: `earrings=stud|hoop|drop`, `headwear=hijab|turban|skullcap|beanie|kufi|cap|backcap` with
  `headwear-color` (the nine `top` colors), and `clothing=crew|vneck|collar|turtleneck|hoodie|blazer`
  (`crew` is the default). Every covering except the hijab is fitted to the face shape (a flatter dome on a round head, a taller one on a long head). A hijab and a turban hide all hair; a skull cap, beanie, kufi and baseball cap (`cap`) hide the fringe and any
  volume above them; a fitted cap worn backwards (`backcap`) sits back on the crown and leaves the fringe showing (a bun, an afro, curls); a hijab covers the ears, so it hides earrings. The Avatars guide, cheat sheet and `avatars.docs.md`
  list them, and `examples/avatars-dress.md` shows each.

- **`backdrop:` register — restrain any finish, per deck or per slide.** `backdrop: 40 clear` dims whatever finish the deck wears to 40% and clears it from the whole content area (eyebrow, heading and body), leaving it only in the margin; `<!-- _class: backdrop-spot-tr -->` shows it in one window on one slide. Works with built-in and fabricated finishes, on every render path including the CLI, and overrides a finish's own baked strength or mask. Strength steps are 20/40/60/80/full; masks are `clear`, `open` and `spot-<tl|t|tr|l|c|r|bl|b|br>`.

- **Added: `tools/wait-for.sh` — the one way to wait for a slow job.** A wait is
  now bounded (default 1800s, ceiling 3600s) and deduped by job name, so a second
  wait on a live job refuses and names the holder instead of piling on. Replaces
  the hand-rolled `until <cond>; do sleep N; done` background call, which had no
  deadline and no identity: one session left fifteen resident, six on the same
  integration run, still polling after five hours. Idling was nearly free; the
  cost was the late fire, which wakes a session past the prompt-cache TTL and
  re-sends the whole conversation at full input price, once per duplicate.
  Contract in `engineering/development.md` §Waiting for a slow job.
- **Added: a PreToolUse hook that coaches toward the bounded wait.**
  `.claude/hooks/warn-unbounded-wait.sh` spots a hand-rolled `while`/`until`
  loop around `sleep` in a Bash call and points at `tools/wait-for.sh`. It warns
  and never blocks, matching `check-commit-msg.sh`'s posture and HARD RULE #29's
  "we warn, we coach" — and it exists because a `check-ownership.js` gate cannot
  reach this at all: that gate walks the repo filesystem, and these waits are
  ad-hoc tool calls that never become files.

- The editable `.odp` and `.pptx` now keep each slide's own background (its fill, border rules, washes and ghost numerals) apart from its content. Slides that draw the same background share one master page (`.odp`) or layout (`.pptx`), so it is not a movable object on any slide. A flat-color background is a plain fill, not a picture. A slide that blends or blurs what is behind it keeps its own opaque picture. `lattice` prints how many slides did.
- The editable export names what each text box is: the slide title is a real title placeholder (Outline view, slide sorter and screen readers list it), the page number is an auto-updating field, and a header, footer or page number that repeats across slides is drawn once on the layout. Eyebrows and subtitles are named "Eyebrow" and "Subtitle" in the selection pane.
- The slide's content picture is locked against moving and resizing in the editable `.odp` (LibreOffice honors it; Collabora is untested) and marked locked in the `.pptx` (PowerPoint's Lock should honor it, untested; LibreOffice ignores it).
- **Added:** the Studio's Editable text export (PowerPoint and LibreOffice) now shares backgrounds across slides, crops photos and charts as pictures of their own, and writes inline code as a text highlight, the same as `lattice --editable`; both run one capture, `captureOfficeSlides` in `@laticent/calco`.

- The editable `.odp` and `.pptx` now draw more of a slide as native shapes instead of pixels in the picture: pills with their dot, ring and icon (grouped as one object inside their card), accent bars, counter text such as "STEP 01", linear gradients (a real gradient fill with its stops and transparency), and sized one-color rules.
- Two outer shadows draw as the wider one and a frosted box keeps its translucent fill; the export line counts both (`approximated: 2 stacked shadows, 1 frosted fill`).
- What cannot be a shape (a photo, a chart, an icon) is now a picture of its own in the editable export, placed in order among the shapes and grouped with its card, instead of one slide-sized picture under everything. A card that holds an icon is a real card with the icon above it. A large photo is a JPEG cut to the photo, so a photo deck is smaller; a small photo crop stays a lossless PNG. The export line reports how many pictures and how many slides kept one whole-slide picture.
- An inline code span or mark is now a text highlight in the editable export, so it moves, edits and wraps with its words (its rounded corners and border are not carried). A finish's decorative monogram or numeral no longer appears twice.

- The editable `.pptx` now carries the deck's own theme instead of Office's: the theme colors are the deck's palette (text, ground, heading, card fill, the accent and the first five chart series colors, read from the theme's tokens under the slide's color scheme), and the theme fonts are the deck's heading and body faces. PowerPoint's color picker, theme fonts and new text boxes now match the deck.
- A slide added in PowerPoint or Google Slides now looks like the deck, on every kind of slide: each layout carries the whole look of its slides, in its own type and ink, so a new divider, topic or closing in a light deck is light-on-dark with its own header, footer, eyebrow and source line. Layouts are named after the slide ("Title", "Content", "Divider", "Topic", "Closing") instead of "Layout 1", …
- A text box, table or chart added on a dark slide in a light deck (or a light one in a dark deck) now reads: the theme is written the Office way, dark colors first, and each such layout maps text to the light pair, as Office's own dark themes do.
- The running header, footer and page number are drawn once on the slide master, so they are edited in one place in Slide Master view and appear on new slides. A slide on a background no other slide uses now shares them too, and a layout whose slides show none (the title slide) hides them.
- A header whose text changes from slide to slide (a section name) no longer splits the deck into a layout per slide: the layout offers a header placeholder in its look, and each slide keeps its own text.
- The page number now reaches the master and layouts in Lattice's own style (letter-spaced, translucent). It used to stay a separate text box on every slide, so a slide added in PowerPoint had no number.
- Existing slides look the same as before in the `.pptx` and `.odp` (checked pixel for pixel in LibreOffice on five decks, an anchor-slide deck among them).

- **LibreOffice Impress export.** `lattice deck.md deck.odp` writes an OpenDocument Presentation: one full-bleed image per slide, like the `.pptx`, with speaker notes on each page's notes view and each slide's `describe:` text as the picture's alt text. Lattice builds the file itself, so exporting needs no LibreOffice install. `--strip-notes` removes the notes.
- **Editable office export.** `--editable` on a `.odp` or `.pptx` turns every paragraph into a real text box in the deck's own font, over a picture of the slide with its text removed, so the file can be edited in LibreOffice Impress or PowerPoint. Both formats embed the deck's fonts, every weight included, so the text looks the same on a machine that does not have them. Charts, diagrams and equations stay part of the picture.
- **Studio: LibreOffice export and editable text.** The Share sheet has a LibreOffice row (`.odp`), and the PowerPoint and LibreOffice options steps have an Editable text switch that does the same as `--editable`.
- **Calco (`@laticent/calco`), the office-export library.** A new sibling library that turns a rendered HTML slide into an editable `.odp` or `.pptx`: a reader that measures each paragraph and hides it for a clean background photo, and writers for both formats. It has no dependencies of its own (JSZip and a font pinner are passed in). Lattice is its first user.
- **`/calco`, the Calco page.** A live demo on plain HTML slides: see what Calco reads, lift the text, and download a real `.odp` or `.pptx` written in the browser. Listed under Libraries.

- `@callout{…}` now draws on nineteen charts, not only the heatmap: `bar`, `stacked-bar`, `line`, `histogram`, `ep-curve`, `waterfall`, `bullet`, `scatter`, `slope`, `tower`, `piechart`, `funnel`, `map`, `quadrant`, `radar`, `gantt`, `hub-spoke`, `risk-matrix` and `journey`. A note names its mark with `for=` (a category, a stage, a task, an axis, a region, a point), the mark is ringed and carries a numbered marker, and the words sit under the chart as a centered group that sets side by side and wraps to a new row when the width runs out (`side=beside` in the `@callout` span puts them beside it instead; a chart's manifest can set its own default with `callout.side`, and the pie and donut do). On a `journey` the task's chip is ringed and the notes read in a list under the board (the board is browser-measured CSS layout, so there is no side to choose), one list per stage on a portrait deck. A slide with no callout renders as before. The rule, the per-chart naming and the limits are in `lib/plugins/callout/callout.docs.md`.
- On these charts a callout's `detail="…"` joins its mark's hover card and the speaker note, the chart's description lists the notes (and any it could not draw), the narrator says each one after the chart, and `lint:deck` warns on a `for=` that names no mark, on a `key` legend (not drawn yet) and on a note past the sixth.
- Not yet: `flowchart` and `state-chart` (the browser lays them out), and `radar` inside a split pane.

- The pre-merge card built by `npm run card` now ends with a GROWTH section, read from git by `tools/pr-growth.js`: lines added and removed, and files touched, for docs, decks, code, comments, CSS, tests, config and generated files. Comment lines are found by a real parser, and the total matches `git diff --numstat`.

- A plain `.html` export now warns, naming the slide, when a card tag wraps far enough to cover the top of its card body. That file has no script to equalize tag sizes, so the PDF of the same deck can be fine while the `.html` is not.

- The `tag:` register gains two axes, so it now takes up to four words:
  - placement: `corner` (the default), `foot` (the bottom-left corner), `notch` (a tab straddling the card's top edge), `band` (a full-width strip across the card top) or `inline` (a chip above the card's first line; list-steps' own place);
  - text alignment inside the tag: `start` (the default), `center` or `end`.
- Every placement works on every tagged layout: `cards-grid`, `cards-stack`, `decision`, `compare-prose`, `split-compare` and `list-steps`. On list-steps, `corner`, `foot`, `notch` and `band` turn the bare `STEP 01` label into a boxed tag. A slide sets one axis with `tag-foot`, `tag-center` and so on and keeps the deck's other words; a placement word on a slide wins over `banner-tag`.
- Tags in each placement keep one size per slide, as corner tags already did, and `tag-budget` gives a `tag-band` label two lines, as it does a `banner-tag` band. Decks that set no placement render unchanged.

- The `tag:` front-matter register sets how every card tag looks: the numbers on `cards-grid` and `cards-stack`, the slot labels and `banner-tag` bands on `compare-prose` and `decision`, the `split-compare` verdict, and the list-steps `STEP` label and `capsule` pill. Two words, one per axis, in any order:
  - color: `color` (the component's own, the default), `plain` (a neutral pill) or `none` (bare text; the label is never hidden);
  - size: `small`, `regular` or `large`.
- A slide overrides one axis with `tag-plain`, `tag-large` and so on, and keeps the deck's word on the other. `lint:deck` flags an unknown word as `unknown-tag`. See `lib/base/base.registers.docs.md` § `tag:`.
- `lint:deck` also flags two words on one axis on a slide (`tag-plain tag-none`, and `backdrop-20 backdrop-40`) as `conflicting-variants`, and no longer reads a comment-only `tag:` or `backdrop:` value as unknown words.
- Every boxed card tag on a slide is now the same size: the widest tag's width and the tallest tag's height. It applies in the live preview and in the CLI's PDF, PNG, PPTX, Marp, `--fluid` and `--player` outputs. A plain `.html` export has no script, so there each tag keeps its own size, and a corner label that wraps covers the top of the card body; the budget below keeps a lint-clean deck clear of it. A short label beside a long one no longer reads as a different component, and a two-line band no longer sits beside one-line bands.
- `lint:deck` warns (`tag-budget`) when a `decision` or `compare-prose` slot label is longer than one line of its tag: 49, 33 or 24 characters for 2, 3 or 4 cards (fewer at `tag-large`, more at `tag-small`), and twice that for a `banner-tag` band. Two labels in `examples/system-design-foundations.md` were over and are shortened.

- The Studio sets card tags without typing. Deck settings gain a **Card tags** group (Tag color, Tag size, Tag placement, Tag text) that writes the `tag:` front-matter line, and slide settings show the same four rows on `cards-grid`, `cards-stack`, `decision`, `compare-prose`, `split-compare` and `list-steps` slides, writing `tag-*` classes on that slide.

- The chart bucket gallery is regenerated from the manifests (`npm run build:bucket-galleries`) and now carries `histogram`, `ep-curve`, `risk-matrix` and `tower` slides (28 members, was 24), so `tools/chart-structure-census.js --check` measures their rendered marks: `histogram-band` (1px, non-scaling) and `ep-dot` are pinned (23 outline marks, up from 21).
- `tools/chart-structure-census.js` judges outline pinning per element instead of per class. `heatmap-cell` mixes canvas-colored separators (measured cells) with dotted outlines (empty cells); the class-level flag read the separators as an unpinned outline. The check now passes with the separators exempt and the empty-cell outline held to the rule.

- The chart taxonomy now covers the two layers above the mark: the **chrome ladder** (grid → rule → tick → label → title → value, one rung per role rather than five different rule colours by accident) and the **figure frame** — a chart's own ground and edge, which it has never had. The ground is declared always so an export can bake it; the edge stays off by default.

- **Correction:** the chart design language was stripping colour where the rule said to *move* it. `engineering/decisions/2026-09-07-chart-design-language/colour-brief.md` states the principle — colour carries context and is never removed as a correction, only relocated, re-ranked or given a companion channel; pattern and shade substitute for hue only where a reader cannot receive it — and restates the encoding axis as a grouping rule: a group shares one hue, a singular may own one.

- `tools/chart-colour-reach.js` asks whether a chart's text wears the colour of the thing it names, rather than whether it is merely coloured — the distinction that matters, since a navy label beside a green line clears any chroma floor and still tells a reader nothing. Reports per member which marks, text and rules carry a category's colour.

- The six competing chart design languages and the judged ranking are recorded under `engineering/decisions/2026-09-07-chart-design-language/` — proposals, not decisions. The losers are kept in full because the recommendation is to graft from them, each carries measurements the winner does not, and a rejected proposal is the cheapest record of why for the next session tempted by the same idea.

- `tools/chart-language-census.js` measures what every chart-family member actually paints — type register per semantic role, fill finish, axis furniture, key model and interaction handles — by reading resolved style out of a real browser render. A census, not a gate: it grounds the chart design-language work in numbers anyone can reproduce.

- `tools/chart-finish-divergence.js` renders one deck under several candidate chart finishes and reports, per member, the percent of pixels a reader would see change — so a finish that silently fails to reach a chart is caught instead of shipped.
- `tools/chart-language-census.js` gains a KEYING arm: which attribute each member carries its mark's colour slot on (`data-cat`, `data-mark`, `data-s`, `data-series`, or nothing at all).

- Chart look becomes an author choice through a `charts:` front-matter register — three coherent presets (`editorial`, `panel`, `material`) rather than a set of independent knobs, following the same shape as the fourteen registers already shipped. The line a preset may not cross is measured, not asserted: it may change how a chart looks, never whether it can be read.

- **`marks:` picks how every chart on a deck spends its color.** Three finishes:
  `pigment` (full-strength bodies under an ink edge), `etch` (a whisper of a body under a
  doubled edge) and `tone` (one hue in eight value steps, every name in its ink). The key
  repaints with the marks it keys. It is a look like `icon:` and `spark:`, so it is always on:
  a deck that names none wears `pigment`, there is no `off`, and every slide is stamped (a chart
  in a pane of a `columns` slide included). A slide can override the deck with
  `_class: marks-<name>`, and `lint:deck` flags an unknown value (`unknown-marks`).
- A finish never costs a reader contrast or the texture channel. Text on a mark (a heatmap
  value, a matrix-grid cell, a status pill) picks black or white from its own mark's color and
  clears 4.5:1 on every theme tested, the a11y and print themes included. On a browser too old to
  pick that ink, a mark that carries text keeps its own colors, and every other mark
  still takes the finish. The a11y themes'
  pattern fills still win over any finish. `line` and `slope` are left exactly as they draw, and
  a status (a gantt bar's `blocked`) keeps its own color under every finish.

- `check-chart-fit` gains a `--style` flag and a falsifiability test. The gate
  learned to skip `visibility: hidden` marks in #2084 — a real fix, since
  `state-chart` keeps a hidden measuring column that was being counted as content
  cut at the stage — but it shipped with no test, and a filter is one edit away
  from swallowing every mark and reporting that everything fits. The test runs the
  gate twice on the same deck: as shipped, and with the scaffold made visible
  through the deck's own `style:`. Verified red under both mutations that matter —
  a filter that counts nothing, and no filter at all.

- The chart finish register resolves to four named looks — **folio** (the newspaper page), **plate** (the bounded illustration plate), **relief** (material, depth across the mark) and **survey** (the surveyor's sheet) — specified as executable token blocks in `engineering/decisions/2026-09-07-chart-design-language/finishes.spec.js`. A finish is 16 lines of tokens with zero per-member rules, so a new chart inherits all four for free.

- Chart design language: the hue count is the texture count — a rainbow single series hands a monochrome reader one hatch pattern per bar for values of a single measure, which reads as a harder categorical boundary than the colour it replaced.

- `tools/chart-hue-jobs.js` measures whether a chart member's categorical colour does a job — binding a mark to a name across a gap, or separating marks that position does not — and reports the verdict beside what the member actually spends.
- Chart design language: the G0 grouping test is replaced by that two-jobs test. G0 could not tell a `bar row` from a `funnel` (both name the mark in a gutter, one spends five hues and the other one), and the measurement flags `funnel` and `timeline-list` as spending categorical hue with no job, and `roadmap` and `state-chart` as having a job and under-using it.

- `lint:deck` warns with `chart-list-split-quote` when a `>` written at the left margin sits between two items of a chart's list. The quote ends the list, so every row after it dropped out of the chart without a word. On a chart that reads a row's quote (flowchart, state chart, and the 13 detail charts: bar, line, stacked bar, slope, bullet, funnel, pie, waterfall, map, scatter, quadrant, radar, word cloud) the fix indents a one-line quote under the item above; a quote of several lines is left for you to indent, and elsewhere the warning asks you to move the quote above or below the list.
- `lint:deck` warns with `chart-row-quote-unread` when a `>` sits under a radar series or a quadrant group. Those rows draw no mark of their own, so there is no card to show the quote in.

- `tools/chart-mark-separation.js` asks whether a rendered chart still separates its categories under a colour-vision condition — scoring each mark's distance from its nearest neighbor AND the spread of its own shading, so a mark that paints over its own categorical read is told apart from a palette that simply collapses. Credits the texture and stroke-dash channels rather than scoring colour a chart does not depend on.

- Bullet and progress read a row's `{…}` record themselves, in the chart and in the narrator, so the fields no old span spelled are now drawn and said: a bullet's `band=[…]` and `floor=`, and a progress row's `note="…"`. A record draws what the older nested `Band`, `Floor` and note rows draw, a keyword row still overrides the record's field, and a deck that writes no record and no `{> …}` renders, narrates and lints exactly as before (475 of 478 chart slides in the repo corpus byte-identical to `main`; the other three are slides of the new demo deck).
- Lint: `chart-row-record-unread` no longer warns on a bullet record with `band=` or `floor=` or a progress record with `note=`, because they are drawn when the record ends its row; it still warns when a quote the chart does not read, or another paragraph, follows the record.

- **Icons on flowchart and state-chart nodes.** A shape's style record takes `icon=` from the icons plugin, which draws the icon beside the name (above it when the chart is pinned `tb`): `` `{#api, diamond, c2, icon=gateway}` ``. `icon-only` draws the icon alone and keeps the name as the hover title and what a screen reader says. `lint:deck` coaches an unknown icon name, `icon-only` with no icon, an icon on a group, and an icon-only row with no words. With the icons plugin off, a node shows its name, as if no icon were written. Charts that write no icon render byte-identically. Demo: `examples/chart-icons.md`.

- A `>` indented under a chart row is that row's description. Bar, line, stacked bar, slope, bullet, funnel, pie, waterfall, map, scatter, quadrant, radar and word cloud show it at the top of the row's hover card. Before, the quote hid the row's value, so bar, map, scatter and bullet dropped the mark and waterfall dropped the chart. The narration reads the description the same way it reads a nested bullet, says a pill as its text, and skips a spark.
- The hover card in the Playground and the Studio renders a row's description and nested bullets as rich content in the deck's own styling: several lines, lists, bold, code, pills and sparks. Before, it showed them as flattened plain text.
- A word cloud with a nested bullet under one of its words keeps every word. Before, the first nested list ended the cloud, so it collapsed to that one word. A nested bullet is now the word's hover detail.
- A description cannot break its slide: an unclosed tag in it (`<!--`, `<div>`, `<textarea>`) stays inside the row instead of hiding the chart or the slides after it, and the hover card keeps it inside the card.
- The hover card closes when its preview leaves the screen, such as on a switch to the Studio's Source or Compose tab, instead of staying on top of the editor. It no longer shows the slide's page number.

- Each of the 16 charts in the chart authoring model now declares its row in its manifest's `segno` block: a `row` slot (a `cell` slot on heatmap and matrix-grid) whose fields are written as one `{…}` record, plus a `rows` block naming the row's shape, whether a `>` under a list row is its description (`quotes`), which rows draw no mark, and how the chart reads the row today. The build compiles each one, so a schema Segno refuses fails the build.
  - Field names follow the model's shared vocabulary: `value`, `target`, `band` and `floor` (bullet), `kind` (waterfall's `total` or `step`), `status` (the shared status words) and `note` (progress), `x`, `y` and `size` (scatter and quadrant).
- `lib/core/chart-rows.js` is the one chart row reader. The narrator and lint take the detail charts, the markless rows and a row's `>` description from it; Compose reads the same schema flag, pinned to the reader's list by a test. It replaces `lib/core/chart-row-detail.js`, and the narrator no longer rewrites a description into nested bullets before reading the slide.
- Narration of a row's `>` description fixes two cases:
  - A description on a bullet row that also has `Floor` or `Band` rows no longer hides those rows.
  - A description holding inline code under a bar, line, stacked-bar or slope row no longer silences the whole chart's narration.
  - Every other description is said as before.
- The new lint warning `chart-row-record-unread` catches a row written as one record, such as ``- Uptime `{4.2M, target=5.0M}` ``, on a chart that does not draw that form yet. Today such a row loses its value with no error: a bar draws no bar, a pie misreads the slice, progress prints the braces. The warning names the spans the chart reads today (`` `4.2M` `5.0M` ``). It has no machine fix, because the model's codemod will write the record form.
- The radar and quadrant docs now describe the rows the charts actually read: a radar series nests one row per axis, and a quadrant's points nest under their groups.
- None of the 895 chart slides in the decks, docs and manifest samples renders, narrates or lints differently.

- Lint: `chart-series-name-inconsistent` warns when a nested bar, line, stacked-bar, slope or radar list spells one series two ways across its groups (`Licenses` / `Licences`), names the intended spelling, and offers a one-click fix. Series that sit side by side in a group, and names that differ only in digits, stay silent.

- Chart design language: the rules for where colour is spent — a hue appears once per link between a name and its mark, and a finish may retreat a mark's fill only where that fill is not the sole carrier of a channel.

- `tools/build-stress-deck.js` assembles a bucket's per-component `stressDoc` ceiling cases into one deck, so the census, the separation audit and any render check can be pointed at a bucket where it actually breaks rather than at the gallery's tidy samples. It reports which components have no stressDoc, so an incomplete corpus cannot look complete.

- Heatmap: a `{> prose}` description in a table cell describes that cell (replacing the `note=` annotation, which still reads), in a header cell it describes the column, and a column headed `{>}` holds one plain-text description per row (only the first such column; lint warns on a second, and on a header description with no column name before it). A description on an empty cell is kept and the cell stays unmeasured, the `{>}` column is taken out before the 12-column cap, and the narrator and the chart's text description say all three.
- Lint: `chart-description-unread` warns on a `{> …}` description in a list row or in a table cell of a chart that does not read one, and moves a list row's description into a `>` quote with a fix.

- A chart is now classified by its **nature** (substrate, whether its marks overlap, whether it carries text), its **use** (what colour encodes, how a mark is named) and its **reception** (the strongest non-colour channel it can support) — `engineering/decisions/2026-09-07-chart-design-language/taxonomy.md`. Every rule in the design language keys on one of those properties instead of on a member's name.

- The chart finish register resolves to three colour-forward looks — **pigment**
  (full strength in the body: pick it when you want colour), **etch** (in the
  line and the letter: the modern look) and **tone** (one hue carried in VALUE:
  the conservative, restrained look) — separating on mark body depth, which is
  present on 20 of 21 members and needs no gradient. The four-finish attempt that
  varied furniture opacity is kept as `finishes.superseded.spec.js`, since nobody
  could tell it apart on a chart without one.
- **The third finish is `tone`, not `ground`.** The competition picked `ground`
  and this line said so; the swap to `tone` was made afterwards with no record,
  which is why the two disagreed for a while. `tone` is the settled answer and
  `engineering/decisions/2026-09-07-chart-design-language/tone-is-the-third-finish.md`
  is where it is written down.
- **The register is a SPEC, not shipped engine CSS.** The three finishes exist as
  a generated stylesheet driven from `finishes.spec.js` and measured against real
  renders; no `finish:` value in `lib/` selects one yet. The `finish:` front-matter
  register that does ship is the backdrop layer, which is a different thing with
  the same word on it.

- The Studio chat now knows which slide you are on and the line your caret is on when you send a message, so "fix this slide" means the slide in front of you. The shell reads the place once per send from the focus hub; the chat never re-renders on caret moves.

- The Studio chat can use the Library. When the Library holds photos or videos, the chat sees a short list of them (name, shape, whether they are kept to this deck, and a caption once it has one), so "make a collage of my photos" writes real `asset:<name>` references instead of placeholders. It can search the Library (`list_assets`) and, on a model that accepts images, look at up to six small thumbnails a turn (`view_asset`), then save a one-line caption on each photo (`caption_asset`). A captioned photo is read as text from then on and never looked at again. A deck with an empty Library sends the chat nothing extra. A model that cannot read images says so and works from names and shapes. Videos are listed but cannot be viewed.

- The Studio chat can change a deck's theme or finish (only to names the Studio ships). It can turn numbers into a bar, line, pie or stacked-bar slide; a value that is not one number is refused instead of drawing an empty bar. And it can look at a slide: on a model that takes pictures, `render_slide` sends it the slide as export would draw it, up to three per turn. Theme, finish and chart changes stage on the draft like any edit.

- The Studio chat has three modes on its composer bar. **Talk** reads and answers and changes nothing. **Review**, the default, stages edits for you to apply. **Auto**, for one visit, applies a clean edit at once after saving a History checkpoint. An edit that deletes slides or rewrites most of the deck still waits for Apply, and Auto never applies during a live session or after a stopped turn. Code enforces the mode twice: the tools each request carries, and a gate on every tool call.
- The Studio chat can create a new deck. It drafts the whole deck and shows a confirm with the title, the slide headings and any checker errors. Nothing exists until you press "Create and open"; the new deck then opens with a chat line pointing back to the conversation that made it.

- The Architect chat header now has a **Chat metrics** dropdown where the bare session figure used to be. It shows what this session, this deck and today have cost (a new spend ledger, bucketed by local day and deck, kept 120 days), how full the model's context window is (a ring beside the figure turns amber at 70% and red at 90%), the share of the prompt read from cache, and the last reply's cost, model calls and thinking tokens. All of it comes from the `usage` block each reply already returns, so it adds no request and no charge.
- Architect replies now have a **Show work** link that opens what the Architect sent, thought and ran: tokens by part of the prompt (primer, deck, conversation, tools, documents, photos), then each model call with its cost, its thinking (rendered as markdown, with a Raw button for the exact text) when the provider streams it, and every command as a link that expands to the arguments it sent and what came back. The trace is saved with the reply (capped near 8 KB, thinking cut first) so it survives a reload. While a reply streams, a one-line excerpt of the model's thinking shows above the status line. None of it adds a request: it reads the thinking, arguments and usage already in the stream, and no `reasoning` setting is sent to get it.
- The Chat metrics dropdown can **compact the conversation** by hand. One model call turns the older messages into a briefing of at most 250 words and keeps the latest six word for word; the dropdown shows the estimated tokens saved per turn and the one-time cost before you press it, nudges past 20 author turns or 70% of the window, and offers Undo until the next send. Nothing compacts automatically, because that would spend credit unprompted. The briefing shows as an expandable divider in the thread.

- The docs site has a **Using the command line** guide: copy-and-paste recipes for rendering, printing, sharing, notes and captions, image sets, packages, video and batch runs. A new **CLI reference** page lists every flag, subcommand, environment variable and exit code.
- The agent kit ships a `skills/cli.md` skill that teaches an agent to pick the right output for a recipient, render it, and check the result before handing it over. It also ships in the npm package under `design/skills/`.
- A unit test ties the CLI docs to the argument parsers, so a new flag that ships undocumented, or a documented flag that no longer exists, fails the suite.
- Fixed: the **Getting started** example deck authored its `big-number` slide with the number as a heading, which renders the number slot blank. The number is now a list item.
- Fixed: `lattice deck.md out/deck.pdf` creates the `out/` folder when it is missing. It used to finish the render and then crash with a Node stack trace at the first write.

- The CLI renders a `.lattice` project file from the Studio: `lattice deck.lattice deck.pdf` (or `.pptx`, `.odp`, `.html`, `.png`, `.zip`). It opens the file with the same checks the Studio uses and takes the photos the deck names from the file as the Library stored them. The saved themes, components and plugins the file carries are used for that render only, never installed, and the ones you installed still work alongside them. A package in the file wins over an installed one of the same name, and the CLI says so.
- `--trust` runs the code in the components and plugins a `.lattice` input carries, for that render only. Without it, or an approval from `lattice packages trust`, a render that needs that code fails and names the package. Nothing is written to the trust store.
- The CLI writes a `.lattice` too: `lattice deck.md deck.lattice` packs the deck and the installed theme and components it uses. It starts no browser and runs no package code. From a `.lattice` input, the deck's title, its review comments and every package the file carried go back out with it. Photos that came in a `.lattice` input go through the same cleaner as the Studio's Library, so one the Studio made comes back out byte for byte and a camera original packed by hand loses its location; only the ones the deck names go, as in the Studio, including a photo named only inside an image plugin span such as `@image{asset:harbor}`. Photos from an `assets/` folder go the way the Studio keeps an original: their location, camera data, text and comments are removed, and the pixels, transparency and rotation stay. A photo the CLI cannot clean (a HEIC, an AVIF, a damaged file), or a link in `assets/` that points outside the deck's folder, is left out and named with the reason, and photos past the size cap are named too.
- `--strip-notes` and `--strip-say` work on a `.lattice` output the way they do on `--reopenable`'s copy: the speaker notes and say lines are removed from the deck it carries, and its review comments stay out.
- `--reopenable` now carries the deck's photos by the same rule, up to 32 MB. It used to carry none, so a re-openable PDF made by the CLI opened in the Studio with every photo missing.
- The CLI now refuses an input that is neither Markdown nor a `.lattice` (a PDF, a picture) at once. It used to read the bytes as Markdown and fail after a 60-second timeout.

- **CLI `--reopenable`** puts the deck inside a `.pdf` or `.pptx` as a `.lattice` project, so whoever you send it to can open it in the Studio with Import deck… and edit it. It is the same payload the Studio's "Re-openable in Lattice" switch embeds: `lib/core/reopenable.js` now builds and places it for both tools, so a deck is re-openable whichever tool exported it. Comments never ride along. Hidden slides do, and so do speaker notes unless you add `--strip-notes`, which scrubs the embedded copy too. The installed theme and components the deck uses travel with it as package folders, and the payload's clock is pinned like every other PDF date, so an unchanged deck still re-renders to the same bytes.

- **`--reopenable` warns when `-p` themed the export but the deck re-opens in another
  theme.** The `.lattice` carries the deck as written, so a deck themed by `-p cuoio` with no
  `theme:` line re-opened in the default theme. The CLI now prints one warning naming both
  themes and the `theme:` line that makes the theme travel, and says nothing when the deck
  already names it. (`lattice-emulator.js`)

- A `code` plugin now renders every fenced block that no other plugin claims, on any slide. It loads highlight.js core plus only the grammars a deck's fences name (and the ones those embed, such as the JavaScript and CSS inside HTML), instead of the full 192-language build the engine used to load in every process. Every highlight.js language colors as the full build did, with one deliberate exception: an `http` block now looks for a JSON or XML body instead of guessing among all 192 languages, which fetched about 190 grammars in the Studio and colored a plain-text error body as EBNF. The `code` and `compare-code` slide classes now declare that they require it. A host that narrows the default plugins without it gets plain, uncolored code blocks.
- Fixed: `_focus: line N` and `_build` line stepping counted a multi-line comment or string as one line, so every later line was off by one, and they added an empty extra line at the end of each block. Line N is now source line N, matching what `lint:deck` counts.
- The Studio and Playground no longer bundle 36 highlight.js grammars up front. A deck fetches the grammars its fences name, plus the ones those embed, so an HTML fence still colors its `<script>` and `<style>`. A deck with no code fetches none. The Studio's ESM engine drops from 271 KB to 228 KB gzipped, and the classic Playground bundle from 498 KB to 454 KB.
- **Breaking:** the twelve `--hljs-*` theme tokens are renamed to role tokens: `--syntax-comment`, `--syntax-keyword`, `--syntax-builtin` (was `built_in`), `--syntax-number`, `--syntax-constant` (was `literal`), `--syntax-string`, `--syntax-entity` (was `title`), `--syntax-type`, `--syntax-variable`, `--syntax-parameter` (was `params`), `--syntax-markup` (was `tag`) and `--syntax-punctuation`. A theme that still sets `--hljs-*` falls back to the engine's default syntax colors, which can be unreadable on a light code panel, until it renames them; `lib/tokens/crosswalk.js` `flip()` does it mechanically, and the build rejects an old name in a theme file. The draft theme spec (`spec/THEME-1.0.md`) is amended to match.
- Every fenced code block now sits on the code panel, on any slide. Before, a fence on an ordinary content slide painted the panel's syntax colors straight onto the slide background, where the pale ones (functions, types, strings) were unreadable on a light theme. The panel also gains a faint inner edge (`--code-edge`), so it stays visible on dark themes whose slide background matches the panel. Escape sequences inside a string (`\n`, `\t`) now take the string's color instead of none.
- `diff` fences color added and removed lines with two new roles, `--syntax-inserted` and `--syntax-deleted`, on full-width tinted bands. Every theme declares its own pair, and the four accessibility themes use pairs that stay distinct under the condition each is built for.
- Configure a code block with a record on the line above it: `` `@code{title=src/load.ts, numbers, focus=4-5}` ``. The fields are `title=` (a file-name bar), `numbers` and `start=`, `focus=` and `mark=` (the `_focus: line` grammar, `3-5 9`), `diff` (each line's `+`/`-` marks it, and the rest is highlighted in the fence's own language), `wrap`, and `format`/`width=`/`dialect=` for the formatter. `code: numbers, wrap` in the front matter sets a deck-wide default. The record renders nothing; a plain caption span above a fence on a `code` or `compare-code` slide is still a caption. A slide's `_focus: line` and `_build: lines` work on a configured block too.
- `lint:deck` adds `code-record` (a record that does not read), `code-record-orphan` (a record with no fence after it) and `code-line-range` (a `focus=`, `mark=` or `_focus: line` past the end of its block, which silently marked nothing).
- `lattice fmt deck.md` pretty-prints a deck's code blocks in place, and **Format code blocks** in the Studio's command palette does the same as one undoable edit. Prettier formats JavaScript, TypeScript, JSON, CSS, SCSS, Less, HTML, Vue, Markdown, YAML and GraphQL, and with its plugins PHP, XML and Java; ruff formats Python; sql-formatter formats SQL (PostgreSQL unless a record says `dialect=`). A record's `format=off` keeps a block as written, `width=48` sets its line width, and `format` (or `code: format` for the deck) keeps a block formatted: the Studio formats it when you leave the editor. Formatting rewrites the source and the render never formats, so a formatter upgrade never changes a deck nobody re-formatted. Code a formatter cannot parse keeps its text and is reported. The formatters are optional dependencies, loaded per language; `lattice fmt --check` exits 1 when a block would change. `lint:deck` adds `code-format-unsupported` for a block that asks in a language no formatter reads.
- Export to Marp colors a shell command list the way Lattice does. marp-core's own bash grammar left `npm`, `docker`, `kubectl` and every flag uncolored. The bundle's `marp.config.cjs` now rebuilds bash on marp-core's highlight.js from Lattice's shell grammar. VS Code's Marp preview does not read that config, so it still shows stock bash.
- In Export to Marp, a fence on a plain slide now sits on the code panel too. Marp renders a fence as a bare `<pre>`, which the panel rule did not match.
- Export to Marp removes `@code{…}` record lines, which Marp would otherwise print as text above each block. Marp does not draw what a record asks for (line numbers, focus, marks, diff bands, a title, wrapping); the bundle's README lists it.
- Fixed: a receded code line (a block's `focus=`, or a slide's `_focus: line`) faded to about 1.5:1 against the code panel, and a receded comment to about 1.2:1, so the context lines read as blank. A receded line now drops to one quiet color held at 3:1 or better on every theme, and the build checks it.
- Copy buttons on a code block, off by default: `` `@code{copy}` `` on a block, or `code: copy` in the front matter for every block (`copy=off` opts one out). Two small buttons at the panel's top right copy the code as plain text, or as HTML with the theme's colors written inline, so it pastes colored into a document or an email. They appear only where someone reads the deck in a browser (the Studio preview, the Playground, the exported webpage) and never in a PDF, PowerPoint, image or video export, in Present, or in a slide thumbnail. A copied `diff` block is the source as written.
- The `code` and `compare-code` layouts follow the `cards:` register. A short block's panel now shrinks to its code and sits at the stage's middle instead of filling the slide with an empty panel; `cards: stretch` (or `_class: cards-stretch` on one slide) brings back the full-height panel, and `top` and `spread` work as on card layouts. The two panels of `compare-code` stay equal height.

- `npm run structure` reports the codebase's parts and layers: each part's size, coupling and cohesion, plus any loop between parts, any import that points up a layer, and any break in the plugin boundary. `build:check` now fails on all three (`tools/check-structure.js`). `lib/` and the docs site no longer form import loops. See `engineering/decisions/2026-10-11-codebase-structure.md`.
- The plugin boundary is the Hollywood contract: the host calls a plugin and hands it what it needs through `ctx`, and a plugin imports only its own folder, the workspace libraries and the plugins its manifest `requires`. The interim `lib/plugin-kit/` is gone. The host tools that still import a plugin's files are listed in its manifest's `hostApi` and held at 14 files by a ceiling that can only fall. See `engineering/decisions/2026-11-01-plugin-contract-hollywood.md` §9.
- The charts are one plugin with many kinds. The 28 chart components now live in `lib/plugins/chart-family/kinds/`, and the engine's chart frame (`lib/transformers/chart-frame.js`) runs the section walk, the title and caption frame, and the record bridging that every chart shares; a kind only draws. The kinds' remaining imports of engine code are listed one by one in `tools/structure.sanctioned.json`: a new one fails the build by name, and the list can only shrink. Every deck renders byte-identically to before. See `engineering/decisions/2026-11-01-charts-one-plugin.md` and `2026-11-02-slide-facts-for-kinds.md`.
- `npm run identity:check` renders every shipped deck (442 of them: examples, the baseline decks and every gallery) through this tree and through another commit (`--ref`, default `origin/main`), and compares the HTML, the CSS and the deck linter's findings. It exits 1 on any difference, so a refactor that must not move output can prove it.
- The tag stripper the engine and the Playground use to read plain text out of markup (`removeTags`, `@laticent/markup`) now runs in linear time on any input; a slide full of unclosed `<` could make the old pattern take quadratic time. Output is unchanged.

- **A generated code map: `dist/engineering/codemap.md`.** It answers "where does X live?" with
  one line per folder, code part (with its layer), plugin and workspace library. `npm run build`
  writes it (so `npm install` and every cloud session have it), and `build:check` fails a PR that
  adds a code part, or a folder directly inside the top level, `lib/`, `docs/`, `docs/src/`,
  `docs/src/lib/`, `test/`, `tools/` or `.claude/`, without a one-line purpose. It checks that
  the line exists, not that it is still true. The purposes come from `PARTS` in
  `tools/structure.js` (each part now carries an `about`), the plugin and library manifests, and
  a short `FOLDERS` table in `tools/build-codemap.js` for folders that hold no code.
  `lib/README.md`'s hand-written folder table, which listed 21 of the 29 folders, is replaced by a
  pointer to the map. New scripts: `npm run codemap:build`, `npm run codemap:check`.

- New `collage` component (imagery): four to six photos of any shape, packed edge to edge into one frame with no cropping. List the photos (`- ![Alt](photo.jpg)`) under an eyebrow, title, subtitle and one description paragraph; the layout reads each photo's size and finds the tightest arrangement. The packer picks the order by default, and `ordered` keeps the order you wrote. `fill` allows up to 8% crop to close empty space, `above` puts the text above the photos, `bleed` runs the photos across the whole slide with no header, footer or page number, under a translucent card that holds the title, subtitle and description, and `mirror` flips the text side. A trailing code span after a photo sets hints for that photo (`hero`, `top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right`, `center`, or a ratio like `3:2`). The page number is hidden on a collage. A collage never splits across slides. Hover focus is in the PDF-safe CSS. Click or tap a photo to enlarge it on the Playground, the Studio preview and the exported HTML player (Enter or Space on a focused photo works too; Escape, a click away or the close button closes it). The player carries the opener only when the deck has a collage, so every other export is byte-identical. The Present audience window does not enlarge in this release.
- `masonry` and `mood-board` join the component tag vocabulary so catalog search finds `collage`.
- Narration names each photo of a `collage` by its alt text, one sentence apiece, and the Present Guide's pointer lands on the photo as it is named. The article view lists every photo, not only the first.
- Four lint rules for the collage: `collage-count`, `collage-alt`, `collage-bg` and `collage-hint`.
- The description sits straight under the header as a plain paragraph. The header's own rule (the `rule:` register styles it) is the only line, with no second hairline above the description and no empty gap between them.

- **Added `dist/docs/components.pick.md` — the component PICK surface: one line per component,
  the whole 61-component catalog in ~3.8k tokens.** `AGENTS.md` draws the line itself —
  "`components.json` is for *picking*; each component's `.docs.md` is for *authoring inside* the
  one you picked" — but the file it pointed at carried the authoring detail too, so choosing a
  component meant a **95k-token** read of slots, skeletons, effective variants and anti-pattern
  prose for all 61. HARD RULE #6 makes that read mandatory before every `_class:` slide, which
  made it the most-repeated read in the repo. Each row carries what a pick actually needs: bucket,
  the three axes, search tags, the **effective `capacity`** as `axis:sweet/soft/hard` with its
  escalation target, the **neighbors** it is most often confused with (`see also`), and a
  one-line purpose cut at a sentence boundary so every row is a complete claim. One line per component also means `grep -i comparison`
  returns rows instead of a walk through a JSON document.
- **`components.json` is unchanged** — it stays the full machine record that the Studio's slide
  picker, deck export, the playground bundle and the LFM spec read, and it is still where
  `whenToUse` / `antiPatterns` / `slots` / `density` live. `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` now route
  *picking* to the pick list and say plainly not to load the full catalog to choose; the detail
  you need after choosing is in the component's own `.docs.md`, where HARD RULE #6 already sends
  you. The pick list is generated by the same `tools/build-docs-portal.js` pass, so it rides the
  existing `docs:portal:check` staleness gate rather than adding a new one.
- The pick list distinguishes two kinds of "wrong component": **`escalates to`** is where to go
  when your count blows the capacity budget, **`see also`** is where to go when the shape is
  wrong. The confusable clusters (`list` / `cards-stack` / `list-tabular`, `matrix-grid` /
  `matrix-2x2` / `roadmap`) are what a one-line catalog most needs to disambiguate.
- `design/skills/deck.md`, `design/design-system.md`, `README.md` and `examples/content-capacity.md`
  now route picking to the pick list too — `deck.md` is the from-blank deck walkthrough and the
  primary path, so leaving it pointed at the 95k JSON would have meant most sessions never
  learned the pick list existed.

- A component manifest can now say `"spectrum": false` (no spectrum: the slide gets `spectrum-off` and `spectrum-edge-off`, so the bar goes and structural accents flatten) or a style name (`"on"`, `"solid"`, `"duo"`, `"mono"`) to pin one. The engine and the browser runtime apply it identically and drop any spectrum class the author set on that component's slides. No shipped component uses it yet. `npm run check:edge-shift` fails if an opted-out component draws a bar or moves with the placement.

- **Fenced code is first-class in Compose.** A fence now renders as a mono panel
  with its language on a chip, instead of inheriting the inline-code chip style —
  which fragmented into one bordered box per line, so a `mermaid` block read as a
  stack of boxes. Click the chip (or the picker in the slide toolbar) to change the
  language; a new toolbar door inserts a fence, tagged from the slide's own layout
  (`diagram` → mermaid, `code` → js) so it is never bare. Typing ` ``` ` does the
  same.
- **Syntax highlighting in Compose comes from the engine's own highlighter**, so a
  fence's colors in the editor are its colors on the slide — Lattice's own mermaid and
  augmented-shell grammars included. An engine sub-language is colored through the body
  grammar it declares: `mermaid` by our mermaid grammar, `anima` and `functionplot` as
  the JSON they are.
- **The language picker offers every grammar the renderer carries** — all 192, the
  three Lattice fence languages first, then the ones this deck already uses — and
  coaches rather than refuses: it names the `shell`-versus-`bash` mix-up that
  silently kills highlighting, and says when a tag has no grammar at all.
- **Fixed: `Tab` inside a fence moved focus out of the editor.** It now indents (and
  `Shift-Tab` outdents). `Enter` on a blank last line leaves the fence, which is the
  only exit reachable from a phone — previously it was `Mod-Enter` or nothing.
- **Fixed: the language picker ran off the edge of a phone screen**, and its search
  field's focus ring was clipped by the panel. It now wears the same
  `useKeyboardInset` + Radix available-height + shared search-box shape as the command
  palette and the component picker, so it caps against the space a software keyboard
  leaves instead of a flat height.

- **Compose names each slide's layout and changes it from the slide bar.** The pill's first button is the slide's component (`cards-grid ▾`), and every other slide shows the same button quietly on its line, so the column of slides reads as a list of layouts. The menu shows a live preview of the slide, its looks, and the layouts its manifest names as alternatives with when to use each. Picks apply at once and keep the slide's other classes (`scale-l`, a tint, a deck's own class); closing keeps them and offers one Undo. A layout that cannot read the slide's text says so and asks before replacing it.
- **Changed:** Undo and Redo moved from each slide's pill in Compose to the editor's edit bar, beside Compose / Source, Reshape and Fix all (on a phone they stay in the header). They act on the whole deck. The pill now holds the slide's layout, Add, Insert and Settings, then the styles of the block under the caret; on a narrow pane the styles take a second row.
- **Find and replace** in the editor's edit bar, for Compose and Source: counts matches, steps through them, replaces one or all (one undo step), with match case. ⌘F opens it on the selected text; on a phone it is in the drawer. In Compose, a slide that can only be edited in Source is left out.
- **Changed:** the edit bar never runs past the editor pane. As the pane narrows, Version history and Slide settings, then Reshape and Fix all, move into a new More (⋯) menu before the Compose and Source words drop to icons; Undo and Redo always stay.
- **Fixed:** changing a slide's layout, or placing a picture on it, no longer drops other settings that share the `_class` comment (`<!-- _class: stats⏎_paginate: false -->` lost `_paginate`). Compose now leaves such a slide's class to Source and says so.
- **Fixed:** choosing a look in Compose's layout menu or in Slide settings' Reshape now replaces any look it cannot combine with, instead of writing both (`cards-grid three four`, `pricing two four`, `flowchart lr tb`). Every component's manifest now says which of its looks are alternatives (`variantAxes`), 36 of them for the first time; looks that combine still combine.

- Compose edits links by pointing. Select words and press **Link** in the selection bar, or choose **Insert → Link**, to give them a web or email address. Click a link to see its address, change it, open it in a new tab, or remove it. Compose refuses an address a slide cannot carry, such as a `javascript:` or `data:` address, and says why. It writes an address the way the engine reads it back, and adds the scheme an author leaves off: `https://` for `example.com`, `mailto:` for `ada@example.com`, `http://` for `localhost:3000`.
- A click on a checklist item's state chip now opens all six answers (Yes, Partly, No, Unknown, Open, Does not apply). It used to switch only between done and open, and one click on a `[!]`, `[?]`, `[-]` or `[/]` item silently turned it into `[x]`.
- The Insert menu adds **Check** (`@check{pass}`, with a selected word as its label) and each inline kind an installed plugin declares with a slot, started from that slot. Compose could already edit both, but adding one meant typing it.

- Compose draws a pill as the slide draws it, in the deck theme's own colors, as one object with no `{SHIPPED, c2}` text and no caret inside it. Tap or click it to change its label, shape, color and size from one editor (a popover on desktop and tablet, a sheet on the phone), so authors no longer type the grammar. Each pick rewrites only the word that was changed (a pill written `{BETA, c4, tag}` keeps its order and spelling, and every other pill is untouched), and opening a deck never rewrites it. Two pills never touch (a space is kept between them), because two code spans that touch are one span in Markdown. "Done" puts the cursor after the pill; "Edit as text" turns it back into text, and it is drawn again when the cursor leaves. The "+ Pill" button on the slide bar inserts a new pill and opens its editor. A pill stays as text on a slide edited in Markdown, and nothing is drawn in a deck set to `inline-code: literal`.
- The slide bar has Undo and Redo buttons for the whole deck, because a phone has no undo gesture that sees Compose's history. On a narrow pane the bar wraps to two rows (history and the insert doors, then the Format group) instead of covering the slide's end caps.
- `editPill` in `lib/core/inline-pills.js` is the matching writer: it changes one word of a pill using Segno's own item offsets, keeps the author's casing and order for every word it does not touch, and returns null (writes nothing) unless the pill reads back as the old fields plus the requested change. A property test runs it over every readable pill in the shipped decks and galleries.

- **Compose edits avatars and icons by pointing.** A tap on an avatar opens a panel for its name, tile color, size, shape, frame and every trait of the face, with "From name" on each trait saying what the name picked. A tap on an icon opens a panel for the icon (the same searchable grid the pill uses), color, size, frame, look, corners and the name a screen reader says. Each pick rewrites only the word that changed.
- **Compose draws images and lets you choose one from the Library.** A Library photo shows as the picture, not a broken image, and a background says which side it takes. An Image door opens a photo picker with thumbnails and search, and a tap on an image opens a panel for the photo, its description and a background's placement. Compose fetches nothing for a web image; the slide preview draws it.
- **One Insert menu replaces the four insert buttons** (table, code, pill, spark) in the slide bar, so it fits a phone. It holds Table, Code, Diagram, Equation, Plot, Image, Pill, Spark, Avatar and Icon, and says why an item is unavailable (a locked slide, a layout a table does not suit, the cursor in a code block) instead of hiding it. Diagram, Equation and Plot write a fence with a body that works at once.
- **A schema-driven record writer** (`lib/core/segno-edit.js`) changes one word of any inline record from its slot spec and refuses a write that does not read back as asked. Avatars and icons use it; a plugin that declares a slot spec can reuse it.

- Compose: Shift+Enter writes one new line inside the paragraph, saved as a plain newline (a line break on the slide); Enter still starts the next paragraph. In a heading or a table cell the key does nothing, and in a code fence it adds a newline.

- Compose draws a spark (`~{12 14 17, bar, c3}`) as the slide draws it and opens an editor on a tap: a grid of number boxes for a trend (or a value and a total for a ratio), the chart type, color, size, and the marks a line can carry (end dot, low and high, zero line, full width). The type chips offer only what the data takes (a trend takes line, area, bars, steps and win/loss; a ratio takes ring and bullet), and changing to a chart that draws no line clears the marks it cannot carry in the same write. Each change rewrites only the word it changed, so `~{12 14 17, bar, c3}` keeps its order and spelling, and an edit the engine would refuse writes nothing and says why. The "Insert spark" button on the slide bar adds a small rising line after the caret's word and opens its editor.
- `editSpark` in `lib/plugins/sparks/sparks.inline.js` is the matching writer, and `read` returns the spark's fields and the numbers as the author wrote them. A property test runs the writer over every readable spark in the shipped decks and galleries, and an edit lands only when the engine's own reader still reads the result as a spark.
- The pill editor takes an icon (`{DONE, icon=api}`): pick one from the icon grid, change it, or take it off. It also warns when a circle or diamond has a label too long for it, using the same check as the linter's `pill-shape-crowded`.
- On a phone, the active slide's bar (Undo, Redo, the insert buttons and Format) stays pinned fully on screen while a long slide scrolls under it, instead of riding half above the top edge with its buttons clipped. "Add a point" in the spark editor focuses the new number box with its value selected, so the next keystroke replaces it.

- **Added: agent sessions get a warning before a catch-up with `main` they do not
  need.** A new Claude Code PreToolUse hook (`warn-needless-catchup.sh`) fires before
  a `git rebase`, `merge` or `pull` of `main`. When the branch merges cleanly with
  `main` on GitHub's terms, it says the catch-up is not needed (HARD RULE #16) and
  re-runs CI for nothing. It never blocks. In the week to 2026-10-06, 7 of 26 agent
  catch-ups were clean, and 5 of them gave no reason.
- **Changed: the pre-push hook stops at its first failing job** (`piped: true`), so a
  failing push no longer pays for every later job.

- `contact` takes separate typed phone lines (`mobile`/`cell`, `office`/`work`, `phone`/`tel`/`voice`), each its own `TEL;TYPE=` entry in the vCard. The ledger now lists every field in the order you wrote it.
- `contact` takes a `qr` key: `vcard` (default), `tel` (a code that dials the first phone line) or `url`. A lean code is 27 to 35 modules wide against 55 to 67 for a full vCard, so it scans from further away; use it for a hall.
- `venueProbe` manifest field: the longest realistic content a component promises to hold at every venue. `npm run check:venue-conformance` renders it, with each component's sample, at four venues and four canvas families and reports clipping, off-frame content and a QR code below the venue's floor.

- **Cover compositions.** The `cover:` register takes a second word that sets how the heading block sits on the front and back cover: `masthead` (a heavy rule over the title), `ledger` (small capitals over a double rule), `column` (an accent column at the right edge, clear of the header and footer), `label` (a gallery wall label, low on the left), `stage` (a stage-size centered title), `frame` (the title in a keyline) and `poster` (a giant title set left). Write it with or without a surface, in either order (`cover: light column`). Each is also a `title` and `closing` variant (`_class: title cover-poster`), and `cover-plain` keeps one slide centered. Every composition reads on both surfaces in both color modes. `plain`, the default, stamps nothing, so existing decks render as before. A `stage` or `poster` heading holds about 60 characters; a longer one grows down rather than into the top band, so an overlong one overflows where the export reports it. See `lib/base/base.registers.docs.md` § cover and `examples/cover-compositions.md`.
- **`closing qr` and `divider qr` follow `headline:` for the eyebrow too.** On the wide QR layout the eyebrow stayed centered while a left-set heading (`headline: left`, or a left cover composition) moved left; the heading column now follows the same alignment. Unset, it stays centered.

- **`cover:` front-matter register.** `cover: light` paints the title and closing slides on the deck's own light canvas, with the heading, subtitle, eyebrow, chrome and logo inks a content slide uses, in both color modes. `cover: inverse` (the default) keeps the dark panel and stamps nothing, so existing decks render as before. A slide opts out with `_class: … cover-inverse`. Dividers and `topic` keep their own surfaces, and `title light` keeps its meaning (a scheme, not a surface). The HTML player export learns the new `cover-light` class, so a light cover stays light when the viewer toggles dark; the player's dark-mode CSS text changes for every export, while what renders changes only on a `cover-light` slide. See `lib/base/base.registers.docs.md` § cover and `examples/cover-light.md`.

- **Craft: a docs track for authoring themes, components and finishes.** Twenty-five
  pages under `/craft/`, three tracks read in order — what a theme, a component and a
  finish each is, what each file controls, how to build one from scratch, and the
  checklist that says it is done. Written for someone who has not written CSS before.
- **A live lab on nearly every Craft page.** Twenty-two labs across nineteen pages,
  each a real slide above a real editor: edit the theme CSS, the component CSS or the
  finish CSS and the slide repaints as you type, with a light/dark toggle and a
  reset. Runs the shipped engine through the existing single-slide renderer, so it
  inherits the same sanitizers and palette tracking as the Playground and the
  component specimens.
- **Worked examples, troubleshooting and a glossary.** Each track's finished artifact
  shown whole; the failures that actually happen, sorted by what you are looking at;
  and every term the track uses, including the three that collide.
- **Every CSS example audited against the prose it illustrates.** The syntax-highlighting
  section now shows the twelve `--hljs-*` tokens it names, at values measured to clear
  4.5:1 on the code panel; the ink ramp teaches seven tokens rather than six (`--text-label`
  was missing); the two example manifests now pass `validate()` — they carried invented
  search tags and, in one case, a `capacity` with no `stressDoc`; the finish pages
  distinguish `--fin-mark` from `--fin-mark-text` and scope the 5–16% accent band to
  layers that cover the whole page, which two shipped presets deliberately exceed in a
  narrow one.
- **The diagram lab shows the categorical cycle it teaches.** The `--cat-*` family is
  the one group with **no engine default** — omit it and the tokens resolve to nothing,
  so every node in a flowchart draws in `--surface-inverse` with body ink on top. The
  themes track said omitted tokens "fall back to the engine's defaults" as a general
  rule; that is true of every other group and false of this one. The seed now carries
  four verified slot pairs, and the track names the exception where it matters.
- **Craft labs serve Mermaid from our own origin**, the copy the Playground and Studio
  already use, instead of falling back to the jsdelivr CDN.
- **A third review pass over the track's claims, run before merge.** Seven refutations,
  two of them things a reader would have shipped. The component scaffold seed did not
  match what `npm run new:component` writes — it is now byte-identical to the
  generator's template, and the capstone lab opens on the real thing, whose selector
  the reader's first move corrects. The finish worked example declared
  `--fin-frame: none`; that slot composes into a box-shadow list where `none` is legal
  only as the sole value, so the declaration went invalid and took the tone rail with
  it (measured live: the rail resolves with `0 0 transparent` and vanishes with
  `none`). Also corrected: the specificity gap is lab-versus-engine, not
  component-versus-engine; nothing gates an empty `whenToUse`; `ledger`'s mark is
  ~14px, not a hairline; `color-mode:` has five values and one of them is `print`;
  and nineteen of twenty-five pages carry a lab, not twenty-two.
- **The specificity remedy the track taught did not work.** Repeating a component's
  class buys back one class, but the `article.lattice >` prefix the engine adds is a
  class *and* an element name — so against a base rule that names a class of its own
  (`section.form > .cell-stage`, the first one an author meets) the doubled selector
  still loses. Measured in the built lab: plain 8px, doubled 8px, tripled 42px. Both
  pages that gave the advice now say what doubling buys and when it is not enough.
- **Following the tracks end to end, rather than reading them.** Running
  `npm run new:theme` and `npm run new:component` and doing what the pages say turned
  up what no reading pass could: the theme scaffold writes four files (the track showed
  three), leaves `build:check` red until `npm run build`, stamps a `#FF00FF` placeholder
  swatch nothing reminds you to replace, and leaves the palette suite red until
  `bless-palette-baselines` has frozen the new palette's measurements — while the
  component scaffold makes `npm test` fail *by design*, which the checklist listed as a
  green checkbox. All now documented where the reader meets them.
- **The scaffold seed is gated, not trusted.** `test/unit/tools/craft-scaffold-seed.test.js`
  renders the generator's own template and compares it byte for byte with the lab's
  seed — the one place the track claims a match with a command the reader just ran.
- **Executing the finishes track too.** Building the worked-example finish for real,
  by following the page, found the same shape of gap as the other two tracks: step 5
  named four fields for the Studio catalog entry where the type requires seven
  (`nature` and `zone` fail the TypeScript build), and it named one of the three
  places a new finish name has to be registered. The other two — the reserved-name
  list that stops a saved user finish shadowing a shipped preset, and the finish count
  the ownership guard reads out of `design/skills/finish.md` — each have a gate that
  fails until you write them. The checklist listed four files to touch; there are six.

- **`npm run score:variance`** decomposes which scorecard categories actually move a deck's
  Craft and Style grades. It prints each category's share of the summed per-category
  variance, attributes that variance to the rules feeding it by **ablation** (drop a rule's
  findings, re-score, see which category moves — so the tool never restates the scorer's own
  mapping and cannot drift from it), and prints a **perturbation ledger** saying what the
  draft models it compares against are really doing to each category's input. `--json` ·
  `--committed` · `--weighted` · `--depths=` · `--reach`. Findings are counted by identity
  rather than netted per deck, so a swap cannot hide inside a zero.
- The Craft-half variance figures published on 2026-08-25 measured the instrument rather
  than the weights, and the corrected reading now ships with them. Those figures ranked the
  three Craft categories over prefix-truncated decks as a draft proxy, but truncation models
  an *unfinished* deck rather than a badly-written one: across all 202 scorable decks it
  creates 166 `contract` findings and destroys none, while creating **zero** `craftProse`
  findings by line and four by character — all four being one-word fragments left where the
  cut landed inside a heading. The band's endpoints were an unstated parameter besides: cut
  depth alone moves `contract`'s share from 10.3% to 71.2%. So `craftProse` is not "the next
  weight to be suspicious of" — it is the one nothing has yet measured.
- **No grade changes.** No weight, rule, or threshold moved; `craftProse` is left un-priced
  and now labeled as such. Widening `label-title` — which the measurement invites, since it
  accepts 8 of the 1,575 headings it is offered, and only through its single-bare-word branch — would push a
  genre opinion into the profile-blind half of the grade, which is what the Craft/Style
  split exists to prevent. It stays a proposal.

- **A ❓ decision card now carries every open item, question and decision.**
  Sessions used to bury a decision inside a status list, so the owner had to ask
  "what are the remaining open items?" to find it. The card lists only the
  choices that are the owner's, in plain words: each has options with what they
  buy, cost and trigger, a recommendation, and what happens if nobody answers.
  It is posted automatically when a session stops with anything open, or on
  request, on the PR and in chat with the same wording. Unanswered items are
  carried into the continuation brief and `followups.d/`.
  (`engineering/workflow.md` §❓ Decision card)
- **The four agent cards (🚦 pre-merge, 📋 standup, 🎯 continuation, ❓ decision)
  now share one phone-width layout, and `npm run card` builds them.** Each opens
  with a BOTTOM LINE (the ask, the pick, the state), then CAPS sections where each
  field is a label line with its value below it, at most 38 columns because the
  chat app shows about 38 characters of a code block. An agent writes the facts as
  a small YAML file, and `npm run card -- card.yml` validates it against a schema,
  wraps it, puts the CAPS on the critical values and prints the fenced card, so the
  layout is correct by construction. It refuses a card with a value that runs past
  two lines, template text left in, a `raise it` of "nothing outstanding" beside an
  unrun check, or a `#N` that YAML would read as a comment. The 🚦 card gains a
  `pick` line (merge or hold, with the one reason) and a `read by` line. The 🎯
  brief keeps its STANDING ORDERS block inline so a cold session needs no lookup.
  (`engineering/workflow.md` §One layout for all four cards, `tools/card.js`,
  `engineering/card-examples/`)

- **Deck presets.** A new `preset:` front-matter key picks a named look — `classic` (the default), `editorial`, `brand` or `minimal` — that sets the backdrop, heading alignment, brand bar, card rails, trim, heading rule, eyebrow, card lift and corners at once, so each preset looks different on every slide, the title slide included. The Studio previews all four live on a sample slide, in your deck's theme and color mode. Any of those keys you write still wins over the preset. The linter flags an unknown name (`unknown-preset`).
- **Basic and Advanced settings in the Studio.** The deck and slide settings panels open on a short Basic list: theme, preset, color mode, size, page numbers and logo for the deck; canvas, type scale, clean slide and the speaker note for a slide. Advanced shows every setting. Search always covers every setting. The deck panel shows how many settings differ from the preset and offers a Reset.
- The "More look settings", "More accent settings" and "Developer" drawers are gone; their rows now sit under plain headings in Advanced.

- **Studio: Lite mode looks lighter.** On a device the Studio reads as Lite (a software-rendered browser, 4 GB or less, 4 cores or less, or a slow speed test), the slide preview's loading screen is the landing page's single pulsing placeholder instead of the three-layer Nacre animation, no panel or bar uses a backdrop blur (the site header and chart pop-ups turn opaque), and a picture still loading in a live slide shows a still painting rather than moving brushwork. Full mode is unchanged, and exports are byte-for-byte the same in both modes. `?tier=lite` and `?tier=full` pin either mode for a page load.
- **Studio: Lite mode uses less memory.** A Lite device runs exports with one picture encoder and one slide in flight, packs narration with one worker, keeps 6 to 12 live slide previews instead of 10 to 28, prefetches no panels or fonts on a guess, and does not offer the downloaded on-device models (Kokoro voice, WebLLM and Transformers.js chat; they show why they are off). Exports are the same files in both modes, only slower on Lite.
