- **Studio: the device check ranks the graphics chip and watches start-up.** The Studio now ranks the graphics chip with detect-gpu, using tables served by Lattice itself (never a CDN), and notices when it fell behind while starting up. Either can switch a session to Lite mode, with a short notice saying why. The System panel shows the GPU rank (or why there is none, such as a chip newer than detect-gpu's tables, Save-Data or a Mac's masked GPU name) and the start-up result.
- **Studio and Playground: a browser Lattice can't run gets told so.** Instead of a broken page, it gets a full-page notice naming what is missing (for example CSS `:has()`) and what to use instead, with "Copy system report" and a small "Continue anyway" that runs the rest of the session in Lite mode under a one-line banner. Workspace settings has a new Performance mode setting: Auto, Full or Lite.

- A `font-embedding:` front-matter line and `--font-embedding` flag choose how much of each typeface an export carries: `exact` (only the characters shown), `used` (the whole face we ship, so edited text keeps every glyph; the default for text), `full`, or `system` (embed nothing). A word ending in `-emoji` sets the Noto Color Emoji font (default `exact`): `font-embedding: used exact-emoji`. The player, PDF and editable PowerPoint and LibreOffice files read it from one shared kernel (`lib/core/font-policy.js`). `unknown-font-embedding` warns on a word it does not know.
- The Studio offered this setting as `fonts:` from 5 November; it is now `font-embedding:`, because `fonts:` read as choosing fonts. The exports ignore a `fonts:` line, and `lint:deck` flags one (`fonts-renamed`) with a fix that renames the key and keeps the words. When the deck also has a `font-embedding:` line that names no tier, the fix stays off, so it never deletes an author's words. The command line's `--fonts` flag is `--font-embedding` too, and the old flag stops with a message naming the new one.
- The exported player now keeps the text faces whole by default (`used`) instead of cutting them to the shown characters, about 130 KB more on a small deck; `font-embedding: exact` restores the old size.
- `font-embedding: exact-emoji` (the default) cuts the player's emoji font to the emoji the deck uses, about 2 KB each instead of a 60 to 700 KB slice. It runs through a color build of HarfBuzz's subsetter (`lib/fonts/hb/hb-subset-color.wasm`), because the stock one drops the color tables and leaves emoji blank. A deck with five emoji went from a 3.1 MB player to 1.06 MB.
- `font-embedding: system` now keeps the engine's faces out of a Studio PDF too. The PDF writer both hosts run skips them, so words set in those faces stay in the page picture. Before, only the CLI honored it.
- The published `lattice` command now cuts the emoji font too (the color wasm is found through the package's `lib/`), and so do `--read` and `--fluid` pages; a character written as an entity (`&#x1F389;`) keeps its glyph, and an emoji in the `title:` gets its slice. The Studio's slide camera no longer inlines every emoji slice into every slide.
- The Studio's Pictures, Resolution and Fonts choices in the Share panel share one dropdown: each row has a title and a one-line explanation, the closed control stays one row tall, and the follow-the-deck row reads `Auto — <what it lands on>` like the other pickers.
- The plain `.html`, `--read` and `--fluid` exports now cut the KaTeX math faces to the glyphs the page uses, as the player already did. Text drawn only at view time falls back to another font.
- `font-embedding: system-emoji` now applies to PDFs, PowerPoint, LibreOffice and image exports as well as web pages: the picture draws its emoji with the computer that makes it (a machine with no emoji font draws boxes), in the command line and the Studio alike. `exact-emoji`, `used-emoji` and `full-emoji` still draw Noto Color Emoji in a picture, because no emoji font file rides in a PDF.
- Editable PowerPoint and LibreOffice exports take the `font-embedding:` text tiers and the `images:` choice: `exact` embeds just the characters the deck draws in each face (capitals from `text-transform` included), `used` and `full` the whole face, `system` none; `images: original` keeps every picture in the file lossless, and the quality now applies to cropped pictures too (default 90, was a fixed 92 for crops). The rules live in one place, `lib/core/office-export-policy.js`, and Calco (the Office writer) is handed finished fonts and plain instructions instead of holding any policy. Emoji are not embedded in these files: Noto Color Emoji is COLR v1, which LibreOffice draws blank, so the reader's own emoji font draws them.

- **Markdown, Marp and re-openable PDF/PowerPoint exports now carry the Library photos a deck names.** A Markdown export of a deck with photos downloads as a `.zip` (the `.md` beside `photos/<name>.<ext>`, references rewritten to those paths); a deck with none is still a bare `.md`. The Marp bundle puts the photos in a `photos/` folder. The `.lattice` inside a re-openable PDF or PowerPoint carries them too, up to 32 MB of photos (smaller than the standalone `.lattice`'s 128 MB so the file stays under the size the importer opens), and the importer reads that larger embedded file. Photos over the cap or missing from the Library are named in the toast.

- **Filo has a page on the docs site.** `/libraries/filo/` runs the real undo history in your
  browser: four writers (an editor, a settings panel, a section list with an AI rewrite, and a lint
  fix) change one document, ⌘Z anywhere on the page undoes the last change whoever made it, and the
  history is drawn as a thread with its saved versions and byte counts. Eight storyboard beats walk
  the guarantees. `/libraries/filo/learn/` explains the model, the calls and the measurements, and
  `/filo` redirects to the demo. Filo gets its own mark (a clew) and a crimson-and-leaf-green palette, measured apart from every sibling.
- **`History.steps()`** lists a history's steps for a panel: the done steps oldest first, then the
  redo branch in replay order, each with its label, origin, patch size and time.
- **`@laticent/filo` is a workspace package** like its siblings: `npm run filo-lib:build` writes
  `dist/` (ESM, CJS and type declarations), and `npm run build` runs it. Publishing to npm waits
  until the Studio's use of it has settled.
- **Tables on every library and plugin Learn page read as tables.** A Markdown table now sits in a
  bordered frame with a header band and column rules, like the page's own tables, fills the column,
  and scrolls sideways on its own on a phone.
- **Filo's demo has "Eight things to try"**, laid out like Suono's and Cadenza's: numbered cards
  under the stage, each naming the call it shows, and a "Play all eight" button that plays them in
  order and stops on a second press.

- **Undo survives a reload in the Studio.** Reopen the Studio and ⌘Z undoes the edit you made
  before it. If the Studio saved text the history had not stored yet, it comes back as one step,
  "Unsaved changes"; if the deck changed outside the Studio (a restored backup, an import), that
  change is one step of its own, and the older steps apply only after it. If you edit the deck in
  the moment before the stored history loads, that session keeps its undo in memory and the stored
  history waits, untouched, for the next load. A second tab on the same
  deck keeps its undo in memory and says so, and Clear all and deleting a deck remove the history
  too. The history is stored in IndexedDB, capped at 50 MB across decks; the heavy work (shrinking
  a broad change to the lines that changed, checking a stored history) runs in a worker.
- **Undo and Redo buttons on a touch tablet.** An iPad with no keyboard now shows Undo and Redo in
  the Studio's top bar, as a phone does. After a reload, Safari offers its own undo (shake, the
  keyboard bar's undo key) only once the page has an undo list of its own, so before this an iPad
  had no way to reach the history that survived the reload.
- **One undo on a Mac takes back one step.** Safari on macOS answers one undo command with two
  undo requests, and the Studio used to run both; now it runs one and only refuses the other.
  Measured through Safari's undo command; a real Edit-menu click has not been tested.

- **A narrated first-run tour in the Studio.** A first-time visitor on the production site gets a start card ("best with sound on", with a Test button that plays left, then right), then a two-minute spoken walk through the editor, preview, slide strip, Add, Reshape, Compose, Fix all, themes, light/dark, the Read·Write·Craft control, search, Present and Share, ending on a choice to open the lessons. The voice is Gemini `Schedar` and leans toward whatever the cursor points at. It is also in the Show me menu ("Welcome tour"), and `/studio/?welcome=1` forces the card.
- **Lessons lean too.** The recorded lesson voice now pans gently toward the control it points at.

- **🛰️ Fleet board.** `npm run card` now builds a `fleet` card: one screen showing every live session, loudest first (🔴 needs you, 🟠 at risk, 🟢 moving, 🔵 review-ready, ✅ done). Each card has clickable Pull Request | Session | Build links under it and numbered actions that wait for the owner's `go`. Ask a command-center session for a board, or run `/fleet`. Contract: `engineering/workflow.md` §🛰️ Fleet board. `npm run card -- --table` prints the same board as one markdown table: status, session (linked), PR, CI run and state.
- **Desks.** Seven skills turn a session into a long-lived desk that owns one kind of problem: `/desk-flaky` (one owner per red or flaky test), `/desk-merge` (the batched merge round and merge order), `/desk-stale` (PRs idle 3+ days) `/desk-deps-nightly` (Dependabot PRs and nightly reds), `/desk-backlog` (issues and follow-ups as one ranked queue) `/desk-security` (every security finding, never dismissed) and `/desk-optimize` (measured wins in engine speed and size, CI time, agent spend and code quality). The fleet board's overview can carry a `spend` line. A desk acts inside its own lane with a fixed list of verbs, never merges, runs only when asked, and spends about 10 new sessions or agents per lane a day. Another session's message is a request, never authorization: it cannot approve a merge or make a session drop its work. A merge approval covers the commit it was given on. `/fleet desk <lane>` starts one. Contract: `engineering/workflow.md` §Desks.
- **A merge needs the owner's typed word, checked by a machine.** A new `PreToolUse` hook (`.claude/hooks/owner-merge-gate.mjs`) blocks the GitHub merge and auto-merge tools unless the owner's own latest message in that session is exactly `merge #N`, or exactly `all` / `all but #N` answering a message whose first line is `🚦 Merge digest` and which lists the PR. It reads the transcript's harness-written `origin`, so a relayed session message, a desk brief or a subagent report can never authorize a merge, and a refusal such as "do not merge #N" never parses as one. Sessions merge only through those tools; the gate does not read Bash, so a Bash merge is a rule breach no machine catches.

- In the `--fluid` viewer, fourteen more chart kinds now redraw for the box they have on screen, as the bar chart already did: line, slope, ep-curve, tower, stacked-bar, waterfall, bullet, heatmap, funnel, piechart, map, hub-spoke, roadmap and journey. On a phone most of them print their labels at the slide's type size (10 to 21px where they were 6 to 10px; a funnel takes its tall shape but keeps its 9px labels), a roadmap turns into its stacked cards, and every chart gets its exported drawing back when the box returns. The data is read back from attributes on each chart's own marks and checked against the exported drawing before it is used, and a chart the viewer cannot read back exactly keeps its exported drawing.
- In the `--fluid` viewer, radar, map, quadrant, word-cloud, pie and hub-spoke charts drew 0px tall at every width, so they did not show at all. They now fill the rest of the slide, as on a paged slide.
- A chart redrawn for a phone prints every label the export printed: no value is dropped and no name is shortened to fit. A chart that cannot fit them all keeps its exported drawing.
- On a phone in the `--fluid` viewer, a tower prints each layer's name and size above its band instead of in a side column, so the bars take the full width, and its key wraps in centered rows at the chart's label size.
- On a phone in the `--fluid` viewer, a roadmap's phase cards are calmer: one line per item with the workstream name beside it, no rule beside each item, and a phase date the size of the phase title.
- A journey on a phone in the `--fluid` viewer shows its whole board as stages stacked down the screen, one compact row per task; it used to show the wide board squeezed to tiny labels.
- Quadrant, risk-matrix, scatter, histogram, radar, gantt and word-cloud charts redraw for a phone too: each now records its values on its marks as new attributes (the drawing is unchanged), and on a phone a quadrant draws a narrower plane so its labels print at the slide's size.
- On a phone in the `--fluid` viewer a risk matrix puts its key under the grid, so the grid takes the full width, and a word cloud's size key prints at the slide's label size.
- A `--fluid` export no longer flashes the exported chart before its redraw: on a phone or tablet the charts are held until their first redraw (they show as exported without script), and on a desktop the first drawing is already the right one.
- Every chart kind records its source (series names, axis lines, layers, bands, groups and the like, as written) as attributes on its marks, so the `--fluid` viewer reads a chart back from its marks alone; the drawing is unchanged.
- In the `--fluid` viewer chart labels follow the slide's text size at every width, instead of the chart's width alone (at 1024 x 768 they printed nearly as large as the slide's heading).
- On a portrait page (portrait, story, mobile), a chart's key sits under the chart in one, two or three aligned columns, whichever leaves the chart largest on that page's shape, so the chart takes the full width instead of shrinking to make room for a tall key. Pie, tower, stacked-bar, bar, line, map, quadrant, radar and heatmap keys all use it (a chart in a half-slide pane keeps its single-column key), a risk matrix puts its key under the grid there too, and a tower's key prints at the size of its own layer labels.
- On a tall page (story, mobile), line, bar, stacked-bar, waterfall, heatmap, histogram, scatter, slope, bullet, ep-curve, tower and quadrant charts draw their plot taller, to the shape of the space under the title, instead of a fixed shape that left up to half of it empty; their text stays the same size or grows (a quadrant's from 24px to 28px). A 4:5 portrait, square and landscape slide draw as before. A slide with an eyebrow, a source line, a title longer than one line or a `venue:` keeps the fixed shape, because its taller header leaves a shorter box and a taller plot would print smaller. So does a chart whose key or notes under the plot would make it taller than its box.

- In the `--fluid` viewer, a bar chart now redraws for the box it has on screen: on a phone it is drawn for the tall, narrow box at the slide's type size (labels about 16px where they were 7px), and it gets its exported drawing back when the box returns. The chart's data is read back from its own marks, so the export carries nothing extra. Other chart kinds keep their exported drawing for now.

- **Added: `@laticent/fluido`, the library that decides how a slide fits its box.** Every surface that splits a slide (the command-line export, the Playground and the Studio) now asks one pure, dependency-free core which slides divide, on which seam, and how many pages each becomes, including the budget cut that breaks one long code block into runs. No deck's output changes: 402 decks at three sizes split byte for byte as before. A slide whose split would produce more than 64 pages, by any route (a plain cut, a component's own recipe, or a long code block cut into runs), now stays one page and is marked instead; the longest run in any shipped deck is 41 pages. Fluido has a page on the Libraries site with a live demo.

- `_focusStyle: highlight` shows the `_focus:` target with an accent tint and an edge, the `preferred` look of `verdict-grid` without the spark, and leaves every other target untouched. It works on every axis `_focus:` addresses: `item`, `row`, `col`, `cell` and `line` take the tint and edge, a `mark` takes an edge, a `series` a heavier line, and `_focusSteps` and the lint and editor completions accept it. Demos: `examples/focus-styles.md` and `examples/focus-highlight-axes.md`.

- **Added: `followups.d/`, a ledger of pending work that has no issue.** A continuation
  brief used to leave an unticketed item only in a PR comment and a chat transcript. Now
  each item gets one file in `followups.d/`, and the PR that finishes it deletes the file.
  `npm run followups` lists them, and `checkFollowups` in `build:check` rejects a malformed
  item. 79 items from the last two months of briefs are backfilled verbatim and marked
  `backfill: true`. They have not been re-checked against `main`.

- `venue:` front matter names where a deck will be seen: `laptop` (the default), `huddle` (4–6 people), `conference` (10–30) or `hall` (50–2,000). Lattice derives the type size from it (1x / 1.15x / 1.3x / 1.5x), lifts labels, captions, the header and page numbers a little more than body text at `conference` and `hall`, and `lint:deck` warns when a slide is over its budget for the room. `engineering/typography.md` §7 "Venue" has the viewing-distance math behind the four bands.

- **A Frame now declares which stage kinds it can host.** `admits` (`flow` · `canvas` · `sovereign`) is the frame side of the `accepts`/`fits` containment contract in `design/forms.md` §7. The component side has shipped since 2026-07-14 as each manifest's `stage` field; the frame side did not exist, so a Frame could not state what it accepts and admissibility lived only in the render. A sovereign Frame admits exactly `["sovereign"]` — it hosts the one component carrying its name, which is what `exemptFromChrome` has always meant.
- Three checks tie the field to the generated stage catalog. A Frame that claims a kind no component declares fails validation; a **chrome-hosting** Frame that leaves out a non-sovereign kind fails validation; a stage kind left with no Frame to compose in fails the catalog load. **For a chrome-hosting Frame this makes `admits` a verified contract, not a declaration:** such a Frame is the fallback host for every component that is not its own sovereign, so its correct value *is* the set of non-sovereign kinds the catalog declares — and `admits` never feeds that catalog back.
- **`kind` and `exemptFromChrome` may no longer disagree.** They encode the same fact and nothing tied them, so a chrome-hosting Frame could label itself `kind: "sovereign"` and skip the check above — the under-claim arm now keys on `exemptFromChrome` (what `sovereignFrames()` reads) rather than the self-declared label, and `validateFrame` rejects the contradiction outright. Two independent guards; each is exercised on its own probe.
- **The remaining limits are enumerated, not summarized**, in the `checkFrameAdmits` docblock and `design/forms.md` §5: a sovereign Frame's under-claim is structurally unreachable; a chrome-hosting Frame's `admits` is now fully derived, so the arm catches a hand-edit rather than a real disagreement; the derived set depends on both manifest sets, so it is independent of `admits` but not of the frame catalog as a whole; and the arm fires on partially-specified synthetic frames, so fixtures assert with `.some()`.

- Fuoco knows lines, columns and what a section is called. `lineAt`, `offsetAt`, `placeAt` and `rangeOf`
  turn an offset into a line, column, unit, part and flat number, and a unit or part into its offsets and
  lines. An outline names its two levels with `kinds` (a deck says slide and page; `createTextOutliner`
  takes `kinds` for chapters, cues or functions), and `focusPlace(hub)` reports the focus in those words.
- Fuoco can keep two views of a document scrolled together. `createScrollMap` pairs the first section at the top, the last at the bottom and every one between centered, and `sectionAt` names the section a view is on.

- **Pane layouts: `columns` and `rows` (experimental).** Name a two-pane slide in `_class` — `<!-- _class: columns ratio-60-40 -->` side by side or `<!-- _class: rows ratio-35-65 -->` stacked, the ratio optional and written as a class word (`ratio-60-40`, never `60/40`) — and write each pane the way you write a slide, one heading level down: `<!-- _pane: bar -->` names its component (default `content`), then its modifiers (`<!-- _pane: team-profile sides -->`), and a `### title` names the pane, set as a label in the eyebrow's voice (an eyebrow pill above it joins it: `Shortlist · Cleared`; a subtitle pill below it stays). Every top-level `###` on such a slide is a pane's title: right under a marker it titles that pane, and anywhere else it starts a text pane. `no-title` hides a pane's title from the eye and keeps it for screen readers, the Read view and the outline. Side by side, the two titles share one line. Demo: `examples/pane-layouts.md`.
- On a slide in the pane syntax, the Key Insight (`>`) or note (`— `) that closes either pane is the slide's, set below both panes; a `>` in the middle of a pane is a quotation and stays, as does what the pane's component uses itself (a quote's attribution, a chart's caption) and a pane that is nothing but a quote. A slide in the experimental comments keeps the rule it had: only what follows the last pane is the slide's.
- `lint:deck` checks the new syntax: `pane-layout` also names a layout with fewer than two panes, a component in the layout's `_class`, a modifier the pane's component does not know, a `no-title` with no title and a deck-wide `class: columns`; `pane-title` suggests one line for a pill above a pane title, and a title of five words or fewer; `pane-insight` names a slide with two Key Insights; `pane-syntax` suggests the rewrite for the experimental `<!-- panes: -->` / `<!-- pane: -->` comments, which still render as before. A pane with a title holds proportionally fewer items.
- **Breaking:** `columns` and `rows` in a slide's `_class` now name a pane layout. A deck that used either as its own class (a Marp idiom: `section.columns { … }` in the deck's CSS) keeps it on a slide with fewer than two panes, but a slide with two or more top-level `###` headings is now laid out in panes. Rename the class (`my-columns`) to keep the old behavior.
- `columns` and `rows` are components, of a new kind: **hosts**, whose body is two other components (manifest `hosts: "panes"`, bucket and function `layout`, substance `mixed`). They have docs pages and galleries, appear in `components.json` and the pick list, and file under **Split layouts** and a new **Layout** function group in the Playground's picker; the Studio's add-slide gallery offers them as **Two columns** and **Top and bottom** (new manifest field `label`).
- The Playground's and the Studio's live previews style a pane's component as soon as the pane is typed, or given a modifier: both used to keep the stylesheet they had, so a list or chart typed into a pane rendered unstyled until a reload.

- `golden-diff` now renders the goldens a pull request's sources can affect and diffs them against the base, so a PR shows its visual change without committing a PDF. A golden that differs from main's PDF is rendered at the base commit too, and only a change this PR made is reported.
- A nightly `golden-bless.yml` bot checks every golden on `main`, re-blesses only the ones that drifted, and opens one PR with them.

- **Added: `node tools/golden-bless-nights.mjs` prints the nightly bless bot's dry-run nights
  as one table.** It reads each run's `golden-bless` artifact, replays rule 4, and scores
  each night twice: the whole bless PR, and only the goldens that night added, because an
  unmerged bless PR carries every earlier night's goldens forward. The last column is left
  empty for a person's label. Goldens rollout step 4 sets its thresholds from this table.

- `npm run gotchas:index` and `build:check` now refuse a gotcha whose index row exceeds 280 characters, naming the entry. The heading is billed twice — once as the link label, once slugged as the anchor — and paid on every read of `engineering/gotchas.md`, so the cap bounds what one new gotcha can add to a block that is already 9,409 tokens. It is a ratchet pinned just above today's widest row, not a target: the live corpus passes unchanged.
- The topic filename is deliberately not billed. It is shared by every entry under the topic, so counting it would let a topic rename and a near-cap new entry each pass alone while the second to merge failed for the other's change.

- **Added: the handoff issue — a continuation brief that survives the session.**
  A session leaving work pending now files one GitHub issue carrying the brief, so
  the next session pulls it from the queue instead of being handed it. The
  contract is `engineering/workflow.md` § The handoff issue, and it names the two
  traps that make the obvious shape fail: `maskFences` blanks a fenced block
  before the Definition-of-Ready gate looks for headings, so a brief pasted
  verbatim inside a fence reads as having no swimlane and no acceptance check and
  the gate strips `status:ready`; and `pr-autoclose-issues.yml` closes every issue
  under a closing keyword, so a nine-item handoff referenced as `Closes #N` by a
  six-item PR loses three items silently.
  The contract was then tested by handing a real handoff issue to a session with
  no transcript. It found the card wanting in two ways the rules now cover: a
  base that named only a sha left it unable to tell whether to continue the
  unmerged PR's branch or cut a fresh one from `main` (the card's constants and
  evidence script existed only on that branch), and an item added by comment sat
  outside the body's own "every item below is ticked" acceptance check.

- **`heatmap`** — a new chart-family member: a numeric matrix read as intensity, for when the finding is where a value concentrates across two dimensions rather than how individual values compare. Authored in the family's existing nested list (top-level item = row, nested items = columns with a value pill), up to 12 columns by 10 rows. It closes the gap the Cartesian expansion named and deferred: the family covered the qualitative grid (`matrix-grid`) and the geographic one (`map`), but nothing put a number at every row-by-column crossing.
- A crossing with no authored value paints as unmeasured — a bare neutral with a dotted edge — rather than as zero at the bottom of the ramp, so a ragged cohort table reads as incomplete instead of as a collapse.
- Intensity rides `map`'s choropleth ramp (one hue mixed into a neutral anchor) rather than a second sequential mechanism, so low values stay above the empty cell on both canvases.
- The cell carries its value, and the ramp is quantized to five stops so that it can. Text on a colored fill is the one placement the chart family does not otherwise guarantee contrast for: measured across all 33 palettes on both canvases, a single ink crossover leaves 318 cells below WCAG AA (worst 2.60:1), and a per-palette crossover cannot be expressed, because `section.dark` flips the canvas per slide while CSS has no numeric `light-dark()`. Five discrete stops turn that per-palette knowledge from a number into a color, which `light-dark()` does carry — see the stepped-ramp entry for the measurement.

- `heatmap` can show a **band key**, naming each of the five ramp steps so a reader can tell why two cells share a tone. Add `scale` to the slide and the chart names the bands itself, by the range of values each covers. The key is opt-in — a heatmap that does not ask for one renders exactly as before.
- **Label sets** — one way to name the members of a set, wherever a chart has one. Write `` `[{1, Cold}, {3, Warm}, {5, Hot}]` `` above the table and those bands take your words; the ones you skip keep their derived range. The construct lives in `lib/core/label-set.js` so the other charts that hard-code their keys can adopt it.
- A heatmap cell's `` `note=prose` `` annotation now reaches both surfaces it was designed for: a hover popover on the live surfaces, and the slide's speaker note so the exported PDF keeps the same words.

- A demo deck for heatmap motion — `examples/anima-heatmap.md` shows the grid building cell by cell across the four motion styles (`build`, `together`, `rise`, `off`), captured mid-build from the live Playground.

- **Hide a slide.** Put `<!-- hide -->` (or `<!-- _hide -->`, `<!-- _hide: true -->`) at the top of a slide and it stays in the deck and the editor, but Present and every export leave it out: PDF, PowerPoint, LibreOffice, PNG and image sets, and the webpage, from the Studio and from the command line. Speaker notes, alt text and review comments stay with their own slides. Page numbers count only the slides that show, so hiding slide 3 of 6 gives a PDF numbered 1 to 5, and a hidden divider opens no section on the progress rail.
- **Studio:** the slide menu has **Hide Slide** and **Show Slide** (the command palette too, as Hide slide and Show slide). A hidden slide keeps its place in the strip and the slide map with an eye-off mark, and the preview bar shows a **Hidden** chip that brings it back. One Undo takes either back.
- **Export to Marp** leaves hidden slides out too. The bundle writes each as `<!-- _hide: true -->` and its engine drops it when you build with marp-cli (`npm run pdf` and the other scripts), numbering the rest without it. The VS Code preview may still show a hidden slide.

- **New `histogram` chart for distributions.** Write each band as a range and its share: `` `$1M..$10M` `55%` ``. Bars touch because the bands join end to end, and each bar's area is its share, so bands of different widths draw honestly. Add `log` to the axis line (`` `[{Annual loss, $1M..$250M, log}]` ``) when the bands widen toward the tail. `lint:deck` names a band written with a dash, bands that leave a gap or overlap, and `log` over a band that starts at zero. Demo deck: `examples/histogram.md`.
- **New `ep-curve` chart for return-period losses.** Write each point as `` `{return period, loss}` ``, such as `` `{100, $410M}` ``, and nest a curve's points under its name for OEP and AEP or gross and net (up to four curves). The return period runs across on a log scale labeled `1-in-10`, `1-in-100`, `1-in-1,000`, and narration reads each curve point by point. Demo deck: `examples/ep-curve.md`.
- **The chart family guide now lists how every chart is written and where its text goes** (`chart-family.docs.md` § How a chart is written): ranges are `a..b`, a position is a `{x, y}` record, an axis is one bracketed line above the heading, and a log axis is the word `log` in it. Its § Axes and labels sets where ticks, axis titles, value labels and series names go, how crowded labels thin or report, and the sizes and baselines they use, each rule naming the code that enforces it.
- **Both charts take a `marks:`.** Under `pigment`, `etch` and `tone`, histogram bars repaint like bar-chart bars do. EP-curve dots repaint under `pigment` and `etch`; under `tone` they keep their curve's color, as line-chart dots do, so a dot never wears a different color from its own curve.
- **Histogram bars look like bar-chart bars.** They use the same soft wash and outline, and a thin background-colored cut separates two touching bars, so neighbors never merge into one shape under any finish, in light or dark.
- **Hovering a histogram bar shows its full outline.** The cuts between bars step aside while a bar is held, and they never catch the pointer, so moving across a bar's edge doesn't close its card. Bars that overlap by mistake also get a cut, so they read as two shapes.

- **Added: `.html` is a real output format — `lattice deck.md out.html` now writes
  HTML.** It previously fell through the format switch to PDF, so that command wrote
  **PDF bytes into a file named `.html`** and put the actual HTML in a second
  `out.html.html`. The rendered HTML was always produced as a sidecar of every render;
  the only thing missing was a way to ask for it without also paying the PDF encode.
  Measured on a 58-slide deck (medians of 3), the `.html` render takes 6.77s
  against the `.pdf` render's 8.24s. **The saving scales with the deck** — about
  18% there and 20% on the chart gallery, but under 1% on a one-slide deck, where
  browser startup dominates and there is barely any PDF to encode.
- **This is still a full browser render, not a browser-free one.** Auto-split and the
  overflow/legibility passes measure laid-out DOM, and the written file is their
  post-split result — an `.html` render pages identically to the same deck's `.pdf`.
  What it skips is the PDF encode and the PDF-only SVG rasterization pass. For markup
  without layout, call `lib/engine` directly instead.
- **`--player` and `--fluid` are the best reason to use it**: they build the viewer
  at the requested `.html` path, where previously they forced a full PDF encode and
  a megabyte-plus artifact nobody asked for. That win holds at any deck size.
- `--notes` writes `deck.notes.txt` rather than `deck.html.notes.txt`, and
  `--strip-notes` scrubs that sidecar exactly as it does on the PDF path.
  `--raster`, `--paper`/`--orientation`, `--present` (including the `present: true`
  front-matter form) and `--embed-source` are PDF-only and now say so instead of
  going silent.
- A failed `.html` render leaves **no** file, like every other format — it no longer
  strands a complete-looking pre-split document at the deliverable path.

- **New chart component: `hub-spoke`** — one center, its satellites, and what flows between them. Write one top-level item (the hub) and nest the satellites under it; the chart draws a heavy neutral hub, solid satellite discs and constant-width connectors, spread across the stage. Use `bar` or `stacked-bar` instead when the claim is a ranking or a share.
- **Satellites are neutral unless you group them.** A word pill (`Retail`, `Wave 1`, `FY26`) groups a satellite, and up to six groups get a hue and a key band; a group never takes the hub's lightness, even on a palette that spends a slot on the heading ink. A status pill (`at-risk`, `blocked`, `on-track`) marks only its own spoke with a halo, a heavier edge and the spoken status word; nothing else on the slide changes.
- **Nothing scales until you ask.** Values print by default. `sized` scales disc area by value (up to 8 satellites), and `flow-out`, `flow-in` or `flow-both` draw arrowheads and step connector weight in four classes. A per-spoke `flow:in` pill changes that spoke's arrowhead only.
- **`tiered`** hangs leaves off each satellite: up to 6 branches and 18 leaves, each branch its own hue. Every connector keeps a visible floor (hub to branch and branch to leaf), no two discs overlap, and a six-branch slide lays out in about 50 ms.
- **Twenty-five `hub-spoke-*` lint rules** say when a pill is dropped, when `sized` or a flow class switches itself off and why, when the hub name will not fit (an error), and when a slide sits outside the layout's proven envelope (`hub-spoke-crowded`). The grammar, the channel rule and the lint live in one module, `lib/core/hub-spoke-model.js`, shared by the kernel, `lint:deck` and narration; the linter and the narrator read the slide's list through one reader, `lib/core/first-list-tree.js`, so an ordered-list hub (`1. Hub`) lints as it draws.
- **Works with `marks:`.** `pigment`, `etch` and `tone` repaint the group discs and the key, and a status disc takes the finish's quieter level while keeping its state hue (`STATUS_MARKS` in `tools/build-marks-css.js`). Under `tone`, a group's connectors, arrowheads and names join the one hue. The hub and neutral satellites carry no color, so every finish leaves them as drawn. On a slide with groups, `pigment` and `tone` draw the hub in the full heading ink, so no group disc reaches the hub's lightness (onyx dark had put a gray group at the hub's exact shade).
- `lib/core/chart-values.js` gains `unitKey()`, the family's answer to "are these two values in the same unit" (`$1.2bn` and `$1.2B` are; `20 mg` is not twenty million).

- Icons draw as glyphs of **Lattice Icons**, our own font of the curated icons, by default. They look the same on the slide (within a third of a pixel), and the PDF, the web page and the player carry the font: in a PDF an icon copies as its label. An editable PowerPoint or ODP draws icons as native shapes (see the office icons entry). A file carries each icon once (about 0.3 KB) in every theme and color mode, sized by the Emoji font setting; under `system` icons draw as SVG. `icon: svg` keeps the drawing for a deck or a slide (`engineering/decisions/2026-11-01-icon-font.md`).
- `npm run icons:font` rebuilds the font from the curated drawings when the icon list changes; `fonts:check` fails while it is stale.

- **Icons draw on a raw Marp render.** An Export-to-Marp bundle, or any Marp preview that loads the Lattice runtime, now draws `^{…}` icons and pill icons. Before, they stayed as code. The runtime fetches the drawings (`lattice-plugin-icons.js`) from beside itself the first time a slide writes an icon, and the bundle carries that file. A bundle whose deck turned the icons plugin off leaves its spans as code.

- **A card opacity level, and hairline dividers, on `image spotlight` and `image statement`.** The backing is now a 0–100% level: the four names stay (`card-solid` 100%, `card-soft` 80%, `card-sheer` 55%, `card-clear` 0%) and every other 5% step is a class too (`card-o5` … `card-o95`). On the deck line, `image-card: 65%` writes a level. In the Studio, Deck settings → Image and a slide's Image tab show the backing as a slider with the four names as chips. A thin backing needs a matching `ink-light` or `ink-dark`.
- **Dividers that take no space.** A stacked card now draws a thin line under its heading, and a `band` draws a vertical line between its heading and text columns. Both paint `--spectrum-structure`, so they follow the deck's `spectrum-trim:` and a slide's own `spectrum-trim` class (a quiet accent tint by default, the deck's spectrum under `on`); `rule: none` drops them. Measured with `check:jank`: the card's geometry is identical with and without them at every heading length. **Existing `spotlight` and `statement` slides with a heading and a body gain the under-heading line.** Demo: `examples/image-band.md`.

- **`band` — a full-width strip for the text card on `image spotlight` and `image statement`.** Add `band` to `at-top` or `at-bottom` and the card stretches across the slide along that edge, heading on the left and text on the right, so the middle of the photo stays clear of words. It keeps the card's inset and rounded corners on spotlight, and shortens the scrim on statement. It composes with every other card control (`card-soft`, `ink-dark`, `card-sm`, `compact`). On a corner, on `at-center`, or in a portrait or square deck, `band` does nothing. In the `image-card:` register it is the new `shape` axis: `image-card: bottom band`; `card-float` is the slide-side way out of a deck-wide `band`. The Studio's **Image** tabs gain a Card shape control. Demo: `examples/image-band.md`.

- **`image spotlight` and `image statement` card controls.** Four new class axes now control the text card over a full-bleed photo. **Placement:** `at-tl` · `at-top` · `at-tr` · `at-center` · `at-bl` · `at-bottom` · `at-br`. **Backing:** `card-solid` · `card-soft` · `card-sheer` · `card-clear` sets the opacity of the spotlight panel or the statement scrim. **Ink:** `ink-light` · `ink-dark` sets white or near-black words, and the backing flips to match. **Size:** `card-sm` · `card-md` · `card-lg` steps the width, padding and type together. `compact` tightens the card's padding and its inset from the slide edge to 70% at any size. The statement scrim follows the card's placement. Slides that name none of these classes render as before. Demo: `examples/image-card-controls.md`.
- **`image-card:` front-matter register.** One line sets the card for every image slide: `image-card: top-right soft sm compact`. It takes up to one word per axis: placement (`top-left` … `bottom-right`, `center`), backing, ink, size and density (`regular` · `compact`). It rides image slides only, because `at-*` and `compact` mean something on other layouts too. A slide's own class overrides one axis and keeps the rest; `card-regular` lets one slide step out of a deck-wide `compact`. Lint reports an unknown or doubled word (`unknown-image-card`). In the Studio, the Deck settings and the slide inspector each have an **Image** tab with one control per axis.

- **A thin spotlight card gets an ink that reads, picked from the photo.** A spotlight card under 60% opaque lets the photo show through, so the theme's own ink was read against the photo and could vanish. In the Studio, dragging a slide's Card backing slider below 60% with no ink set on the slide or the deck now samples the pixels behind the card in the live preview and writes `ink-light` or `ink-dark`, whichever has the higher contrast ratio (WCAG 2, counting the card's own fill at that opacity). It never overwrites an ink you set, Card ink → Auto removes it, and a photo the browser cannot read (a cross-origin image) gets no automatic ink. For everyone else, lint warns when a thin spotlight card has neither: `thin-card-no-ink`. The rule and the choice share one kernel, `lib/core/card-ink.mjs`.

- **New plugin: avatars.** Write `` `!{Ada Okafor}` `` in inline code and Lattice draws a
  head-and-shoulders portrait. The name picks every trait you leave out, so it is the same face on
  every render. Pin the ones that matter by name: `skin=1`–`8`, `hair`, `hair-color`, `face`, `eyes`,
  `eye-color`, `brows`, `nose`, `mouth`, `beard`, `glasses` and `top`. `gender=woman|man|neutral`
  changes which defaults the name draws from, and a trait you write always wins over it.
- **The tile takes the deck's colors.** `c1`–`c12`, `sm` `md` `lg` `xl`, `circle` `rounded` `square`,
  `framed` `bare` and `border=cN`, plus an `avatar:` register and `avatar-*` slide classes. Skin, hair,
  eyes and clothes keep their colors in every theme, as a photograph does.
- **In a team-profile roster an avatar is the portrait.** Write it where the photo goes; it mixes
  with photos and monograms. With the plugin off, that person gets a monogram, never their role.
- **Inline code that opens with `!{` is now notation.** `!` joins `~` (sparks) and `^` (icons) as a
  record tag. A span that starts with `!` and no brace (`!important`) renders as before.
- **The website teaches avatars.** A new Avatars guide, with live examples you can edit, and an
  Avatars cheat sheet sit beside Sparks under Inline elements. "Things you put in a line" now
  covers four elements.

- **`inline-code: literal` turns the inline pill and mark grammar off for a whole deck.**
  Every single-backtick span stays exactly as typed — `` `{STABLE}:c2` ``, `` `[x]` ``,
  all of it. The grammar reads every such span in every deck, so a deck written elsewhere
  whose prose happens to say `` `[x]` `` or `` `{LABEL}` `` now renders a disc or a pill
  where it rendered text; the per-occurrence backslash escape is the right tool for one
  span and the wrong one for ninety. Default is unchanged (`rich` — the grammar runs), so
  no existing deck moves a pixel.
- **It works on a Marp-kit deck too, through Marp's own `class:` directive.** On a
  marp-core render the register cannot reach the runtime at all: marp-cli loads a deck over
  `file://`, where `fetch` is CORS-blocked outright, and over http(s) the answer arrives
  after the pills are drawn. So the CLASS is the contract that always lands:
  `class: inline-code-literal` puts the token on every section by marp-core's own doing,
  verified against real marp-cli. Through the Lattice engine, and in any export (which
  bakes its front matter), the register does it for you.
- **Known limit: a marp-core render carrying no baked front matter.** That is a
  hand-authored marp-kit deck (`marp --pdf`, `marp --html`, the VS Code preview) or an
  `.html` export predating the bake — the runtime is the only implementation, and it has to
  fetch the sibling `.md`, which either fails outright on `file://` or answers after the
  pills are drawn. `class: inline-code-literal` covers every one of those; re-exporting
  covers the old export. Making the runtime WAIT instead cost every other deck a full extra
  transform pass (1 to 3 on a 40-slide deck carrying no register at all) and needed a
  wall-clock guess that rendered wrong at 3.2s and again at 10.2s, so the limit is pinned
  rather than papered over.
- **An unknown value keeps the grammar RUNNING, and says so.** `inline-code: off` — the
  value most authors will try first — is not a known value, so the deck keeps rendering
  pills and `lint:deck` warns with `unknown-inline-code` naming the two real values. The
  opposite mapping would let a typo silently change what a deck looks like.
- **A literal deck keeps a backslash you typed.** With no grammar running there is nothing
  to escape from, so `` `\[x]` `` renders as `\[x]` rather than being quietly rewritten.
- **In the Studio: Deck settings · General · Inline pills and marks.** Toggling it off
  writes `inline-code: literal`; toggling it back on removes the key rather than writing
  `rich`, so a deck that never opted out carries no trace of having been switched.
- **It works per slide, and in the deck's own chrome.**
  `<!-- _class: inline-code-literal -->` turns the grammar off for one slide and composes
  with a component class; a literal deck's `header:` and `footer:` go literal with the
  body, which matters because those are the two directives a deck written elsewhere is
  most likely to carry. Both render paths gate on the resolved section class rather than
  on front matter, so the register, Marp's `class:` and a per-slide `_class:` are one
  mechanism instead of three that can disagree. (The engine builds chrome eleven ruler
  rules before that class exists, so it reads the class first and re-derives the deck-level
  answer from the front matter when it is not there yet — a timing exception, same inputs
  and same answer. The runtime needs none: chrome lives inside the section.)

- Every inline kind that takes a record has one more spelling, `` `@kind{…}` ``, the form plugins will use for
  their own inline syntax: `` `@icon{database}` `` is `` `^{database}` ``, `` `@avatar{Ada Okafor}` `` is
  `` `!{Ada Okafor}` ``, `` `@spark{12 14 17}` `` is `` `~{12 14 17}` ``, and `` `@pill{LIVE}` `` is `` `{LIVE}` ``.
  The short forms stay, and both spellings draw identically. `@` without a brace right after the name
  (`` `@ada` ``, `` `@laticent/segno` ``) is still plain code.
- In the Studio editor, typing `` `@ `` lists every inline kind with its short form, and inside `@kind{` the menu
  offers what the short form offers (spark types, pill shapes, icon names).
- `lint:deck` warns on `@name{…}` when no kind is called `name` (`unknown-inline-kind`), with a one-click fix to
  the nearest kind, and its pill, spark, icon and spelling checks read the `@kind{…}` spelling too.
- A plugin from a zip can bring its own inline kinds: its manifest declares them under `contributes.inline`, and a deck
  that lists the plugin calls one as `` `@kind{…}` ``. The plugin's code draws each span in the same sandbox as its
  fence, after you approve it (`lattice packages trust`, or Approve in the Studio). Until the deck lists the plugin, the
  Studio shows a small chip where each span is; a span that cannot draw stays as code, and the Studio or the CLI says
  why.

- **`{LABEL}` in inline code renders as a pill, anywhere in any deck.**
  `` `{STABLE}:c2` `` draws a capsule; `:tag` `:tag-bordered` `:chip` `:circle`
  `:chevron-right` `:chevron-left` `:diamond` pick the shape, `:c1`–`:c12` pick an
  ordinal categorical slot (not a color — the same slot is sky blue on `indaco` and
  deep red on `burgundy`), and `:sm` / `:lg` scale it from the type. Modifier order is
  free. Shape and color now belong to the VALUE, so one ledger can carry four different
  statuses without a variant class on the slide — which is what five of `list-tabular`'s
  eight variants were doing, none of which ever moved a grid cell.
- **Nothing existing changes.** A pill needs a brace pair whose label is trimmed and
  comma-free; every other inline code stays literal, including `` `[x]` ``,
  `` `[data-mark]` ``, `` `{ ok, scene }` `` and `` `getUserId()` ``. Measured across
  every inline-code span in every deck we ship — thousands of them: 36 dispatch, and they
  sit in exactly two decks — 22 in `examples/inline-pills.md`, which demonstrates the
  grammar, and 14 in `examples/inline-code-literal.md`, which turns it off. Zero in any
  other deck. That is a measurement, not yet a gate: the corpus-wide census that would
  re-walk every deck on every run is deferred to its own change, so re-derive before you
  rely on the number. An unknown modifier (`` `{X}:c13` ``) falls back to literal rather than being ignored, and double backticks
  force the literal for a label that would otherwise qualify.
- **The four state markers are reserved inside `{}`.** `` `{x}` `` `` `{-}` `` `` `{/}` ``
  and `` `{ }` `` render literal, with a `lint:deck` suggestion pointing at the bare
  `- [x]` form. Without the reservation `{x}` drew a capsule pill containing the letter
  `x` — not an obvious no-op but a plausible-looking wrong artifact — and the four
  behaved three different ways, since `{ }` already fell to literal on the space.
- **Fixed before release: a pill in a `list-tabular` row was not placed at all.** Every
  placement rule in that component selects `code` — the element — so a pill auto-placed
  into the first free cell instead. Measured on a row carrying both a `` `META` `` and a
  pill, the pill landed in the label column and shoved the row name out to the counter
  column at x=0. A pill now takes the same cell its variant gives a `code`, and a census
  test fails if a future variant places a code without placing a pill.
- **`` `[x]` `` in inline code draws the state disc, anywhere inline code can go.** The
  six state markers an author already writes bare at the start of a bullet — `[x]` `[-]`
  `[!]` `[?]` `[ ]` `[/]` — now work in a sentence, a heading, a table cell or a ledger row's
  trailing column. Brackets make a mark, braces make a pill: one vocabulary in two
  positions. Each mark names itself with the universal word (yes, partly, no, unknown,
  open, does not apply) on `role="img"` + `aria-label`, putting no word in the document, and every `checks-*`
  style variant reaches it because it carries the same classes a checklist row does.
  Only the six exact forms dispatch — `` `[~]` ``, `` `[data-mark]` `` and `` `[0]` ``
  stay literal.
- **`stateClassesFor` is one kernel again.** The marker-to-semantic decision lived twice,
  in the markdown-it plugins and in the runtime, which is the drift HARD RULE #1 exists
  to stop. Adding the inline consumer forced the unification rather than a third copy;
  both originals import `lib/core/state-marks.js` now, and a test fails if one grows back.
- **The escape is a backslash, and it works on every render path.** `` `\{LIVE}` `` and
  `` `\[x]` `` render the literal with the backslash removed. It replaces a
  double-backtick escape that worked only on the engine path: marp-core renders
  `` `{LIVE}` `` and `` ``{LIVE}`` `` to the same `<code>`, so the runtime's DOM mirror
  could not tell them apart and converted both — a divergence the fidelity probe now
  pins. A backslash survives into the DOM, so both paths agree. It only escapes what
  would otherwise dispatch, so `` `\[a-z]` `` and `` `\d+` `` keep their backslash and
  a regex is safe. Fenced and indented code blocks were never affected — they are not
  inline code, so no directive is ever read inside one.
- **Pills and marks now clear the text either side of them.** Measured as the only
  mechanism without wrapping every one in a spacer element: on the same pill,
  `padding-inline` grew the chrome 58.9px to 73.3px and gave 0px of outside space, while
  a horizontal margin left the chrome alone and opened 5.59px. Horizontal only, and there
  is deliberately no vertical padding — these are atomic inline boxes, so block padding
  enters the line box and gives one line of a paragraph leading its neighbors lack
  (measured 75.6px to 82px). Vertical room stays the container's, through `line-height`.

- **Inline sparks.** A `~{…}` in inline code now renders as a word-sized chart that sits wherever inline code can go: a `kpi` line, a table cell, a `big-number` caption, a sentence. `` `~{12 14 13 17 21}` `` draws a line; `:area`, `:bar`, `:step` and `:winloss` draw the same series other ways; `` `~{72%}` `` draws a ring and `` `~{72/80}:bullet` `` a bar against a target. `:sm` / `:lg` / `:fill` size it, `:c1`–`:c12` color it, `:end` / `:minmax` mark values, `:zero` starts a line at zero. Every spark sits in a squared 3:2 frame by default. A **look** decides how its one color is spent across the tile, the edge and the marks: `:pigment` (the default, the color fills the tile), `:etch` (a clear tile, the color is the line) and `:tone` (one hue stepped by value), the same three finishes Lattice's charts use, drawing from the chart color cycle so a spark and a chart show a slot in the same hue. A spark that names no color is `:c1`. `:bare` and `:rounded` change the frame and corners. Each is set for one spark, for one slide with a `spark-*` class, or for the whole deck with the new `spark:` front-matter register (`spark: bare`, `spark: etch rounded`). A span that doesn't parse stays code, and `lint:deck` warns with the reason (`spark-literal`). In the Studio, typing `` `~ `` offers starter sparks and `:` after the brace offers the next step only (a type, then a size, then a color …), limited to what the spark can take — and pills now complete the same way, a shape, then a color, then a size; a spark measured too big for where it landed (past its space, or more than 1.5 lines tall) gets a `spark-too-big` warning with a one-click fix to the size that fits. See the docs site's new **Sparks** guide, under a new **Inline elements** sidebar group (`/guides/inline/sparks/`), `lib/base/base.docs.md` § Inline sparks, and `examples/inline-sparks.md`.
- **Sketch mode draws sparks by hand.** On a `mode: sketch` slide a spark's tile edge, its line, its bars' outlines, a bullet's tick and a ring's arc are drawn by the same rough.js hand as the tables around it; fills keep their look.
- **Fixed: sketch-mode ink sat 4px low.** Every hand-drawn table frame, row rule and ledger rule was drawn one section-border-width below where it belongs; the rules now sit on the row edges.

- **Added: the intake gate now asks whether anyone can actually work a card.** A
  card missing a swimlane or an acceptance check gets `needs:definition` and one
  comment naming what to add, clearing once both are written. The Definition of
  Ready was previously checked only when someone applied `status:ready` — a
  transition nobody performs — so measured across all 318 open cards, 218 had
  never been asked for it, and every one of those 218 is missing the swimlane.
  The work-item form already required both fields; the gap was the paths that
  skip the form. Grandfathered to cards opened on or after the cutoff in
  `.github/scripts/triage.js` (a replay over the real queue flags 7 rather than
  218), and end-user `feedback` reports are exempt — a bug reporter cannot name
  the decision doc their crash belongs to.
  The cutoff governs what the **gate** flags, never what a human may flag: a
  `needs:definition` applied by hand to a legacy card sticks, because that
  labeling pass is how the backlog gets swept.
- **Added: `npm run audit:queue`.** Counts open cards against the Definition of
  Ready and replays the intake gate over them, with and without the cutoff, so
  the numbers above are re-derivable instead of asserted.
- **Fixed: the BACKLOG triage banner read "1 card need triage".** It agreed the
  noun and left the verb plural.

- **Added: `tools/jank-census.js` — the jank sweep, pointed at the whole catalog.**
  `check-jank` answers one question about one component; nothing had ever asked it
  across the catalog, so the only jank evidence in the repo covered essentially one
  component. The census runs `--anchors` over every manifest class and variant (272),
  ranks what moves, and reports a class it could not measure as UNMEASURED rather than
  as clean.
- **Added: `--marks`, which sweeps the running marks a component census cannot reach.**
  `mark-orbit`, `stamp-seal` and the rest are base MODIFIERS, not manifest variants, so
  a catalog sweep never renders one — and a `section::before` running mark is the
  archetype `check-jank` was built from. All 23 hold position across the sweep; that is
  the first time it has been measured.
- **Added: `engineering/jank-census.md` — the committed table**, regenerable by the one
  command printed at the top of it.

- **Added: `check-jank` measures an anchor's SIZE, and sweeps `topic` with its track.** Every
  anchored run prints a `GROWTH` line, and `--max-growth PX` fails a mark that must hold one
  size — DRIFT deliberately ignores a mark pinned at one edge that grows. The heading sweep
  now carries per-slide directives from the manifest sample (such as `_track`), so
  `node tools/check-jank.js topic --anchor 'ul.tile-track > li.on' --max-growth 2` measures
  the lit tab on every step instead of on none.

- **Added `examples/kaizen-craftsmanship.md`** — a 14-slide mentoring deck on craftsmanship, Deming's view of quality, kaizen, and modularity, built for an observe-first experiential session. Carries a speaker note on every slide.

- A `dead-code` pre-push job holds knip's unused files, exports and packages, imports of undeclared packages, and every other knip finding at zero in `.js` files (`node tools/quality-assessment.js --check --only dead-code`, about 5 s). Of the 20 files knip flagged, 19 are used through a route knip cannot follow and are now listed with their reason in `knip.jsonc`; the 20th, `lib/core/transform-dsl/index.js`, is an unwired prototype waiting on an owner decision. All 16 flagged packages are used. `pngjs`, `puppeteer-core`, `marked` and `js-yaml` are declared devDependencies at their installed versions instead of resolving by accident. `.mjs` files are not covered yet.

- Every page of the site (the landing page, the Studio, the Playground and the docs) now tells a browser too old to run
  Lattice so, instead of showing it a broken page. The notice covers the
  page with the site's own background, shows one real Lattice slide, and says what this reader has and what Lattice needs
  ("You have Safari 15.6. Lattice needs Safari 16.4 or newer"), how to update that browser, with a link to its vendor's
  update page, and that browsers this old no longer get security fixes. "Continue anyway" dismisses it for the tab. Current
  browsers download nothing extra.
- Getting started has a new "Supported browsers" section: Chrome and Edge 111, Firefox 128, Safari 16.4 (iOS 16.4 on
  iPhone and iPad), Samsung Internet 22 and Opera 97 or newer.
- The Studio and the Playground now decline browsers older than Chrome 111, Safari 16.4 or Firefox 128 (they need CSS
  `color-mix()` and `@property`, which the site's CSS framework relies on), and the decline screen names the versions to
  update to instead of "a current browser".
- The notice is built for every reader: a screen reader hears its heading and lead as it opens, the update steps are a
  numbered list, what each missing capability does sits behind "Capability requirements", links that open a new tab say so, and keyboard
  focus stays inside the notice instead of wandering into the page beneath.
- The notice also reads correctly in the original Edge (EdgeHTML): readable selection colors, a narrow card where CSS
  grid is missing, and steps that install the current Edge, since the original one no longer updates.
- The notice is self-contained: it lists the supported browsers itself, in a collapsed "Supported browsers" section
  beside "Capability requirements", instead of linking to another page of the site, which an old browser could not show
  properly either. Both sections open with the same simple button in every browser. Its only link goes to the browser maker's own update
  page.
- An old browser no longer glimpses the broken page while the notice loads: the page stays hidden until the notice
  covers it.
- The notice looks like the rest of the site: the site's top bar, its flat background, its card and button styles, with
  no color jump as it appears.
- The notice is written for readers who aren't technical: what each missing capability does in plain words, a way
  forward for anyone who can't update (on a work device, their IT team; on their own, the browsers that work), and corrected steps for Macs,
  older iPhones and Android phones.
- The page beneath the notice is not drawn at all while the notice shows, so an old browser no longer flashes the
  broken page's colors (a mustard flicker in the original Edge) as the notice appears.
- In the original Edge, the page's background no longer turns the site's accent color. The site's tinted text-selection
  and link-highlight colors now apply only in browsers that support `color-mix()`; the original Edge painted them onto
  the whole page, which was the mustard flash on every refresh of the old-browser notice.

- **`lat` is a short name for the `lattice` command.** After `npm install -g @laticent/lattice` (or in your project's scripts), `lat deck.md deck.pdf` works exactly like `lattice deck.md deck.pdf`, and tab completion covers both in bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell. Don't run it through `npx` in a folder without Lattice: the unscoped `lat` package on npm belongs to someone else.

- **Added: the `legend` plugin, and heatmap callouts as its first capability.** A heatmap can now
  point at a cell in one line under its table:
  `` `@legend{{Onboarding change, tag, c4, row="Feb 2026", col=M2}}` ``, naming the cell by
  its row and column labels (`for=14` or `for=Feb 2026/M2` is the short form). The label sits in a lane
  beside the grid, and a number ties it to its cell: the cell is ringed and carries a numbered
  marker, and the same marker leads the label. No line crosses the grid, and a marker goes only
  where it covers no printed number or name (where none is clear, the ring alone marks the cell). The marker is a circle in its number's color by default, sized
  from its cell, and the pill's shape and color words restyle it. `detail="…"` joins the cell's hover card and the speaker note, and
  narration reads each callout after the rows. A target that names no cell is listed in the
  chart's description, and `lint:deck` rule `legend-span` warns on a span that does not read
  or that sits on a slide where no component reads one yet. It is the first wave of one model for every chart key and label
  (`lib/plugins/legend/legend.docs.md`,
  `engineering/decisions/2026-10-19-universal-legend.md`).

- LFM 1.0 is ratified, with an owner. Its shared test cases live in `spec/conformance/lfm/`: small decks, each with what a Markdown viewer, a Lattice renderer and a linter must produce from it, so another tool can check itself against the same cases. `node tools/lfm-conformance.js` runs them against Lattice.
- LFM 1.0 §2.3 now matches the engine: `boardroom`, `sketch` and `sketch-clean` are `mode:` values, and `finish:` names a backdrop such as `halo`. §3.3 lists the `math` fence, and §2.2 says when splitting at headings changes a deck's slides.

- LFM 1.1 is drafted for the owner's sign-off in `spec/LFM-1.1.md`. It specifies every front-matter setting a deck can use (26 of them, each with its values and the warning an unknown value gets), how slides divide at headings, the `_lens` tag, and the inline notation for pills, marks, sparks and icons. Each part has shared test cases in `spec/conformance/lfm/`.

- The Library's Images tab now opens a detail view for each photo: the picture large, with its description, credit, date taken and name editable. The description shows on the card, and the chat reads it too.
- Renaming a photo keeps its old name as an alias, so `asset:<old-name>` in a deck keeps showing the same photo with no deck edited. Names and aliases share one namespace, so a new upload cannot take a name that is an alias of another photo. Removing an alias frees the name.
- The delete warning on a photo now counts decks that still write one of its old names.
- A workspace backup now carries each photo's description, credit, date taken and old names, and a restore puts them back. An older backup without them still restores. An old name that another photo already holds is dropped on restore instead of refusing the photo.
- A description keeps the quotes you type. The chat still gets a cleaned copy of it, so a quote mark cannot break out of its prompt. Date taken is a date picker.
- A photo whose name is only an old name on this device no longer makes a restore or an upload fail with "delete it first": it is renamed on clash (or reused when the bytes match), and the decks a restore wrote are pointed at the right photo.
- A photo keeps at most 20 old names. A rename past that is refused.
- A Library photo's description now fills an empty alt on its image in a deck: `![](asset:roof)` is announced as "The team on the roof" in the preview, the exported page and a collage's lightbox caption and narration, and it updates when you edit the description. An alt you write yourself is never replaced, and a deck with no described photos exports the same bytes as before.
- A photo's own file is read when you add it: the artist or copyright becomes the credit, the date taken fills in, and a description from the file's XMP, IPTC or EXIF is offered in the photo's detail view under "From the file" with a **Use as description** button. A camera's default text ("SONY DSC", "IMG_2041") is not offered. A photo that carried a location says so there; the location itself is removed from the stored photo and kept nowhere.
- Saving a photo's name and details together is one step: a refused name leaves the details unsaved too, and Enter in a field saves.
- A photo's detail view lists its old names with how many decks still write each, and **Use new name** rewrites those decks to the current name. Each deck gets a Version history entry first, and a code sample that mentions the old name is left as written.
- **Suggest a name and description** in a photo's detail view asks your image model to look at the photo and draft both, for you to edit. A camera's name such as `img-4568` is replaced by the suggested one (the old name stays working as an alias); a name you chose is only offered. It sends a picture only when you press it, to your own OpenRouter account, and saves nothing until you press Save. With no model connected, or a model that cannot read images, it says so instead of doing nothing.
- **Workspace → Model → Image model** picks the model that looks at your photos (vision models only; the latest Claude Sonnet by default), and **Look closer** sets how closely: Quick, Careful (default) or Thorough, which sends a larger picture and asks the model to think first. The panel shows the cost in tokens.
- Each photo card has an **Edit** button beside Delete. On a phone the detail view no longer pans sideways, the date field is short, and the picture is not left broken after you save.
- A suggested name is made unique against your other photos, and a backup file can no longer choose which model looks at your photos. A `.lattice` file now carries a photo that a deck still names by an old name, and a code sample in a table cell is no longer rewritten by **Use new name**.
- The photo detail view is fully keyboard-driven: Enter on a card opens it, Tab stays inside, Enter in a field saves, and Escape closes it and returns focus to the card.
- A photo's description is never read as a slide directive: a description such as "bg contain" stays alt text.
- Reading a photo's own details is safe against crafted files, including a packet built to freeze the page, and a file's text is cleaned the same way text you type is.
- **Use new name** reports honestly when the browser has no room to save: it rewrites nothing it cannot undo, and says how many decks were updated.
- **Use new name** reads markdown the way the renderer does: a list item, heading or quote ends an inline code span, an HTML `<pre>` block runs to its closing tag, and a code fence inside a list item ends with the item, so the count of decks and the rewrite agree with what a slide really shows. A very long block no longer crashes the detail view.
- A description keeps a family emoji, a flag and a Persian word's joiner when it is saved, while hidden-text characters are still removed. A **Suggest** answer from a cancelled visit can no longer overwrite what you typed after reopening the same photo.
- **Use new name** now asks the same markdown parser the slides render with where code, tables, lists and quotes are, instead of guessing, so the count of decks that still use an old name is exactly what a slide shows. Every place the engine resolves a photo name follows the rename (a video poster, a background directive, an inline image tag); only code is left alone. A flag emoji and a family emoji survive a description; hidden text made of invisible characters does not.
- Fixed a photo going broken after you edit it: on iPhone and Safari, saving a description or a new name could leave the stored picture unreadable. A photo's bytes are now rewritten safely, and a photo the browser cannot draw shows a Lattice placeholder (a lattice with one cracked tile) instead of the browser's broken-image mark.
- The photo detail view is laid out as one tight column on every device: every field the same height, Credit and Date side by side at the same width, the picture capped so Name and Save are on screen without scrolling, a full-width **Suggest with AI** button under the Description field, and old names and the file's own details folded away until they matter.

- The Studio Library has an **Images** tab. Add photos from your camera roll, camera or files (on Android and iOS the picker opens natively), or drop them on the panel. Each image can belong to **all decks** or to **this deck** only, and moves between the two without renaming. JPEG and HEIC photos are resized to a 2560 px long edge and re-encoded, which also removes their embedded location. Photos are included in workspace backups and come back on restore: a restore never deletes or overwrites a photo already on the device, a photo it already holds is reused, and a different one under a taken name comes back under a new name with the restored decks updated to match. A file's bytes, not its extension, decide how it is treated, so a JPEG renamed `.png` still loses its location. PNG, WebP and GIF keep their pixels but lose every metadata block (only a picture's rotation survives), AVIF is converted to JPEG, and a backup's photos get the same cleaning on restore, so no photo's location rides into an export. Share tells you which photos a Markdown or Marp file does not carry, and names any photo it could not read for a picture export. In a browser that refuses to store files (Safari in a private window), the Library keeps the photo as raw bytes instead of failing, and says so if it cannot store it at all. Adding a photo whose name is taken keeps the old one and says which name the new one took. Deleting a photo that decks use, or a deck that owns photos, asks first. Deleting a deck deletes the photos kept to that deck only, and the Workspace storage line now counts photos by their size.
- A deck can show a Library photo by name: `![](asset:team-photo)`, `![bg](asset:hero)`, or in a `collage` photo list. The name is the one the Images tab shows on the card. The reference works in the live preview and the Present overlay; the Library card counts the decks that use it. A photo that was deleted, or that belongs to another deck, shows the drawn missing-image stand-in instead of a broken picture. PDF, PowerPoint, image-set and webpage exports carry the photo as pixels, never as a link that dies with the tab. Markdown and Marp exports keep the reference as written, and a `.lattice` carries the photo itself. The CLI keeps the reference, because a Library lives in the browser.
- The Studio editor completes Library photos. Typing inside the parentheses of any image (`![alt](`, `![bg](`) offers `asset:<name>` for the photos the open deck can see, with their size and whether they are kept to this deck. On a `collage` slide, a bare list item (`- `, then a letter or Ctrl-Space) offers whole `![Alt](asset:name)` lines with the alt text selected so you can replace it. The shelf is read on first use, so a deck that never names a photo pays nothing.

- **Libraries and Plugins hubs on the website.** `/libraries/` introduces all nine libraries, grouped by the job each one does, and `/plugins/` introduces the six plugins an author writes: Math, Mermaid, Icons, Avatars, Function plots and Code. It also explains how plugins load, how a plugin differs from a component or a library, and how to write your own. Each library and plugin has a live demo and a Learn page beside it. The Learn page covers the problem it solves, the idea, how to use it, where else it fits, how Lattice uses it and what it doesn't do, and ends with links to the repository docs.
- **Plugin demos.** Each plugin has a live, editable slide at `/plugins/<name>/`, with captioned examples that open in the Playground.
- **A plugin manifest can carry its icon.** The new optional `icon` field holds path data tagged `line`, `accent` or `fill`, and the website's Plugins hub draws it in the active theme's colors, so a plugin's mark keeps its contrast on every palette and can't carry a color or markup of its own (spec/LPM.md §3.1, `lib/plugins/plugin-icon.mjs`). Math, Mermaid, Icons, Avatars, Function plots and Code ship one.

- The Studio's Library has a **Plugins** pill. An imported zip plugin is listed there with what it draws (its fence and `@kind{…}` spans), whether this browser has approved its code, and whether the open deck lists it, with a Remove button. A plugin-only zip opens on the pill, the empty state no longer shows beside an installed plugin, and the status line counts plugins. Plugin cards have no select box and no Share: a plugin's code never leaves the browser.
- The import toast names only what landed ("Imported 1 plugin(s)…"), not "0 theme(s) + 0 component(s) + 1 plugin(s)".
- While a zip imports, an empty Library shelf says "Importing…" instead of "No saved assets yet". A plugin import takes a few seconds on a phone (the sandbox starts), and the empty-shelf message made it look as if the import had failed.

- Live calls get a per-person **High fidelity (music)** toggle in the microphone menu (the arrow beside Mute). It re-captures the microphone with echo cancellation, noise suppression and automatic gain off and sends 128 kbit/s mono instead of 64 kbit/s, for music or a demo. Wear headphones with it on. Stereo is not offered: the transport gives us no way to ask the other side for it.

- Live calls get a per-person volume control: a speaker button on every other person's row, always there, that opens a popover with a 0 to 200 % slider (kept for the session). Above 100 % the voice plays through Suono's new `stage.amplify(stream, gain)` gain stage, for calls that play quiet (an iPhone with its microphone on). Where it cannot act yet, the popover says why (join the call; they are not on it).

- Live calls show each person's call quality in the popover from the speaker button on their row: the bitrate you hear, the share of packets lost and the jitter (*Audio: 64 kbit/s · 0.4 % lost · 18 ms jitter*), plus what you send them. It reads WebRTC stats every 5 s while both of you are on the call, so a choppy call can be told apart as network loss or as the phone.

- Live: **Your settings → Connection → Copy connection log** copies a timeline for bug reports: every connection attempt from its start (ICE state changes, candidates found, STUN/TURN errors), peer joins and leaves, a round-trip sample every 10 seconds, each connection check and its state, your role, and whether the screen wake lock is held. Addresses are never included.

- **Live sessions show how each person is connected.** Each row in the Live panel carries an icon for the connection: same network, direct across networks, or through a relay. The person's ⋯ menu spells the connection out with the raw candidate pair, so a two-device test can be recorded from a phone (`engineering/decisions/2026-10-06-studio-live-collaboration.md` §8.1).
- **A live session keeps going while the host is away.** If the host's connection stays down for about half a minute, the next person who can edit hosts until the host is back. Everyone else rejoins without knocking, chat keeps flowing, and new people can knock again. When the host returns, they take the session back, with the chat and the people let in meanwhile. The host's panel names who stands in. Tavola's wire protocol moves to version 2, so a tab still open from before shows *Reload to join*.
- **Live sessions have audio calls.** *Join with audio* in the Live panel or the header pill sends your microphone to everyone in the session, with echo cancellation and noise suppression. You can mute, pick a microphone, or leave the call. Each person shows their mic and a speaking ring while they talk, and the tab title starts with *On air* while your microphone is live. Audio goes only to people the host let in.

- Live calls get a **Hearing** section in the Your audio popover: one **Everyone** volume (0 to 200 %) multiplied into each person's own, and a **speaker** picker where the browser allows it (not Safari, which says so). The popover now fits the room on a phone-size screen.

- Live calls get a **Your audio** popover on your own row (the arrow beside Join audio or Mute, there before you join too): a live level meter of what you send, so you can see your microphone work with nobody else on the call; the microphone list; a **Mic level** slider (0 to 200 %) that changes how loud you are to everyone else, through Suono's new `stage.gainStream`; and High fidelity as a real toggle switch.

- Live: **Your settings** now starts with **Your name**. Change it after you join and everyone's panel, cursor label and (for the host) the lobby invite follow. The host refuses a name another person already has, so nobody can pass for someone else.

- Live: a **⋯ on your own row** opens **Your settings**, where you choose what others see of you: your cursor, which slide you are on, and when you are typing. Withholding your slide shows "Slide hidden" on your row for everyone else.

- **Added: `logo: lattice`, a built-in mark that works on every surface.** A `logo:`
  path only means something where the deck FILE is — the CLI resolves it against the
