  `.md`, and the web cannot, so a deck carrying `logo: ../lib/base/_logo/…` showed no
  mark in the Playground, none in the Studio, and failed the PDF export outright. The
  built-in name inlines Lattice's own mark, so it paints in the CLI, the Playground,
  the Studio, an exported `.html` opened offline, and on a phone. Your own mark still
  takes a path or a URL — on a web surface it needs one the viewer can fetch. The
  jargon gallery now uses the name, and its rendered pages are unchanged.

- `logo-finish:` styles the deck logo on one line, one word per axis, autocompleted in the editor: a placement (`top-left` … `bottom-right`), a color (`auto`, `accent`, `ink`, `muted`, `canvas`, `inverse`, `brand`, or the blends `accent-ink`, `accent-canvas`, `ink-canvas`), a size (`sm`, `md`, `lg`) and a scope (`all`, `title`). Naming a placement hides the header, footer or page number in that band, since the logo wins. Colors follow light and dark mode. `_class: no-logo` hides the logo on one slide.
- Studio → Chrome → Logo has a Position, Color, Size and Show on control, all writing that one line.

- The Lattice Timing Track spec is published at `/spec/ltt/`, from its new home `spec/LTT-1.0.md`, and the home page has a Specs group listing LFM 1.0, the Diagnostic Protocol and LTT 1.0. LTT's card moved there from the Libraries group; `@laticent/ltt` is named as its reference implementation.

- **The Vetrina page records and replays a tour.** `/vetrina` gains Record, which writes its
  "Point at a thing" beat down as a seekable timing track (`.ltt.json`), and Replay, which plays the
  committed recording back so each stroke lands on the word that names it, as recorded;
  `/vetrina?replay` starts the replay on load. The beat's four strokes now land on their words
  ("rule", "boundary", "swept", "tapped") when it plays live too. A test checks the recording against the page's own storyboard, so an edited line
  is flagged as stale instead of replaying out of step.

- **Video export: `lattice video <narrated-export.html>`** renders a narrated HTML export to an
  MP4 (1920×1080, 30 fps, H.264 video, AAC audio, a caption track) and a `.vtt` sidecar.
  The video is the export's own player, played on a clock the capture controls and captured frame
  by frame, so it shows exactly what the export shows; the audio is mixed from the export's own
  clips at the times the player started each sentence. It needs a Chromium whose WebCodecs encodes
  H.264 (Chrome or Chrome for Testing), and checks before capturing. AAC is encoded by FFmpeg's
  encoder compiled to WebAssembly (`@mediabunny/aac-encoder`) where the browser has none. The
  frame follows the deck's canvas (long side 1920 px), and a failed or interrupted run leaves no
  file behind. It plays in QuickTime and on phones; PowerPoint and Keynote are not yet verified.
- **The exported player gains a render mode** (`window.__lpRender`, set only by the video
  capture), so a narrated HTML export's player script grows by a few hundred bytes; an export
  without narration is byte-identical. A viewer's browser never enters it.
- **`lattice video --help` carries FFmpeg's LGPL-2.1 notice** for the AAC encoder, and the
  license text ships as `assets/licenses/LGPL-2.1-ffmpeg.txt`.

- **Every hand-authored manifest is now checked against its JSON Schema.** All
  five families already shipped a `*.schema.json` beside their manifests, and all
  five already declared `additionalProperties: false` — but nothing in the repo
  ran a JSON-Schema validator, so each family grew its own hand-written checker
  and the three disagreed about how much they checked. `tools/manifest-schemas.js`
  now holds one registry of the families and validates all 131 manifests with
  `ajv` (a devDependency, build-time only; `checkAjvBoundary` gates it out of
  `lib/`, where it would ship to consumers and into browser bundles). It runs inside `check-ownership.js`, which `npm run build:check`
  already invokes in CI and the pre-push hook — no new CI step, no new git hook.
- **The Form model's frames, cells and tiles were never checked at all.** Their
  validators never read their schemas — the enums are hand-copied — so unknown
  keys passed silently across 37 files. Renaming the optional `slicing` block on
  the `standard` frame to `slicng`, a one-letter typo that deletes the frame's
  whole responsive behavior, returned zero errors from every checker in the repo.
  It now fails the build.
- **Three component manifests carried undeclared fields two levels down**, where
  the component validator does not look: `adapt.capacity.axisRetired` on
  `matrix-2x2` and `split-compare`, and `adapt.capacity.wide.note` on `kpi`. Both
  fields are legitimate and are now declared. `axisRetired` is a tombstone whose
  point is the *absence* of `axis` — `splitFactsFor` reads that key as a split
  opt-in, so restoring it re-enrolls a component in a per-item split its own
  design resolution forbids. `note` is the per-family counterpart of the flat
  `capacity.note` and already ships into `dist/docs/components.json`.
- **The gate also catches a typo'd keyword inside a schema file** (`patttern`),
  a manifest belonging to no registered family, and a `$schema` link resolving to
  another family's contract — the link editors follow for inline completion.
- `themes/theme.schema.json` moved from JSON Schema draft-07 to 2020-12, matching
  the other four schemas.
- **The gate closed a hole of its own kind in `slots`.** `slots.<name>` accepted
  any key, leaving 180 nested paths unchecked — and `slot.required`, which 61
  manifests set, drives the "required" column of every generated Agent contract.
  A `requird` typo silently flipped it. Now closed; all 180 slots already used
  only the three declared keys.
- **The sweep no longer walks dot-directories**, so a `.claude/worktrees/`
  checkout (reserved in `.gitignore`) stops failing `build:check` with a bogus
  error per manifest. It also skips `_`-prefixed directories, matching the two
  runtime loaders, which treat a parked `_draft/` as outside the catalog.
- The swept filename set is derived from the family registry rather than
  hardcoded, one schema typo now reports one error instead of 62, and a missing
  or absolute `$schema` is caught rather than exempted.
- The sweep skips `node_modules` and `dist` at **any** depth, not just the repo
  root — `docs/` is its own npm package, so a root-anchored skip walked 4,193
  third-party directories and would have failed the build on the next dependency
  shipping a bare `manifest.json`. Dot-directories are skipped at the root only,
  because `loadAll` does not skip a nested one and doing so hid a component the
  engine really loads. The flat theme family applies no `_` filter, matching
  `listThemeManifests`.
- `checkAjvBoundary` covers the whole ajv package family (`ajv-formats`,
  `ajv-keywords` are the same devDependency leak), dedupes per file, and now has
  tests that watch it fail.
- **The `if`-error filter can no longer swallow a manifest's last error.** Dropping
  ajv's bare `must match "then" schema` line risked the gate's worst outcome — a
  manifest that failed validation and reported nothing, indistinguishable from one
  that passed. A fallback now fires if every error was filtered, naming it a gate
  defect and carrying the raw ajv text.

- The Export-to-Marp folder now opens as a ready VS Code project. VS Code offers to install Marp for VS Code when the folder opens, and **Terminal → Run Task…** lists *Marp: export PDF*, *PowerPoint* and *HTML*, each running `npm install` first, which downloads marp-cli the first time. `npm run pptx` joins `npm run pdf` and `npm run html`.
- The folder's README is rewritten as two step-by-step quick starts, one for VS Code and one for the command line, plus a troubleshooting table. Every step and every quoted prompt was checked on VS Code 1.142.0 with Marp for VS Code 3.6.1 and on marp-cli 4.5.1. It now says plainly that scripts need VS Code's *Disable* preview level, that a PowerPoint export is one picture per slide, that an HTML export needs the folder beside it, and that Marp picks the export format from the file name.
- The Export-to-Marp README no longer says Mermaid diagrams render as a code block in Marp. The bundled runtime draws them, and the fidelity ledger now says so.

- **The copy-and-go Marp kit is published to the orphan `dist-kits` branch**, under `marp/`, so it is browsable and raw-fetchable straight from the repo again — the surface lost when `dist/` stopped being committed to `main`. npm install and the GitHub Release zip already carried it; this restores the third.

- A `@video{…}` record (or its short form `>{…}`) now draws in a deck written in Marp, the copy-and-go kit's or a record typed into an Export-to-Marp bundle: the same poster figure and `video` card Lattice draws, in `marp --pdf`, in a `marp --html` file, and in the VS Code preview at the *Disable* security level. It used to print as a line of code. The address comes only from your Markdown (marp-cli reads it as it parses; VS Code reads the saved file), so a record you have just typed in VS Code draws when you save.
- The kit and the Export-to-Marp bundle state the Marp versions they work with: marp-cli 4.x (marp-core 4.x) and Marp for VS Code 3.x. Lattice's CI now renders every Marp suite on the oldest of that range (marp-cli 4.0.0 with marp-core 4.0.0) on every change and on the newest 4.x every night, and both READMEs print a line generated from the same record. The bundle's `package.json` asks for `^4.0.0`.
- On a Marp slide whose Lattice stylesheet did not register, the runtime now says so once in the console, with the fix, instead of leaving plain-text slides and no message.
- The kit README says what its settings allow (raw HTML, local files, and the VS Code preview at *Disable*), and that they apply to every deck in the folder.
- The kit's readable `lattice-runtime.js` no longer carries its 8.5 MB DevTools source map (the file drops from 11 MB to 2.7 MB), and NOTICE.md names the repository the kit's engine files are built from.
- The kit's sample deck states the current layout count (80) and what a render loads (13 MB), and a test now holds both to the catalog and the build. Its "what renders where" slide marks charts and diagrams in the VS Code preview as working once the preview runs scripts, which is what a real VS Code shows.
- Typing in the VS Code preview no longer blanks a diagram or leaves a chart unbuilt on every keystroke: the runtime now lays the slides out in the same task as the preview's re-render, so Mermaid finds its cached drawing (0 frames with a missing diagram or chart, from 25 and 34, typing on those slides in a real VS Code).
- Typing in the VS Code preview of a kit deck or an Export-to-Marp bundle is about four times faster: a keystroke shows in ~0.3 s instead of ~1.0 s (p50, typing on a diagram or chart slide in a real VS Code). Marp for VS Code used to re-process Lattice's 1.1 MB stylesheet on every keystroke; VS Code now registers only each theme's name and sizes, and the deck links the stylesheet, packed once when Lattice is built. Slides look exactly as before, pixel for pixel, on every Marp for VS Code 3.x release (3.0.0 to 3.6.1), and a deck's own CSS (a `<style>` block or `style:`) still beats Lattice's there, as it does in marp-cli. Keep the deck's last lines: the `<link rel="stylesheet" …>` line is what styles the preview. A bundle carrying a Studio library theme works as before.
- A Mermaid diagram no longer lays out with the fallback font's widths when the deck's font arrives late: the diagram now waits for the body font (at most 1.5 s) before it measures.
- Typing inside a Mermaid diagram's source in the VS Code preview no longer blanks the diagram on every keystroke: the previous drawing stays until the new one is drawn (0 frames with an empty slot across 22 keystrokes, from 67 to 76).
- The Marp kit and every Export-to-Marp bundle now carry VS Code completions for all 80 layouts: in the deck, type `lattice-` and press Ctrl+Space, pick a layout, and VS Code writes its slide skeleton. The six layout snippets whose skeletons hold a dollar sign (`math`, `kpi`, `pricing`, `stats`, `tower`, `ep-curve`) used to insert mangled (`$2.4B` became `.4B`, `$0` vanished); they now insert exactly as written, and the snippets apply to Markdown files only.

- **`npm run merge:order` finds digest PRs that conflict with each other and lands the smaller of each pair first.** It checks every pair of ready PRs for conflicts the way GitHub merges (in memory, merge drivers ignored), holds back any PR that already conflicts with `main`, and orders the rest: a PR built on another's branch after it, the smaller of two conflicting PRs first (the other rebases after it lands), otherwise oldest first, with the reason on each row. Every PR lands in exactly one list: ordered, held (it or the PR it is built on conflicts with `main`), or unordered (a dependency cycle). It checks pairs only, so a conflict that needs three PRs together, or a later change to `main`, is still the queue's to catch. `/desk-merge` step 3 now uses it. On its first run against nine real ready PRs it found two that conflict with each other (#3351 and #3361) and one that conflicts with `main` (#3345).

- **Mermaid diagrams now animate under `motion:`, like charts.** A deck with `motion: on` (or a slide with `motion-on`) builds each diagram in: subgraph boxes first, then nodes, then the arrows between them, then the words. `motion-style` and `motion-speed` apply, `motion-off` opts a slide out, and a viewer who asks the OS to reduce motion sees the diagram settled. It runs in the Playground, the Studio, Present and the exported HTML player. Twelve families are mapped (flowchart, state, class, ER, mindmap, sequence, pie, gantt, XY chart, quadrant, git graph, timeline); any other family, a diagram with clickable nodes, and a very large diagram (past ~65 nodes) stay still pictures. The PDF is unchanged.

- **Added: the Mosaico demo page shows more than the two strategies.** Five one-click sets show
  what each strategy does, including one where the search takes margin rather than shrink a box to a
  sliver. The live CSS grid that `toGrid()` returns for the current layout, a speed test that runs
  in the reader's browser, Lattice's two layouts before and after, and a comparison with diorama and
  justified-layout follow. The page and the Learn page now say what the `tree` search keeps: the
  least empty space and crop, with a penalty on boxes that shrink to slivers, not simply the least
  empty space. The README's CSS recipe now scales the `fr` tracks by 1000, because row tracks sum
  below 1 and a grid with `fr` factors under 1 leaves part of its height empty.

- **Added: Mosaico takes padding, separate column and row gaps, alignment, and pixel sizes.**
  `pack()` accepts `padding` (one length or one per side), `columnGap` and `rowGap` for both
  strategies, and `align` (`start`, `center`, `end`; `rows` also `justify`, with `lastRow`). Give
  the container a `width` and `height` and every length is read in that unit, so a 16 px gutter
  is `gap: 16` whatever the strategy. Each result now carries `frame`, where the layout sits in the
  container, and `placed`, one box per item ready to draw; a `tree` layout that is too wide for its
  box keeps every gutter exact as it shrinks, and so does `fit: 'fill'`. Lattice's collage and logo
  wall lay out exactly as before. Two edges move for other callers: `toGrid` on a `rows` result now
  uses `rowGap` for the row tracks, and a `tree` arrangement whose gutters span the whole box
  yields to the next one that has room; when none has (gutters about as tall as the box), `pack`
  refuses with `no-valid-layout`. The demo page gains sliders for gap
  and padding and a control for alignment.

- **A narrated deck can open with a greeting and end with a closing.** Set `greeting:` and `closing:` in front matter, as `true` or custom text. `{greeting}` in the text becomes "Good morning", "Good afternoon" or "Good evening" from the listener's own clock (04:00, 12:00 and 17:00 boundaries, never "good night"). The greeting plays before slide 1 when narration starts there. The closing plays after the last slide when narration reaches the end by itself, including autoplay onto a silent "Thank you" slide. Each plays at most once, and pausing or going back never repeats it. Both work in the Studio's Present view and in an exported player, which carries all three greetings and picks one when Play is pressed. A video export and a downloaded `.vtt` say "Hello", because they have no listener clock. A line the deck already says is not repeated: when slide 1 already opens with a greeting ("Welcome…", "Good morning…"), the greeting is skipped, and when the last slide already says "thank you", the closing is skipped. The linter warns about a greeting that hard-codes the time of day (`greeting-hardcoded-period`), a `{…}` that would be read aloud (`unknown-bookend-placeholder`), and an English salutation in a non-English deck (`greeting-not-english`).
- **The timing track (LTT) gains an optional `bookends` section** beside `segments`, holding the greeting's four variants and the closing, each laid out like a narrated slide. `timeline()` takes a `greeting` variant and returns `greeting` and `closing` entries, with `segments[i]` still slide i + 1. An export's audio blocks for them are keyed by name (`greeting-morning` … `closing`).

- **Added: charts are now explained, not just read.** A chart whose substance lives
  in an `<svg>` used to reach the caption voice as a list of labelled numbers with
  nothing saying what they measured. Every picture-bound chart now opens with what
  its encoding means — *"each bar's length is its value, measured from zero"* —
  declared in the component's own manifest (`projection.frame`), so a chart added
  later is covered the day its manifest lands.
- **Added: `bullet` narration names the measure, the target and the attainment
  between them.** It read *"New ARR, four point two million, five million"* — two
  numbers in authored order, with nothing saying which was the plan. It now reads
  *"New ARR, four point two million against a five million target — eighty-four
  percent of plan, closing on plan"*, counts how many rows cleared the line, and
  measures attainment **from the row's floor**, so a 99.4% uptime against a 99.9%
  target on a 99.0% floor is spoken as 44% of the way to plan rather than 99%.
- **Added: `word-cloud` narration reads rank instead of reciting counts.** The
  component's docs say the rank matters more than the count and that it is not a
  precise data viz; narration recited every weight anyway, twenty numbers deep on a
  large cloud. It now names the encoding, the biggest term and its margin, the tiers
  under it and the quiet tail — enumerating only clouds small enough to hold, and
  naming the remainder on the rest so nothing is silently dropped. It states no TERM
  COUNT, deliberately: the packer drops a word it cannot seat, so a source list and
  the drawn canvas can disagree (2 of the 34 word-cloud slides in this repo), and
  narration runs on markdown before any render.
- **Added: `state-chart` narration opens with the machine's shape.** Every edge was
  read in authored order and the topology was not, so a listener rebuilt the graph
  from a serial list. Slides now open with the size, the endpoints, where the machine
  decides, what steps back and what loops — plus three hazards no surface named
  before: a state whose only exit is a self-loop, a state nothing leads to, and a
  state that stops without being marked an ending.
- **Fixed: a `bullet` row's `Band` and `Floor` bullets are no longer read aloud as
  prose.** They are structural inputs to the chart's zones; the caption track spoke
  them as content at the end of the slide.
- **Fixed: the same number now narrates the same way however it was typed.** `900k`
  and `0.9M` both read as *"nine hundred thousand"*; `1.2M` and `1200k` both as *"one
  point two million"* — narration was reading the author's spelling rather than the
  value, so two decks carrying identical data narrated differently and `1200k` came
  out as *"one thousand two hundred thousand"*.
- **Fixed: a European-spreadsheet paste no longer narrates a hundred times too big.**
  `1,25M` read as *"one hundred twenty-five million"* over a chart correctly drawing
  1.25M — the voice took the decimal comma for a thousands separator where the chart's
  parser did not. A bare number is deliberately left alone, so `Closed \`2024\`` still
  reads as a year.
- **Fixed: a state chart's shape no longer arrives as one thirteen-second breath.** The
  machine-shape sentence joined every clause with a semicolon, and since one sentence
  becomes one caption cue — and one TTS clip — the hazards slide produced a 39-word
  utterance a listener cannot scrub back into. It is two sentences now: longest cue
  13.2s → 10.1s, p90 7.6s → 6.9s.
- **Fixed: a `bullet` chart's spoken tally no longer contradicts the chart.** A row
  whose key is written as a code span (`- \`Target\` \`80%\``) was invisible to
  narration and fully scored by the chart, and one with a note nested under it was
  the reverse — so the caption said "none cleared its target" over a chart drawing a
  cleared bar. Measured over 400 generated decks: 91 of 356 that spoke a tally spoke
  one the render contradicts, now 0 of 351.
- **Fixed: a `bullet` row that CLEARED its target no longer swallows its `Band`
  lines.** Narration absorbs them so they are not read back as prose, and the clause
  that voices them sat below the cleared branch — so on a cleared row they reached no
  surface at all.
- **Fixed: a rounded attainment no longer argues with its verdict.** 99.1 against a
  99.5 target is 99.6%, which rounds to "one hundred percent of plan" on a row that
  MISSED. It reads "just short of plan" now, and "just above plan" on the mirror case.
- **Fixed: a heading carrying any two numbers no longer deletes the tally.** "Three
  pilots, five weeks in." reports nothing and suppressed the one summary fact a
  five-row chart has. The tally SHAPE (*"two of five…"*) is what states it; anything
  else needs a verb, and `over target` and `against plan` join that list. A trailing
  prose bullet did the same and no longer does.
- **Fixed: a `state-chart` no longer claims a route to a state it cannot reach.** "A
  three-state machine from Draft to Draft and Filed. … Nothing leads to Filed" asserted
  a route and denied it two sentences later. Endpoints are now the terminals the start
  can actually get to.
- **Added: a `state-chart` names an ISLAND — states that point at each other and that
  the machine can never get to.** Nothing found those before; an in-degree test cannot,
  because each of them has an edge pointing at it. It is a separate sentence from
  *"nothing leads to X"* on purpose: on an island the picture draws the arrow that
  would refute that one.
- **Fixed: `$-0.8M` and `0.5k` are spoken.** The first rebuilt as the literal
  `-$-800k` and reached the voice as glyphs; the second read as *"zero point five
  thousand"* rather than *"five hundred"*. **One spelling changes in a way worth
  knowing:** `$−0.8M`, with a Unicode minus *behind* the currency symbol, used to
  reach the voice as unreadable glyphs and now reads *"eight hundred thousand
  dollars"* — positive. That is what the chart plots for that pill (`parseValue`
  reads a U+2212 in front of the symbol and not behind it), so the voice and the bar
  agree; the parser asymmetry itself is tracked as #2287.
- **Fixed: a `bullet` row whose nested structure cannot be read from the Markdown is
  no longer narrated at all — and its line is read aloud verbatim instead.** A tab, a
  marker gap wider than one space, a one-space indent, an indent four columns past
  its parent, or prose after a blank line each make markdown-it nest differently from
  anything a line scanner can compute — and narration runs on Markdown, before any
  render. The rule is one rule: if the structure cannot be proved, the row is not
  narrated and its line is left for the flattener, so the listener loses the SENTENCE
  and not the numbers. The slide speaks no tally either way.
  Earlier drafts of this refused only what a row's children could have changed, and
  kept the row's own pills. That was never safe: the measure is exactly as derived as
  the target, because a child `Actual` overrides the row's own first pill and a
  malformed row line voids it. What settled it was changing the ORACLE — comparing
  narration's measure, target, floor and bands against `parseBullet`, the transform's
  own reader, rather than against the SVG `<desc>` that every earlier check went
  through. On the decks in this repo the refusal costs exactly zero: 501 of 3,734
  sections narrate, and not one reads differently than before.
- **Fixed: a `bullet` or `word-cloud` slide whose list is not the one the picture is
  built from no longer speaks a claim about the whole chart.** Every chart in the
  family is drawn from ONE list. Five things end it or replace it, and narration read
  straight through all five: a note paragraph between rows, a fenced code block, a
  change of bullet character, a list sitting ABOVE the data, and a marker indented one
  to three spaces — which CommonMark makes a top-level item the chart draws and scores
  while a column-0 scan cannot see it at all. Each gave a wrong whole-chart claim on
  the real export — *"one of three cleared the plan line"* over a two-bar chart,
  *"none cleared its target"* over a chart whose first row cleared at 125%, *"all two
  cleared their target"* over a five-row chart, plan-line readings for two rows over a
  chart drawing ONE bar, and a word cloud announcing the wrong biggest term. Narration
  stops where the list does, tells its callers the row set may be a prefix, and stands
  the tally down; every line past the boundary is read aloud verbatim, so the listener
  loses the summary sentence and none of the numbers.
- **Fixed: a `state-chart` no longer says a state "stops without being marked an
  ending" over a slide that draws it into the finish marker.** It reads *"nothing
  leads out of X"* — true of both rules the chart uses to decide that. A state
  stranded on both sides gets one clause rather than two, and a state whose only
  inbound arrow is its own self-loop is no longer told that nothing leads to it.

- Narration can now spend time on what matters. Cadenza's `buildTrack` takes an optional `emphasis` map — `[{start, end, weight}]` char ranges over the narration text — and a cue where an emphasized passage ENDS holds a beat afterwards, so a deck's key claim no longer gets exactly the same pacing as a footnote. The hold sits in the gap between cues, the one place both playback paths already insert real silence. An unweighted deck is timed byte-for-byte as before.

- **Added: every picture-bound chart reads its numbers aloud.** A bar chart used to say
  "Revenue · FY26. Growth is concentrated in two regions." and stop — the four regions and
  their four values never reached the voice, because the speech walker skips the `<svg>`
  they live in and only six hand-written narrators existed to replace it. A generic
  data-series narrator now covers every component whose manifest declares `data: true` and
  an `svg`/`spatial` figure, in three list shapes plus a markdown table. Measured with
  `node tools/measure-narration-coverage.mjs`, real CLI and real `--captions`: mean coverage
  0.674 → 0.839 across 71 components, with `line` 0.09 → 1.19, `map` 0.12 → 1.25, `slope`
  0.14 → 1.19, `piechart` 0.16 → 1.03, `word-cloud` 0.16 → 0.88, `stacked-bar` 0.19 → 1.14,
  `heatmap` 0.22 → 1.26, `waterfall` 0.23 → 1.38, `bullet` 0.26 → 1.47, `bar` 0.28 → 1.33
  and `scatter` 0.35 → 1.83. No component regressed.
- It computes nothing and claims nothing. A `scatter` row binds each value to the axis the
  eyebrow names; a `bullet` row's two pills read in authored order, because nothing in the
  Markdown says which is the measure and which the target. The roster is derived from each
  manifest's own `projection` block, so a new SVG chart is covered the day it declares
  itself.

- **Added: `lint:deck` says which tokens will read as glyphs.** A slash means a ratio, a
  rate, a date or an alternative, and nothing in `A/B`, `24/7`, `P/E`, `16:9` or `ID-4471`
  says which — so the normalizer deliberately has no rule, and guessing would make the voice
  state a fact the slide does not show. The deck lint now names each such token and shows the
  `lexicon:` line that fixes it, beside the acronym hint that already worked this way.
  Advisory, never blocking, and it goes quiet as soon as the author answers it. 56 distinct
  tokens across 35 of the 186 shipped decks.
- **Added: `tools/measure-token-narration.mjs`.** The boardroom token corpus the
  2026-09-20 narration audit's "19 raw of 52 → 9 of 59" came from was a scratch script, so
  neither number could be re-derived. It is committed now, grouped by the class that audit's
  own table names, and it separates deliberate passthroughs from gaps: 11 of 66 raw, 8
  deliberate, 3 unhandled.

- **New lint rule** `nested-render-target-key` — the deck linter warns when `fluid:`,
  `player:` or `present:` is written indented. The export reads an indented key as the
  deck's own register, so a nested `fluid: "true"` ships the fluid viewer even when a
  top-level `fluid: false` says no. The warning names what the export does and points at
  the line; it reports only lines a reader arm really reads, so it never claims the export
  acts on a line it ignores.
- The fix text names an escape that keeps a legitimate nested entry. `lexicon:` and
  `acronyms:` take arbitrary word keys, and `present` is a word an author might well teach a
  deck to pronounce — quoting the key (`"present": pre ZENT`) is the same mapping to YAML
  and stops the export reading it as the register. The rule carries no autofix: de-indenting
  the key, quoting it and deleting it are all plausible, and the source does not say which
  was meant.
- The reader is unchanged, deliberately. Narrowing it to read only column-0 keys would turn
  off decks in the field — six measured input shapes read as on today and would stop — so
  the kernel keeps believing an indented key and the author gets told instead
  (`lib/core/render-target-keys.js`).
- The Studio editor anchors a warning to the line a finding quoted VERBATIM, indentation
  included, before falling back to a trimmed match. Without it a nested `fluid: true` on a
  deck that also carries a top-level `fluid: true` underlined the innocent top-level line
  while the message said it was indented.

- In an editable PowerPoint or ODP, an icon's name (its `label=`, or the icon's own) is now the icon shape's description, so PowerPoint's Alt Text and a screen reader name it.

- An editable PowerPoint or LibreOffice file draws each icon as a native outline shape, so apps that ignore the file's fonts, such as Google Slides and iPhone Preview, draw the icons too, not only desktop PowerPoint. Each recolors as a shape.

- Nine new skills for work on a deck you already have: `edit-deck`, `restyle-deck`, `fix-findings`, `chart-from-data`, `diagram`, `math`, `import`, `accessibility-review` and `studio`. The Studio chat offers every one except `import`, and Claude Code and the agent kit get all nine through the skill index.

- **Added: `lattice packages list | add | check | export | remove`.** Install a theme or
  component exported from the Studio with `lattice packages add <file>.zip`, and every
  deck that names it renders from the CLI. Finishes and motions install and export too,
  but the CLI doesn't render them by name yet. Packages live in
  `~/.lattice/packages`, or `$LATTICE_HOME/packages`, or the folder `--packages <dir>`
  names for one run. `add` runs the Studio's import checks, so CSS that loads from
  the network is refused by name. A component that carries JavaScript installs only in
  the one form a code package takes, and runs only after you approve its code.
- **Changed: a deck naming a theme Lattice doesn't have fails with that name.** The
  error prints the `lattice packages add` command that fixes it.
- **Added: a `.lattice` project carries the saved theme, components and finishes the
  deck uses.** Opening it on another machine adds them to that Library through the
  same checks as a `.zip` import.
- **Changed: `jszip` is a declared runtime dependency.** The CLI reads and writes zips
  at run time. It used to arrive only through `pptxgenjs`'s own dependency, which a
  strict installer such as pnpm does not expose to Lattice.

- **Shipped motion library.** Lattice now ships four motion scenes as packages in
  `lib/motion/<name>/`: `rotor`, `pipeline-beats`, `arrivals` and `ring-marker`.
  `lattice packages list --type motion` lists them, `lattice packages export motion/<name>`
  zips one, and the Studio's Library lists them on its Motion tab under "Shipped with
  Lattice", where Insert places one in the deck like a saved scene.
- **Theme manifests take `type` and `format`.** `themes/theme.schema.json` accepts
  `"type": "theme"` and `"format": 1`, and every shipped theme manifest carries both, so a
  theme exported from the Studio or the CLI is a valid `themes/` manifest as written.
- **Library motion thumbnails draw every stroke.** A motion card in the Studio's Library
  dropped each stroke painted from the categorical ramp (`--cat-N-mark`), because the
  Studio page does not define it; the cards now use the Motion faculty's fallback ramp.
- **A palette a bundler can import.** Each shipped theme now also publishes as
  `@laticent/lattice/palette/<name>.css`: its tokens with every `@import` resolved, dark
  variants carrying their base. It imports cleanly in Vite and webpack, where the theme file
  fails (`ENOENT: open 'lattice'`), because its `@import 'lattice'` is a Marp theme
  reference, not a file. A palette is for tokens, not for showing slides: to render slides in
  a web page, use `render()` from `@laticent/lattice/engine`, which matched the CLI's render
  pixel for pixel. The themes guide has the recipe.
- **The docs no longer promise that a stylesheet pair renders slides.** The README called
  `dist/lattice-default.css` "browser-droppable" and its browser embed linked the engine and
  a theme. Neither sizes the slide, and a `dark` slide keeps the light canvas. The README and
  the themes guide now point to the engine for slides, and the README no longer says the
  runtime fetches a Mermaid section from the palette file (it reads tokens from the slide).

- **Added: the package spine (`lib/packages/`).** One shape for themes, components,
  finishes and motion: a folder named for the item, a `<name>.manifest.json` that
  owns the name, and role files named `<name>.<role>`. The build now discovers
  themes and components through it, writes one generated index
  (`lib/packages/packages.generated.json`), and fails when a package's folder or
  file names disagree with its manifest — for every kind, not only themes. Component
  manifests may now carry `"type": "component"` and `"format": 1`.

- **New gate:** rendered-DOM contrast is now measured on **every shipped palette**, not just `indaco`. `tools/palette-sweep.js` renders a deck once and re-themes it in place, so all 32 palettes are probed in ~2 minutes instead of the ~7 that re-rendering the matrix costs. Verified against native renders of all 32: the sweep and a real render agree palette for palette.
- **New nightly referee:** `tools/palette-native.js` re-renders every palette for real and reconciles against the fast sweep, so the per-PR gate cannot drift back into measuring something the engine does not paint. It also scores the runs the sweep drops by construction (Mermaid bakes its own stylesheet into the SVG at render time, and no palette swap can move it).
- **Fixed:** `mustard`'s `--accent` was ink on both plain canvases at 4.35:1 and 3.89:1 against a 4.5 floor — 79 sub-threshold runs across fourteen component classes (glossary terms, stats figures, every leading-zero list counter, `big-number`, the `cards-grid` / `compare-table` stars, `cycle`'s chevrons, `timeline-list`, `split-compare`). Deepened `#8C6A18` → `#7B5D15` (5.31:1 / 4.75:1).
- **Fixed:** the `journey` mood legend's numeric keys (1–5) carried an `opacity: 0.85` wash over `--text-secondary` — 35 sub-threshold runs on seven palettes, worst 3.72:1. The wash is gone, matching the `PAIN` / `DELIGHT` labels beside them, which had theirs removed for the same reason.
- **New checks:** `tools/contrast-audit.js` now scores `--accent` **as ink** on `--bg` and `--bg-alt`. It was scored on `accent-soft` and as a backdrop under `--on-accent`, but never as the foreground it most often is — the same shape of hole as the `--text-muted` one, and the reason a palette-wide defect read as clean.
- **Fixed:** the contrast probe scored the CSS source inside an SVG-scoped `<style>` element as if it were visible text, so a Mermaid diagram's own stylesheet was reported as a 1.17:1 contrast offender.

- The Studio's Compose editor edits a `columns` / `rows` slide's panes. Each pane opens with a
  bar that names its place ("Left pane 60%") and what it holds. "Change" opens the slide gallery,
  showing only the components that fit that pane, and each tile says what picking it does: "Keeps
  your text", or "Starts with an example", which swaps the pane's body for the component's starter
  and offers Undo. The pane's `###` title reads as a labeled field, and a pane with no title gets
  an "Add title" button.

- **Panes (experimental — the syntax may change)** — put two components' body content on one slide, side by side or stacked, under the slide's one title and chrome. Mark each body with `<!-- pane: <component> -->`; set the split with `<!-- panes: 40/60 -->` (25–75 in 5% steps) or `<!-- panes: stack 35/65 -->`. The Key Insight, below-note, header, footer and page number stay the slide's. Decks without pane markers render byte-identical markup. Demo: `examples/panes.md`.
- Panes carry a **spine** between them — the accent rule that separates a chart from its key — vertical side by side, horizontal when stacked. Add `no-rule` to the `panes:` marker to drop it.
- Every component declares how it behaves in a pane — a `pane` field in its manifest, also in `dist/docs/components.json`: the least share it reads at side by side (`side`) and stacked (`stack`), measured with the new `tools/measure-pane-fit.js` and reviewed; a pane `form` (`image` renders as `content`); and a pane **budget**, measured with `tools/calibrate-capacity.js --pane` where it can be, judged and explained where it cannot.
- A pairing that does not fit is never drawn: when both panes fit the other direction the slide re-orients (side by side to stacked, or the reverse), and otherwise it splits into one slide per pane. `lint:deck` says which (`pane-arrange`), and checks each pane before you render: `pane-overflow` and `pane-crowd` (past the pane's budget, counted per pane). A panes slide's bullet ceiling in `wall-of-text` is now per pane.
- A chart in a pane lays out at the pane's size: bar values and axis ticks print at the size a chart slide prints them, and the plot gives way instead. A pie, map or quadrant key prints larger where the pane has room. Radar and Mermaid still scale into the pane.
- The Studio's editor shows the pane warnings as you type, the same ones `lint:deck` prints.
- The `cards:` register (`top`, `center`, `stretch`, `spread`) and a slide's `_class: cards-*` reach a card row or list in a pane, as they reach a slide.
- On a square, portrait, story or mobile deck, a panes slide splits into one slide per pane — each an ordinary slide of its component under the same title — because those sizes set type too large for two components to share a frame.
- A speaker note written between a chart's title and its data now reaches the export's notes; chart slides used to drop it.

- **Added: the Studio's exported PDF now carries its text.** Every page was a
  picture of a slide, so Cmd-F found nothing, a cursor selected nothing, and a
  screen reader was handed blank pages. The export now measures each word in the
  capture frame and writes it over the page image in PDF text rendering mode 3 —
  invisible ink, the same mechanism OCR output uses. `pdftotext` on a real
  18-page export returns 1,214 words in reading order, and the picture is
  untouched: the image streams are byte-identical page for page and the
  rasterized pages match at AE = 0. The file grows 0.7%.

- **The Coach's photo-contrast finding offers the card ink when no pin clears.** When neither pinning the slide dark nor light lifts the text on a photo to 4.5:1 (the theme's muted body ink can stay under it on both), the finding now offers **Set card ink light** (or **dark**) if that ink clears the floor, measured in the live preview like the pin. A pin is still offered first whenever one clears. When nothing clears, the message says so and suggests a stronger card backing or another photo.

- **The Studio Coach warns when text on a photo will not read.** With the Coach open, the slide on screen is measured in the live preview: the photo behind the card, the card's fill over it, and the ink on top. A spotlight or statement slide whose text falls below 4.5:1 gets a `photo-contrast` finding, for example dark ink on a dark photo under a thin card. When pinning the slide dark or light would clear the floor, the finding carries a **Pin this slide dark** (or **light**) button that writes the class. Nothing flips on its own, a pin that would not clear 4.5:1 is not offered, and a photo the browser cannot read (a cross-origin image) gets no warning rather than a guess. The finding is outside the deck's Craft and Style grade. The arithmetic is `lib/core/photo-contrast.mjs`, built on the same contrast function as `thin-card-no-ink`.
- **The `thin-card-no-ink` tooltip has a fix button that picks the ink from the photo.** Hovering the warning on a thin spotlight card with no ink now offers the one ink that reads (**Add ink-light** over a dark photo, **Add ink-dark** over a light one), It never offers both. The warning appears at once; the photo is checked when you open it (a **Checking the photo…** note shows meanwhile), from the live preview when it shows that slide and from the photo file otherwise. The answer is kept in the browser, so it survives a reload and is not worked out again. When neither ink reads (a mid-gray photo under a clear card) or the photo cannot be read (a relative path, a cross-origin image), the tooltip says so and offers **Use a solid card** instead, which always reads.
- **On a phone, the Source tab's live preview now follows the caret to another slide.** It draws once per slide crossing (never per keystroke), so the editor's tooltips can read the photo on the slide you are editing. `DeckPreview` has a new `followWhenParked` option, off by default.

- **The Coach's photo-contrast check now covers statement slides.** A statement's white words sit on a scrim; with `card-clear` the scrim is gone and the words can vanish on a bright photo. The Coach now flags that slide and offers **Set card ink dark** when the dark ink clears 4.5:1. It judges a statement against its scrim at its strongest, so a statement the scrim already rescues is never flagged, and when a partial scrim is on it says the text reads "at most" the ratio shown.
- **Fixed: the Studio editor's "spark too big" warning now shows when the slide comes into view, not on the next keystroke.** The editor re-ran its lint pass on a new preview measurement with `forceLinting`, which does nothing to an idle linter. It now dispatches its own re-lint effect.
- **Fixed: a one-click edit to the slide on screen no longer sends the preview to the last slide.** A Slide-panel row or a Coach fix rewrote the whole deck and dropped its final newline, which moved the editor's caret to the end. The edit now changes only that slide.
- **The editor and the Coach now give one answer about text on a photo.** Both show the same message and the same fix button, read once from the slide on screen. A statement the Coach flags is also underlined in the editor, with the same fix. On a thin card, the fix both views offer is the card ink that reads (or a solid card), because a pin would leave the editor's thin-card warning standing. The tooltip's button now reads **Set card ink light** (it said **Add ink-light**). A Coach warning no longer lingers for a moment after you move to another slide.
- **Fixed: an editor photo tooltip opened before the photo was measured now takes the Coach's words and fix when the measurement lands,** instead of keeping an estimate while it stays open.

- Adding photos to the Library now asks how to store them, with the size each choice would make for your own photos and what it means: Keep original (no resize, location removed), JPEG, WebP (about a third smaller than JPEG) or PNG (lossless, several times larger for photographs). Your last choice is remembered.

- **The docs site documents pills.** A new **Guides → Pills and marks** page covers
  all three routes to a pill in one place: the universal `{LABEL}` brace grammar
  (eight shapes, twelve ordinal color slots, two sizes, the escape and the
  `inline-code: literal` off switch), the trailing-inline-code metadata pill, and the
  chart components' ten-word status vocabulary. It carries three live labs, so a
  reader edits real deck source and watches the pills redraw rather than reading a
  table of modifier names. Until now the grammar was documented only in
  `lib/base/base.docs.md`, which is the agent reference — an author working from the
  site had no way to discover that `` `{STABLE}:c2` `` draws anything.
- **The page states two limits the reference glossed over.** The status vocabulary is
  not reachable from the brace grammar — a `{LABEL}` pill can take any of twelve
  categorical slots but cannot say "this is failing" — and date pills are positional
  per-component conventions, never parsed, so a `timeline-list` leading chip renders
  whatever you put in it.
- **Fixed: two components documented a status vocabulary narrower than the one they
  accept.** `timeline-list.docs.md` listed seven of the shared ten (missing `warn`,
  `fail`, `pilot`) and `progress.docs.md` listed eight (missing `pilot`, `decision`),
  against the frozen `CHART_STATUS` in
  `lib/components/chart/_chart-family/transform-utils.js`. Both also claimed an
  unrecognized word "renders as a plain pill"; it renders a pill tinted with the
  default info hue, so a typo reads as a deliberate blue verdict rather than as a
  mistake. Both now name all ten, say the matching is case- and hyphen-exact, and say
  what an unknown word actually does.

- **Warm harness for the macOS and Windows platform suites.** Dispatch `platform-suites.yml` with `harness=<PR number>` and one runner installs and builds once, then runs `/harness` commands posted on that pull request (a suite, a shell block, a re-run), syncing each new push and replying with the result. Only the person who dispatched it can post commands, and an edited comment never runs; with watch on, a push to the branch re-runs the last job. One harness runs per OS, so a macOS and a Windows harness can serve the same PR: every reply names its OS, and `--on=<os>` sends a command to one of them. An iOS round no longer pays about 17 minutes of queue wait and setup each time (`tools/platform-harness.js`, `engineering/development.md` §Platform suites).

- **Added: `--player-consent <origins>` lets a reader choose to load a player's web pictures.** Each
  picture from a named site ships as a placeholder. A banner names the sites and says what loading
  sends them, and the pictures load only when the reader presses **Load pictures**. With JavaScript
  off nothing loads, and the banner lists the pictures as links. The player's policy never lets the
  deck itself reach those sites: only its script can, after the reader agrees. The site must allow
  cross-origin reads. Off by default.
- **Fixed: `--player --allow-remote` embeds the deck's web pictures.** It used to ship them as links
  the player's own policy refused, so the reader saw broken images. A picture that cannot be
  fetched ships as a placeholder, and the run says so.

- **Fixed: a palette or light/dark change in the Playground no longer blanks the preview
  or throws you back to slide 1.** The preview used to rebuild its whole document for a
  theme change, which hid every slide until the new one loaded and reset the scroll. It
  now swaps the stylesheet in place and keeps your place. Decks with a Mermaid diagram
  still rebuild, and the preview then reopens at the slide you were reading.
- **Fixed: in Explore, Next and Prev land the whole slide in view.** A step placed the
  slide 16px too low, so a strip of the previous slide showed above it and the bottom of
  the one you asked for was cut off. On desktop a stepped slide now stands alone, centered,
  with no part of its neighbors showing.
- **Fixed: a collapsed preview no longer leaves Explore blank.** Collapsing the preview in
  Edit and then picking a component, loading a gallery or switching to Explore showed an
  empty stage. Entering Explore now opens the preview.
- **Fixed: a scroll right after resizing the window in Explore is kept.** The deck used to
  jump back to the slide it was on about a tenth of a second later.
- **Fixed: in Edit, the preview follows what you type.** Typing or moving the caret into
  another slide scrolls the preview to it, so an edit no longer lands off screen. Scroll
  the preview yourself and it stays put until you type again.
- **Fixed: typing in the Playground costs less per keystroke.** The status line no longer
  flips to "Rendering…" and back on every key, the toolbar re-renders once when you pause
  instead of on every key, and the preview's fit step rewrites only the slides whose size
  changed. Measured against `main` on the built site, five alternating runs of a 31-key
  burst at 4x CPU slowdown: the page's own JavaScript fell from a median 817ms to 608ms,
  and the preview frame's from 477ms to 401ms. Long-task totals stayed within run-to-run
  noise.
- **Added: Look settings in the Playground's Deck settings.** Preset, headline
  alignment, heading rule, eyebrow, slide corners and venue join theme, finish and size.
  The sheet is grouped into Look, Format, On every slide and Editing, and each
  control now sits under its label at full width, so values like "HD · 1280×720 (16:9,
  default)" no longer cut off. The trigger reads "Deck settings" (it read "Deck
  Setting").
- **Changed: the Playground preview renders only the slides you can see.** The rest of
  the deck waits as empty, correctly sized placeholders and fills in as you scroll, and a
  fast fling skips the slides it passes. On a 522-slide deck the first slide shows in 3.4s
  instead of 8.5s, and the preview frame holds 722 nodes instead of 25,494. On the
  58-slide Jargon gallery it shows in 2.1s instead of 3.8s.
- **Changed: a first visit to the Playground shows a real slide sooner.** The site now
  builds the preview a first-time visitor opens on, and the page loads it before the rest
  of the Playground has downloaded. The app then takes it over as it is, with no reload.
  With no network throttling the first slide shows in 0.6s instead of 1.4s, and over fast
  4G in 1.8s instead of 2.5s. The page skips
  this on a connection your browser marks as slow or data-saving. The home page fetches
  that first slide and the theme ahead of time, so following its Playground link over
  fast 4G shows the first slide in 0.8s instead of 2.0s.
- **Fixed: the Playground preview downloads only the fonts its slides use.** It used to
  fetch every typeface the engine knows, including the hand-drawn ones, on every visit.
  Exported decks still load every face, as before.

- A deck that does not load a plugin now draws none of it on any surface that shows the engine's
  render. The engine marks such a
  plugin's code fence `data-lattice-off="<plugin>"`, and the browser runtime's Mermaid pass, the
  Studio's drawn-fence probes and the preview's ink-withholding rule all skip it, so the Studio's
  preview and export and a `--fluid` or `--player` page show the source instead of a diagram.
  `--disable-plugin` now reaches `--fluid` and `--player` pages too.
- `--default-plugins <names|none>` narrows the CLI's default plugin set for one run. The CLI decides
  admission once and hands it to the engine, the plugins' bakes and its source-side slide splits.
- `LatticePlayground.setPluginDefaults(names | null)` and `render(…, { pluginDefaults })` let a
  browser host narrow the default set per bundle or per render; the Studio's one-slide renders
  take the whole deck's admission (`pluginAdmission`), since a slide class anywhere loads its plugin.

- A plugin that declares `contributes.returns` can put `${field}` in the drawing it returns, and the host fills it with the checked value: a word, number, flag or text value as escaped plain text, a markdown value as the host's own sanitized HTML (bare tags, no attributes). A slot fills in visible text only, never inside a tag, a comment, `<style>` or `<script>`, so a returned value cannot become a link or a style; a `${name}` that is not a declared field stays as written. A markdown value fills only in a block fence, outside `<svg>` and `<math>`; in an inline span it fills as its escaped source text. The fills of one render are budgeted at 2 million characters. Works in the CLI and in the Studio. Demo: `lib/packages/_demo-host-slots/host-slots.md`.
- An installed plugin's `styles.css` now reaches the CLI export and the Studio's previews and exports. The host parses the sheet and writes every selector back behind the plugin's own root (`[data-lattice-plugin="<name>"]`), so it can style that plugin's drawing and nothing else, then passes it through `sanitizeStyleText`. A sheet may hold style rules and `@media` / `@supports` blocks; an unbalanced brace, a nested rule, `&`, a leading combinator, `@keyframes`, `@font-face`, `@import` or any other at-rule is refused when the plugin is added.

- **A plugin system, with math as its first plugin.** A plugin is one folder under
  `lib/plugins/<name>/` — a manifest that declares what it contributes and which plugins it
  needs, a grammar module, a renderer module, docs and conformance fixtures — and the build
  freezes every plugin into one registry the engine, the boundary parser and the linter all read.
  The build fails, naming the plugin, when a manifest and its code disagree, a required plugin is
  missing, the dependencies form a cycle, or two plugins claim one syntax trigger or token. Math (`$…$`, `$$…$$`, the `math` slide class) moved onto it with **no change to any
  render**: 4,059 engine renders across every tracked deck at three slide sizes and three math
  settings, and every boundary-parser token stream, are byte-identical before and after.
  `lattice packages list --type plugin` lists it. `createEngine({ math: false, mathOutput })`
  keeps working; `createEngine({ plugins: { disabled, options } })` is the general form. Design
  and roadmap (function-plot, Mermaid and the chart family next):
  `engineering/decisions/2026-09-27-plugin-system.md`.
- **Breaking:** math's internals moved into the math plugin. `lib/engine/math.js` is now
  `lib/plugins/math/math.render.js` and no longer exports `installMath`: install math (and every
  other plugin) on a markdown-it instance with `installPlugins(md, { family, options, disabled })`
  from `lib/plugins/host.js`. `lib/engine/math-detect.mjs` and `lib/core/math-block-rule.{js,mjs}`
  are now `lib/plugins/math/math.syntax.mjs`, which keeps the `sourceHasMath`, `hasDisplayMath`,
  `hasInlineMath` and `mathBlockRule` exports. Only code that deep-imports these files through the
  `./lib/*` export is affected; `@laticent/lattice/engine` and `createEngine` are unchanged.

- **`npm run pr:park -- <PR>` and `npm run pr:ready -- <PR>`** drive the draft-iterate CI procedure. `pr:ready` waits out the push's draft run before marking the PR ready and confirms a real CI run started, closing a race that left a ready PR with only a skipped `ci` run. Both are allowed in `.claude/settings.json`, so a session's permission check no longer refuses them.

- **Every merge ask now carries a fenced 🚦 pre-merge card — what, why, how, evidence, risk,
  what's unverified, and a confidence level.** The merge gate is the one place a human is
  required, and the ask used to arrive as a bare "it's green, may I merge?" — putting the
  decision on the human while the evidence stayed in the agent's head. Green CI is weak
  evidence by construction: it confirms only what CI exercises, and the things that should
  most often block a merge (an unverified surface, a claim resting on a proxy, a defect
  knowingly shipped) are exactly what it cannot see. The confidence level is **derived, not
  asserted** — five axes (evidence, blast radius, reversibility, unknowns, independent eyes)
  graded separately, and **the lowest one sets the level**, so a change with thorough tests
  and one unverified load-bearing claim reads `medium` rather than "high with a caveat".
  Every card also names the single thing that would raise it, which turns "are you sure?"
  into a decision the human can act on. (`engineering/workflow.md` §Pre-merge card)

- **Present goes full screen.** A toggle in the Present overlay's top bar (and
  the `f` key) hides the browser and the OS around the deck, so a laptop or an
  iPad on a lectern shows only slides. Escape leaves full screen; a second
  Escape exits Present. Closing Present hands the window back.
- The button appears only where the browser can actually do it — shown on
  desktop and iPad, absent on iPhone Safari, which ships no Fullscreen API for
  anything but native video. The capability is detected, so nothing needs
  updating if that changes.
- If a browser refuses full screen, Present says so — carrying the browser's own
  reason — instead of leaving a button that appears to do nothing. Where the
  refusal is structural the button retires itself for the session, which is what
  happens in Firefox, Chrome and Edge on iPad: those are WebKit shells, and the
  API is off by default for non-Safari apps however capable the engine reports
  itself to be. Safari on iPad is unaffected.
- **Present's staging controls read as one set.** Slides, Rehearse, Fullscreen
  and Presenter screen are now the same pill, and all show their labels at the
  same width, collapsing to bare icons together below it. They used to disagree
  three ways — one hid its label early, one never hid it, and Presenter screen
  was not even a pill. Presenter screen also keeps a stable label instead of
  swapping to "Presenter on", which a screen reader announced as the control
  becoming a different control.

- **Preset hooks: five tokens for a deck's weight.** `--rule-w`, `--rule-style` and `--rule-mark` set the heading rule's weight, line style and ink (the `form` masthead hairline, `rule: full`, the `rule: short` / `accent` segment, the `split-panel` kicker and the five split-page runheads); `--rail-w` sets the `spectrum-card:` rail's thickness; `--radius-card` sets the corner of every card that can carry a card tag, such as `cards-grid`, `stats`, `decision` or `statute-stack`, and of the tag sitting in its corner, without touching `corners:`, pills, quote panels or diagram tiles. Unset, each falls back to today's value, so no existing deck changes. Presets will set them; a deck can set them today in a `style:` block. See "Preset hooks" in `lib/base/base.docs.md` and the demo `examples/preset-hooks.md`.

- **Added: a judging gate for deck presets.** `node tools/preset-gate.js` renders the new
  30-slide preset corpus deck (`test/fixtures/preset-corpus.md`) under a preset or a candidate
  recipe, in its own palette and mode, the opposite mode and indaco light, as PNG and as the
  exported PDF. It runs the machine gates first (overflow, text contrast at 4.5:1, chart-mark fill
  contrast at 3:1, `check-jank`, and `pixel-check` against an earlier run), stops a preset at
  its first failure, and writes one contact sheet per row plus `summary.json`. The judge
  protocol that follows it is in `engineering/decisions/2026-11-20-deck-preset-study.md` §8.
- **Fixed: `check-jank` no longer reads a deck finish as content.** A `finish:` adds a
  full-bleed backdrop layer to every slide, and the sweep counted it as ink, so under any
  preset with a finish (Editorial, Brand-forward) every step measured the same and the verdict
  was meaningless. The sweep now skips the slide's backdrop layer.

- A `preset:` can now recommend a palette (`theme:`), a color mode (`color-mode:`), a rendering hand (`mode:`), a mark finish (`marks:`) and a finish restraint (`backdrop:`), and every render path, the CLI, Export to Marp, the Playground sheet and the Studio read the recommendation. A key the deck writes still wins, a deck-wide `class: dark`, `light` or `print` (or a `-dark` theme) keeps its color mode, and the Studio's preset picker and Reset never remove the author's `theme:` or `color-mode:`. In the Studio drawer and the Playground sheet, Auto follows a recommended palette or color mode and names it (`Auto — Cuoio (preset)`). No shipped preset sets these keys yet, so every existing deck renders as before.
- A preset can carry internal design tokens: a deck on such a preset gets a `preset-<name>` class on every slide, and the build generates the matching rule. None of the four shipped presets carries tokens.
- Export to Marp now reads a `theme:` with a trailing comment (`theme: cuoio  # brand`) as `cuoio`, as the renderer does, instead of shipping the default palette.
- The Studio and website preview read `theme:` and `color-mode:` with a trailing comment the way the renderer does.

- `pricing` now splits at portrait, square and other tall page shapes: an accent
  cover leads in, then each tier gets a page of its own carrying the component's
  own card — the featured flag, the accent border and the tinted fill all
  survive. Every page carries a derived `Option N of M · comparing …` signal, so
  the pages still read as one comparison. The `two` and `four` variants follow
  the same rule, and landscape is unchanged: a wide page still renders every
  tier in one row.
- **Fixes content loss.** At portrait an un-split `pricing` slide showed one tier
  of three with its text cut mid-word and roughly two thirds of the page blank.
  Nothing is lost now. See `examples/split-pricing.md`.

- **Added: a dated triage of the open issue queue, classified by cost of delay.**
  `engineering/decisions/2026-09-20-issue-queue-triage.md` assigns all 317 open cards to
  one of 14 work classes — eight defect classes ordered by what each costs while it stays
  open, six feature tracks — because the board's four label axes answer "which column" and
  none of them answers "what does this cost open". It reports 30 cards in the three hottest
  classes carrying `priority:medium` or lower, a duplicate pair, a subset pair, and 50 cards
  still labeled for the model dimension HARD RULE #27 retired. § 3 is a cross-cutting jank
  view, linked from `engineering/jank.md` § Canonical sources.

- **Added: `npm run audit:hygiene` and a `queue-triage` skill — the repeatable half of a backlog triage pass.**
  `tools/audit-queue-hygiene.js` audits the queue *itself* in four arms: labels no
  `.github/labels.json` entry declares (which is how 50 cards kept a `model:*` label for a
  dimension HARD RULE #27 retired), cards missing a required axis, duplicate leads, and cards
  holding an outsized share of all comments. It is the sibling of `audit:queue`: that one asks
  whether a card can be pulled, this one asks whether the board is telling the truth.
  `.claude/skills/queue-triage/SKILL.md` carries the judgment half — the cost-of-delay classes,
  the cross-cutting-view rule, and the discipline that label writes go to the owner in one
  batched round and are recorded in the note because they leave no diff.

- **`--read`** exports a deck as its reading article — the prose, with real headings, paragraphs and lists, and charts and tables re-hosted as figures — instead of the slide stack. This is the form a reader mode or a "summarize this page" feature can actually read: a slide stack is headings and short list items inside `<section>` elements, which those tools do not score as article text, so most decks were invisible to them. Instead of, not beside — a page carrying both copies would feed a summarizer the same deck twice. The PDF, PPTX and PNG outputs are byte-identical either way, it composes with `--captions` and `--notes`, and it is also available as a `read: true` front-matter key.

- The Studio can show the active deck as an article. Run **Read as an article** from the command palette (⌘K) and the deck's prose renders as real headings and paragraphs in the page itself, with a table of contents. That is also what makes "summarize this page" work on a deck — Firefox's shake-to-summarize, Safari Reader and the Edge/Chrome reading modes only read the top-level document, and every other slide surface here lives inside an iframe they never look into.

- Reader views now carry a **depth model**: a view is either a **rung** (an altitude in the deck's one containment-checked ladder) or a **cut** (a standalone slice). `kind: rung` in the front-matter `lenses:` block declares an altitude; absent means cut, so a view nobody declared a rung — a custom view, or one a deck already wrote out for itself — is never enrolled in a ladder.
- The ladder is **derived from what each rung shows**, not declared — `ladderRungs` orders rungs narrowest first with the full deck on top, so adding views in a different order never re-orders the depth chain (`order:` stays a picker position).
- New `validateLadder` reports, per slide, any slide a rung shows that the rung above it does not — the invariant that makes "go deeper" additive, now enforced for hand-tagged membership rather than only proved for the suggester. The Reader views panel surfaces these on the offending view, with a `Ladder` marker on its row.
- New `deeperLens` read-path primitive: the next rung that is reader-eligible *and* strictly contains the current view, or nothing. It fails closed, so a deck with a broken ladder still reads safely — it just cannot climb. The "go deeper" affordance in Present is a separate, not-yet-built slice.
- **The two starter views are rungs.** A deck inheriting the workspace defaults ("Default reader views" on, the shipped setting) now shows a `Bottom line → The evidence → Full deck` ladder without doing anything — deliberately, since those two are exactly the pair that provably nests. If such a deck's hand-tagged membership breaks the nesting, the Reader views panel now says so where it was previously silent.

- **New lint rule** `bad-render-target-value` and two new autocomplete keys ship here, which is why this fragment is `added` rather than `fixed` — the category picks the release bump.
- `fluid:`, `player:` and `present:` no longer fall silent on a trailing YAML comment.
  The export matched these three keys with a `$`-anchored regex, so `fluid: true  # for the
  web` enabled nothing while every other key in the same block stripped the comment and read
  normally. A quoted value (`fluid: "true"`) now works for the same reason. Both are
  widenings — a deck that was off becomes on — and no deck that already enabled a target
  loses it: the reader is the union of the old matcher and the shared front-matter scalar
  rule (`lib/core/render-target-keys.js`), pinned by a parity sweep over whole front-matter
  blocks.
- The deck linter reports a `fluid:` / `player:` / `present:` value that is neither on
  (`true` / `yes` / `on`) nor off (`false` / `no` / `off`) — new rule
  `bad-render-target-value`. A typo like `fluid: ture` reads as off, writes the ordinary
  artifact without complaint, and looks correct on every surface the author can check. The
  rule carries no autofix on purpose: a typo's polarity is ambiguous (`of` is one edit from
  both `off` and `on`), so guessing would risk enabling a target the author opted out of.
- The Studio editor's front-matter autocomplete offers `fluid:` and `player:` alongside
  `present:`, and all three now name the full six-word vocabulary rather than `true / false`.
  Only `present:` was listed, so the other two were reachable only by already knowing they
  exist. None of the three gets a settings-panel control — they name the artifact a render
  emits, not a property of the deck, and the Studio sets them at export time.
- The reader answers one question of a deck rather than two. The scalar and legacy arms
  disagreed about *which* line to read — first-match versus any-match — so a trailing YAML
  comment or a pair of quotes, both no-ops in YAML, could flip a deck from on to off when an
  earlier line for the same key held a typo. Both arms now read every line for the key: the
  target is on if any line for it says an on-word. Reordering complete `key: value` lines no
  longer changes the verdict as a result; a value folded onto the following line is the one
  exception, since reading it depends on the two lines staying adjacent.

- **Tables reflow when they run out of width.** A record list (each row one thing: a person, a file, a risk) becomes one card per row, its first cell the card's title and every other cell a `LABEL value` line, the values aligned in one column (a label past 10 characters sits above its value); a two-column table puts each label above its value. Every other table keeps its grid. The engine names each table's kind on its own (`lib/core/table-shape.js`), and the switch is a container query on the table's own box, so it fires in a narrow pane, on a portrait canvas or on a phone, and never on a full-width or half-pane 16:9 slide. On a slide it switches only where the new layout fits: when the cards would make the slide overflow, the table keeps its table form and the export says so with an `ⓘ` line. Overrule a wrong guess per slide with `table-cards`, `table-pairs` or `no-table-reflow` (a slide's override reaches its panes; a pane marker can name its own). The components that own a table follow: a `glossary` puts each term above its definition, a `math derivation` puts each justification under its step, and `obligation-matrix` and the `statute-stack lane` take the cards; `matrix-grid` and `roadmap` keep their grid. In a table that reflows, each body cell carries its column header as `data-lat-col`, and the table carries ARIA table roles.
- **`npm run lab:build`**, the Frame Lab: every component's gallery in a frame you can narrow, with type held at slide size and no height limit, to see how each one responds. **`npm run tables:bakeoff`** scores the table-kind detectors against 225 independently labeled tables.
- **Rows of cards drop columns when their box narrows.** `cards-grid`, `verdict-grid`, `pricing`, `stats`, `statute-stack`, `decision`, `list-steps`, `compare-prose`, `team-profile`, `cards-stack horizontal`, `q-and-a`, `inventory cards`/`timeline`, `kpi` and `list principles` respond to the width of their content area, not only to the deck's aspect, through one shared rule (`lib/base/base.card-reflow.css`); a full-width 16:9 slide never changes, and on a slide a row that would overflow keeps its columns. statute-stack's status pill no longer lands on the label in a narrow card.
- **Fixed:** a `cards-grid three` grid stayed three across on portrait and mobile decks wherever nothing splits the slide (the live preview, an exported Marp bundle, the fluid view); it now stacks one card per row, as `cards-grid` always intended. That reaches exported PDFs too where the grid sits in a tall pane of a wide deck (it rendered three squeezed cards across); a full portrait or mobile export was not affected, because its auto-split already put one card per page.

- **New `risk-matrix` chart for risk registers.** Write each risk as its name and `{likelihood, impact}` (1 to 5), with an optional second record for where mitigation takes it. The chart draws a 5 × 5 grid shaded low, medium, high or critical by likelihood × impact, places each risk as a numbered marker (an arrow and a dashed ring show the planned move), and lists the risks worst first beside the grid. Narration reads them worst first in words ("likelihood likely, impact critical, rated critical"). Demo deck: `examples/risk-matrix.md`.

- Scrollbars in the Studio, the Playground and the docs are now thin everywhere, not only on the page itself. Inner panels such as Compose and the filmstrip used to draw the thick system scrollbar on Windows.
- Long panes now offer jump to top and jump to bottom: Studio Compose, Source and the reading view, and the Playground editor and preview. The buttons appear while you scroll content longer than two screens and hide 1.5 seconds after you stop. With a mouse they sit as a small rail beside the scrollbar; on a touch screen they stack bottom-right, above the New slide button.
- A mouse wheel now scrolls the Studio's slide pills and the slide map sideways, wherever the pointer is on the strip. Before, a plain wheel did nothing there unless the pointer sat on the strip's scrollbar.
- The slide map no longer shows a scrollbar. It used to reserve an empty bar strip even when nothing scrolled; you move through it with the mouse wheel, a trackpad swipe or the keyboard.

- `lint:deck` warns (`bracket-list-closed-early`) when a stray `]` right after a quoted name closes a bracketed axis or key list early, as in `["Cost, excluding tax"]], Value]`. The notation cannot read such a span, so the axis silently showed as plain text. The fix line gives the list the author meant.

- Segno grammars can name `stops`, node kinds that end a parse where they close, and `parse(input, rule, from)` resumes at an offset (grammars without stops generate the same parsers as before).

- Segno: a record whose first character is `>` is a description, `{> prose}`, with prose to the first unescaped `}` (`\}` and `\\` escape). The reader returns a `description` value, and a slot that takes values reports `description-not-here`. A record's first bare item can no longer start with `>`: `{>5}` is a description, not the number 5 (no deck in the repo wrote one); later items keep it (`{3, >5}`).

- **Segno can read whole files, not only short spans.** Three additions to the grammar engine:
  `greedy()` marks a loop that takes the longest match; `until("*/")` skips ahead to a fixed
  string of up to 64 characters; and a grammar can raise its nesting cap from 64 to 1,000. Each
  one keeps Segno's guarantee that a parse takes time proportional to its input and never throws.
  Grammars written with them read every CSS, HTML and Markdown file in the repository
  (`npm run parser:bakeoff:languages`). Nothing in a deck changes: Lattice's inline notation
  parser is byte-for-byte identical.

- **Added: the Studio's deck and slide settings panels can be searched, and can
  drop their tabs for one continuous list.** Two controls sit at the top right of
  both panels. **Search** filters every control across all sections at once, so
  "pagination" finds the Page numbers row without opening the Chrome tab to look
  for it; opening the field hides the view toggle and takes the whole row, which
  is the width a phone needs. **View** switches between `Grouped` (the pill-tabbed
  panel, still the default) and `List` (every section down one scroll under its
  own sticky heading). The view choice persists and is one choice for both scopes.

- **Deck settings covers nine registers it never offered.** A deck logo (with its
  placement, size, treatment and which-slides modifiers), the masthead meta line,
  `corners:`, `claim:`, the deck-wide stamp and tone shapes, `pace:`, and — new to the
  Studio — slide splitting, deck chrome, auto-glossary and the default slide class. Each
  was already honored by the engine and reachable only by hand-writing YAML.
- **Every settings row now carries a ⓘ** with the full explanation, on both the deck and
  slide panels. It opens on tap as well as hover, so the help is reachable on a phone.

- **Tab completion for the `lattice` command in bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell.** `lattice completion <shell>` prints a script you install with one line (for example `eval "$(lattice completion bash)"` in `~/.bashrc`, which works from bash 3.2, the macOS default, up). Tab then completes the subcommands, every option, the values an option takes (palettes, `--size` canvases, `--paper` sheets, plugin names, the image-set settings) and the packages you installed, and narrows paths to the files that fit. A Tab press costs one Node start, about 50 ms.

- `mode: sketch` (and the legacy deck-wide `class: sketch`) now carries into Mermaid
  diagrams. Flowchart, state, class and ER nodes are drawn with Mermaid's native
  hand-drawn renderer, so a sketch deck no longer wraps a hand-drawn slide around a
  crisply machine-drawn diagram. Per-slide `_class: sketch` opts one diagram in on a
  plain deck; `_class: boardroom` opts one out of a sketch deck.
- The categorical palette survives the hand look: rough nodes cycle `--cat-N-fill`
  the same way classic nodes do. It goes on as a `stroke`, because a rough node has
  no fill — its "fill" is a bundle of stroked hachure lines.
- **Themes that carry categories by texture keep crisp shapes.** On `a11y-*`, `onyx`
  and `concrete` the per-category pattern is the redundant encoding a color-blind or
  monochrome reader depends on, and it cannot survive being painted through a stroke
  (it reads as speckle). Those decks still get the hand type everywhere; only the
  diagram shapes stay machine-drawn. This is not overridable per slide — style does
  not outrank an accessibility affordance.
- No change to any non-sketch deck: the engine emits no `look` key at all unless the
  slide resolves to hand-drawn, so an existing deck's Mermaid directive is
  byte-identical to before.
- Diagram LABELS still use the mono face under `sketch`. That is a separate,
  pre-existing gap in the diagram font path (`engineering/mermaid.md` §5.3), not
  something this change regressed.

- Every Lattice skill (`design/skills/*.md`) now opens with front matter (`name`, `description`, `kind`, `studio`), and `tools/skill-index.js` generates one index from it: the README table with a read cost per skill, `design/skills/index.json`, the agent kit's skills index, and a `.claude/skills/lattice-<name>/SKILL.md` per skill so Claude Code can pick a skill from its description. The Studio chat's guide list now comes from the same index instead of a hand-kept table.

- `lint:deck` now checks every slide against its layout's slot contract (`slot-contract`, an error). A required heading, list, blockquote or table that is missing, a heading written at the wrong level (`#` where the layout reads `##`), and a list written with a marker the layout does not read (`agenda` with `-`, `journey` with `1.`) are reported. Before, `lint:deck --strict` passed a slide with its required heading deleted on 67 of 69 layouts; now it passes none.
- Each manifest slot carries a structured `match` (what the author writes, in Markdown terms) that `lint:deck` executes, and a variant can change a slot's shape with `variantSlots` (`statute-stack lane` takes a table, `split-panel pullquote` anchors on a blockquote).
