The component guides list each slot as what to write, not as a CSS selector.
- `lint:deck` warns (`variant-inert`) on a variant that does nothing as written: `numbered` on `cards-grid` and `cards-stack`, whose numbers come from a `1.` list.
- `quote` styles only the paragraph right after the quotation as its attribution. A later paragraph renders as body text instead of a second credit in tracked capitals.
- `closing` and `divider` declare `#` as well as `##` for their heading, `agenda` declares its list optional (it fills itself from the dividers), and `glossary`, `image`, `math` and `table` declare the other forms they already render (a table, `@image{…}`, a ```` ```math ```` fence, a raw `<table>`).
- `lib/base/base.manifest.json` declares every class word a slide accepts without a component (48 modifier groups) and every front-matter register with the groups it stamps. `MODIFIER_GROUPS` is built from it, and `lib/base/base.modifiers.docs.md` is generated from it: every group, every register, and a one-line test that tells a component, a variant, a modifier, a switch and a register apart. 43 words the engine already accepted joined the registry: the `mode:` words, seven switches, 16 tints and marks, the `tint-at-*` and bare placements, `bleed` and `watermark`.
- `lint:deck` no longer accepts a class word because it starts with `no-`, `with-`, `at-`, `tone-`, `fill-`, `checks-`, `treatment-`, `tint-` or `mark-`: a typo such as `no-heaer` is now `unknown-class`. Only `finish-*` stays open, for saved finish names.
- `lint:deck` warns (`foreign-variant`) on another layout's variant (`kpi gallery`), which renders as if it were absent.

- Every spec in `spec/` now names its schema, reference implementation and shared test cases in a short block under its title, and `npm run build:check` fails when a spec loses one or names a path that no longer exists.

- `split-compare` now splits at portrait, square and other tall page shapes, on the
  owner's ruling: an accent cover carrying the question, then one option card per
  page, then the **recommendation on its own closing page**. The question rides
  every option page, because a comparison read one answer at a time needs the
  question beside each. See `examples/split-decision.md`.
- **Fixes content loss.** At portrait an un-split `split-compare` slide kept both
  option cards and pushed the `RECOMMENDATION` block — the slide's conclusion —
  off the page entirely, with no warning.
- New `compare-options` split strategy. `split-compare`'s transform builds
  `.option` divs rather than a list, so a plain item axis had nothing to slice and
  paginated an option's inner rows instead; this strategy reads the rendered shape
  the component actually produces.

- **Added: Squadra's demo and Learn pages, and its mark.** `/libraries/squadra/` runs the real library in the browser: six rules for a small notes language, three honest and three broken, and the reader turns them on to watch the compiler refuse each broken one by name before it can touch the text, then edits the notes and presses Fix all. The Learn page at `/libraries/squadra/learn/` carries the code, the refusals and the whole-deck comparison behind Lattice's Fix all. The mark is a copper set-square with a graphite scale on its hypotenuse.

- **Added: "Fix all" says which fixes it did not apply, and why.** The Studio's Fix all (its button, the command palette and the phone drawer) and the Playground's Alt-Shift-F now end with a notice: how many issues it fixed, then each fix the fix driver refused, by slide, rule and reason ("Slide 2, card-style-inline-title: Fix all stopped before reaching it; press Fix all again."). A refused fix keeps its underline, which before this came with no explanation. The fix driver also stops listing one refusal twice, and stops reporting a refusal whose issue a later fix resolved anyway.

- **Added: `@laticent/squadra`, a lint-and-fix library that refuses a rule it cannot prove works.** A rule must fire on its own bad examples at the spans they mark, stay quiet on its good ones, and its fix must turn each bad example into its fixed partner and keep the document's shape, or the rule does not load. Findings carry spans, not line text, and one fix driver checks every fix: no overlapping edits, no edits inside code fences, and no fix that changes the number of slides or drops the front matter unless its rule declares it. The core has no dependencies, no DOM and no file access, so the same rules run in Node and in the browser.

- `state-chart` now lays out **branching** machines with a real graph layout (dagre) instead of forcing them into one column: a state with several outgoing transitions fans out across a rank, and terminal states converge on one exit marker. **Chains are unchanged** — `state i at row i` is the right answer there, and every machine in the six shipped galleries keeps byte-identical geometry. Self-transitions keep the existing router, so one machine can use both. The numbering remains the stable ref either way; it just no longer dictates the row on a machine that branches.

- `dagre-d3-es` and `lodash-es` are now direct dependencies, self-hosted and inlined into the shipped bundles — nothing is fetched at run time. Their MIT notices travel with the marp kit's `THIRD-PARTY-LICENSES.txt`. The state-chart's browser pass can now reach a graph layout engine on all three render paths.

- `state-chart` edge labels now sit **off the line** — below it on `lr`, to the right of it on the default — so a multi-line label no longer knocks a hole through its own edge. Event text accepts explicit breaks (`\n` or `<br/>`) and wraps on its own when it is still too long, never mid-word.
- Edge length is **responsive**: the rank gap stretches so a `tb` machine fills the stage's height and an `lr` machine fills its width, floored at the room the labels actually need — so a sparse machine gets air and a label can never reach a node.
- The clearance each axis asks for now follows **where the label sits**: a `tb` label sits beside the vertical run, so its height is no longer stacked into the rank gap as well, and it wraps late because on `tb` the cross axis is the cheap one. A four-state `tb` machine gets its full width back and 17% of its height, which the fit spine spends scaling the diagram up.
- **Fixed:** a re-ranked chart no longer feeds its own output back into its next draw. The size pin the layout puts on the scale box was still there when the next draw measured the nodes inside it, so the column was narrower each time and labels wrapped that did not need to; on a live preview one chart alternated between two sizes forever. The pin now comes off before measuring, alongside the fit transform it sits next to.
- **Fixed:** an `lr` edge label no longer cuts the connector it labels. The offset positioned the label block's *center*, so the first line's box top landed half a pixel below the edge and the label's halo reached back across it — visible on two edges of the branching demo deck.

- `state-chart` transitions and states accept `:::token` to name a **theme token** to paint with — `1. Draft `start`:::state-info-hue`, `- `{reject, to=3}`:::state-fail-hue`. A transition takes an optional second slot for its edge-label background (`:::state-fail-hue/surface-raised`). The token is used as `var(--<token>)`, so a tinted deck still re-themes with the palette; there is no syntax for a hex literal. Malformed names are dropped whole and the element keeps its inherited paint.
- **Fixed:** the tint channel no longer erases what it cannot paint. A `:::token` naming a token that does not exist used to make the custom property invalid rather than fall back, which sent a transition's `stroke` to `none` (the edge vanished), dropped a state's border, and painted the state solid black. Each inline value now carries its own fallback, so an unknown token renders the untinted default — which is what every doc surface already promised.
- **Fixed:** the start marker's arrowhead is painted from the palette again. It reads `--edge-tint`, which was declared only on the edge group — and a start marker sits outside every group, so the arrowhead fell to the SVG initial and painted pure black on every machine, chains included, and invisibly against a dark canvas.
- **Security:** tints read back out of the DOM by the browser pass are re-validated against the token grammar and escaped at the sink. The build-time parser refuses anything but a bare token, but the pass reads `data-tint` and the transitions JSON from the document — where a deck author's raw inline HTML also lands — and interpolated them into a `style` attribute unescaped, which let a crafted value inject live markup into the preview frame (HARD RULE #22).

- **`npm run check:glance` checks whether status reads at a glance from the back row.** It renders a
  deck, simulates a projector in a lit room and the blur a 20/40 viewer sees at the venue's back row
  (and a designer's squint), then measures every status mark: whether it still stands off the slide
  (3:1 floor) and whether two statuses on one slide can still be told apart. It writes a contact sheet
  with failing marks boxed. Every other contrast check scores the pixels as painted, so a pale pill
  held off the slide by a thin border passed them all. On its first run, over three shipped themes
  (mustard, indaco, crepuscolo), 48 of the 54 status marks on their dark faces fell below the floor
  at the back of a hall in a lit room (2.1–3.1:1), and none of the 54 on their light faces did.
  (`tools/check-glance.js`)

- **Added: a "Status and labels" guide on the docs site, replacing the single "Pills and marks" page.** Seven pages, read in order: a start page on which tool to reach for (state mark, pill, status word or label set) and which ones work on every slide versus only in certain components; the six answers and how to choose between the ones that look alike; each layout's words for the six answers, renaming them with a label set, and the `checks-*`, `heat` and `state-cells` switches; brace pills; the pills a component places from position; upgrading a deck written before the six answers; and a one-page cheat sheet. `/guides/pills/` redirects to the new start page.
- The component reference pages for the layouts that read marks, status words or positional pills now carry a **Guides** section linking to the page that teaches that grammar.
- The checklist, verdict-grid and pricing references now name the same words the engine speaks for each marker: checklist `[/]` is "skipped", verdict-grid `[-]` is "partial" and `[/]` "not applicable", and pricing `[/]` is "not included". An inline mark's accessible name for `[x]` is "yes", not "done", as `base.docs.md` had said.
- The docs-site glossary adds the status terms and lists **mark** as a fourth word with more than one meaning, and the theme track explains why the unknown, open and does-not-apply marks share one gray.
- **Added: a "Deck settings" guide and a generated front-matter reference.** The guide explains how the front-matter block works — it applies to every slide, one slide can differ, a wrong value is linted, and the Studio's Settings writes it — then walks the settings most decks want, with live examples. The new **Reference → Front matter** page lists all 60 keys with their accepted values, default, Studio control and per-slide form; its keys come from the Studio's autocomplete list and its values from the list `lint:deck` accepts, so it cannot drift from either.
- **Fixed: four false claims on the docs site.** The introduction said Lattice has no animation or presenter timer; it has chart motion, `_build` reveals and a rehearsal clock in Present mode (the PDF stays still). Getting Started sent readers to the removed Drawing Board for the Marp export (it is **Share → Marp bundle** in the Studio) and quoted stale layout counts. The authoring guide listed `loose`, which is not a modifier.
- The Studio's front-matter autocomplete now describes four keys correctly: `spectrum-trim` also takes `restrained`, `motion` reaches the exported player, `paginate` treats anything but `false` as on, and `debug` accepts `off`. The logo-size help text says an out-of-range value is clamped, which is what the engine does.

- The Studio editor now completes everything the Playground editor does, because both run one shared list of completion sources: slide directive names after `<!-- _`, `_focus:` axes and `_focusStyle:` values, the keys of a nested `backdrop:` map, Mermaid keywords inside a `mermaid` fence, a component's slot skeleton on an empty slide, and region names on a `map` slide. Inside a nested `backdrop:` map the editor used to offer the deck's top-level keys; it now offers the map's own.
- Each platform's usual key opens suggestions in every Studio editor and the Playground: Ctrl-Space, plus Option-Esc on a Mac, where macOS uses Ctrl-Space to switch the keyboard input source. Tab now accepts a suggestion as Enter does, and only while the menu is open. Where nothing completes, the editor shows "No suggestions here" instead of doing nothing. The `?` shortcut list has an Editor section with these keys.
- Picking a front-matter key whose value completes (`theme`, `finish`, `pace`, …) opens its values at once, and a key the front matter already sets is no longer offered again.
- More of the slide body completes, in both the Studio and the Playground:
  - **Directive values.** `<!-- _paginate: ` offers the same words as the front-matter key.
  - **Note channels.** `<!-- ` offers `say:`, `describe:`, `reader:` and the pane keys.
  - **TeX commands** after `\` inside `$…$`, `$$…$$` or a `math` fence. A command that takes arguments writes its braces, with the caret in the first.
  - **Flowchart slides.** The chart's own shape and group names after an arrow, the arrow forms after a name, and the span words (outline, color, status, line) inside a backtick, all from the flowchart grammar.
  - **Sample art.** `sample:` inside an image reference offers Lattice's sample pictures, so an image completes even with an empty Library.
  - **A blank line.** Ctrl-Space offers what a line starts with: a layout directive, a record, a say line, a speaker note, a heading, a list item, a fence or a new slide.
- **Fixed:** the editors no longer offer `chart` as a fence language; the engine renders it as plain code. Fence languages now come from the plugin registry, which adds `functionplot` and `anima` to the Playground's list and `math` to the Studio's.
- **Fixed:** the Studio's CSS fields (Theme CSS, Component CSS, the Craft lab) had no completion at all, because the field replaced CodeMirror's own CSS completion with nothing. CSS properties and values complete again. Inside `var(` the fields now offer the token names: the palette contract grouped by role, and the type scale with each token's role, listed first after `font-size`.
- **Fixed:** typing quickly into a Studio CSS or JSON field (Theme CSS, Component CSS, Manifest JSON) could drop letters. The field mistook the page's late copy of its own earlier text for a new value and wrote it back over what had just been typed. On Firefox at full typing speed, 4 of 5 runs lost a letter.
- While the Studio's component catalog is still loading, an empty Ctrl-Space says "Loading suggestions…" rather than "No suggestions here".

- **Engineering:** `tools/chat-figures-bakeoff.mjs` and an isolated harness page (`/proto/chat-figures/`) measure what it costs to draw a mermaid, math, plot or slide figure in a chat bubble under four strategies; the result and decision are in `engineering/decisions/2026-10-12-chat-figures-bakeoff.md`.

- **Studio chat:** a reply's ` ```mermaid `, ` ```math `, ` ```functionplot ` and ` ```lattice ` fences (a diagram, an equation, a plot, one slide) are now drawn in the bubble, in the open deck's theme, instead of printed as source. Each has a Source toggle. Figures share a small pool of frames, so a long conversation does not grow in memory with its figure count.

- **The Studio chat checks that its slides fit.** Each edit is rendered off-screen and the
  agent is told which slides overflow, cut text or shrink type below the legibility floor. An
  overflow on a slide it wrote counts as an error, so it fixes the slide before you see the
  change. (`docs/src/components/studio/draft-fit.ts`)

- **Studio chat:** the paperclip now takes a photo. "Add a photo…" opens the device's own picker (Photo Library, Take Photo or Choose File on a phone), and you can paste an image into the message box. The photo goes through the Library's intake (EXIF and GPS removed, capped at 2560 px) to this deck's shelf, shows as a thumbnail in the thread, and goes to a vision model as an image, with its `asset:<name>` so you can ask for it on a slide. A model the catalog lists as text-only refuses the photo before you send.
- **Studio chat:** a short video can be attached the same way, up to 15 seconds and 15 MB, to a model the catalog lists as reading video. It shows as a poster with its length and goes to the model for that turn; it is not stored (the Library has no video shelf yet).

- **Import deck… now sits in the deck switcher, under New deck, and in ⌘K.** It used to be
  in the Lattice brand menu, where people looking next to "New deck" didn't find it. It now
  opens **`.lattice`**, **Markdown**, a **webpage (`.html`) export**, and a **PDF or
  PowerPoint exported from Lattice** with the new switch below. The importer detects the
  format from the file's contents, so a renamed file still opens. A PDF or PowerPoint that
  carries no deck is refused with a message saying how to get one that does. Import never
  tries to rebuild a deck from slide pictures. (`docs/src/components/studio/deck-import.ts`)
- **New: "Re-openable in Lattice" on PDF and PowerPoint export.** With the switch on, the
  exported file carries the deck's `.lattice` project, so anyone you send it to can import
  it and edit the deck exactly as you wrote it. In a PDF it is an attachment named
  `deck.lattice`; in a PowerPoint, a package part. The switch is **off by default**,
  because the embedded deck includes your speaker notes and hidden slides. Each deck
  remembers its own setting. Review comments never ride in a PDF or PowerPoint this way;
  to pass them along, send the `.lattice` file. PowerPoint now opens an options step
  before downloading, as PDF already did. With the switch off, PDF and PowerPoint files are
  built exactly as before. (`docs/src/components/studio/embedded-source.ts`,
  `engineering/decisions/2026-10-05-reopenable-exports.md`)

- **The Studio's deck settings now choose the Guide's delivery.** Settings ▸ Speech has a Delivery menu under Pace: Restrained (the default), Expressive or Somber. It writes the deck's `delivery:` line, and choosing Restrained removes it, so the choice travels with the deck the same way typing it did.

- **Studio: bring your own OpenAI, Anthropic or Gemini key.** Workspace → AI → API key now has a provider picker beside OpenRouter (still the default). A pasted key is checked with its provider, stored sealed in this browser, and runs every Studio AI feature on that provider. Spend shows an estimate from token counts, priced from OpenRouter's public catalog, plus "Balance not available for this provider" with a link to the provider's billing page. Errors name the provider ("Your OpenAI account is out of credits").

- **Drop a deck file anywhere on the Studio to open it.** A `.lattice`, `.md`, `.html`, or a
  PDF or PowerPoint exported "Re-openable in Lattice" now opens as a new deck when you drag it
  onto the Studio, through the same reader and checks as **Import deck…**. A sign shows where
  the drop will land. The Library and the editor keep their own drops, and a drop never changes
  the deck you have open. (`docs/src/components/studio/deck-drop.ts`)

- **Added: the Studio's edit→paint budget is now a committed baseline with a gate.**
  `bench:check` ratchets the engine in Node; nothing held the warm keystroke a person
  actually feels. `npm run perf:frame:bless` / `perf:frame:check` (in `docs/`) drive the
  real built Studio under CPU throttle and compare against
  `docs/scripts/frame-baseline.json` — FRAME patch 1.1 ms, TOTAL edit→paint 11.4 ms,
  engine RENDER 3.6 ms. A metric must break both the 25% band and an absolute floor to
  fail, so sub-millisecond jitter on a ~1 ms needle cannot redden the gate while a real
  regression still does. A metric the run cannot measure is recorded as null and skipped
  rather than blessed as zero.

- **Studio Inspector covers four more deck settings.** Look ▸ More now has **Card rows** (`cards:`) and **Text overflow** (`guards:`). General has **AI writes in** (`ai-lang:`). Motion has **In the exported player** (`player-motion: off`), shown once chart motion is on.
- **Editor autocomplete knows every deck front-matter key.** It now offers `guards:`, `player-motion:`, `inline-code:`, `captions:` and Marp's `color:` / `background*:` keys. It also completes the VALUE of every register with a fixed vocabulary (`cards:`, `guards:`, `claim:`, `corners:`, the `spectrum*` family, `rule:`, `motion-speed:`, …), using the engine's own lint vocabulary, so it offers exactly the values `npm run lint:deck` accepts.

- **Browse every icon in the Studio.** The command palette (⌘K) has **Insert an icon…**, a grid of all 265 icons, drawn and grouped by category. Search by name, alias or category (`db`, `serverless`, `storage`). A pick inserts `` `^{name}` `` at the cursor, or `icon=name` when the cursor is inside a pill or a chart record. The drawings load the first time the grid opens.

- Studio lessons now speak. Every line of the six Basics lessons plays a clip recorded with Kokoro, the Studio's own voice, so no key and no model download are needed. Captions still show every line, and a line without a clip falls back to its caption. `node tools/record-lesson-voice.mjs` records the clips, and a unit test fails when a lesson line has no current clip.

- Nine new Studio lessons, all voiced: adding a chart, a table, a comparison and an image; speaker notes; checking a deck with Coach; Fix all; changing a slide's layout with Reshape; and switching light or dark. Search finds each one by the question or by words like "graph", "notes" or "dark".
- The command palette gains four rows: "Coach — check this deck", "Fix all issues" (shown while there is something to fix), "Switch light / dark mode" and "Slide settings — look, notes".

- The site-wide search finds Studio lessons: type "pdf" on any page and "How do I export a PDF?" opens the Studio running that lesson (`/studio/?lesson=<id>`).
- Finished lessons are remembered. Search marks them "Done", and the end of a lesson offers the next one.
- Opening Coach or Slide settings for the first time offers its lesson, once.

- Two new Studio lessons, both voiced, complete the curriculum's Sharing track: "How do I share a deck that plays in a browser?" walks to the Webpage export, and "How do I get a PowerPoint file?" walks to the PowerPoint export. Each opens Share and the format for a learner who waits, then leaves the Download button to them. Search finds them by words like "html", "offline", "pptx" or "powerpoint".

- **The Studio teaches through search.** Type what you want in the command palette and you get the action and a short lesson for it: "pdf" offers **Export as PDF…** and **How do I export a PDF?** A lesson points at the real control and waits for your click; if you wait, it does the step for you and moves on. Six lessons to start: a new deck, writing a slide, adding a slide, changing the theme, presenting, exporting a PDF. Lessons run on the deck you have open and change nothing until a step does.
- **Export as PDF…** in the command palette opens Share straight on the PDF step.

- **Added: the deck switcher is in the header at the Read stop.** Read drew a plain
  title before, so a reader whose saved posture is Read had no way to reach their
  other decks.
- **Added: the Studio's brand mark links to the home page.** The mark and the
  wordmark are two controls now — clicking or tapping the mark goes to the site
  home, while the wordmark and its chevron open the workspace menu (Decks ·
  Fabricate · Import).

- `dist/styles/` — `lattice.css` cut into ordered style modules (187 today) plus a `manifest.json` (id, file, bytes, SHA-256, source). Joined in manifest order (the manifest's `note` gives the separator rule) they are `lattice.css` byte for byte, and no existing file changes. The package gains this folder and `dist/styles-min/` (about 0.94 MB gzipped together). First step toward loading only the CSS a deck uses (`engineering/decisions/2026-10-18-on-demand-styles.md`).
- `dist/styles-min/` — the minified twin of `dist/styles/`: same ids, file names and order; concatenating the files is `lattice-min.css` byte for byte (about 0.98 MB raw, 0.14 MB gzipped).
- `tools/style-baseline.mjs` — prints how much CSS a rendered deck carries and how much it uses, on Chromium and WebKit.
- `tools/style-needs.js` and `tools/style-needs-audit.mjs` — say which style modules a rendered document needs, with an audit that checks no needed module is skipped, in Chromium and WebKit (results in the decision note).
- `npm run branch:owner` (`tools/branch-owner.sh`) — lists the sessions whose commits are on a branch, so a session does not push to one another session owns (HARD RULE #31).

- **Added: `examples/system-design-foundations.md`, a 232-slide system-design tutorial
  (233 pages with its generated glossary) for engineers in their first
  years.** It opens on one engineer's Tuesday told wake-to-sleep with
  no vocabulary at all, then names each thing she met — system, purpose, boundary, environment,
  process, model, constraint, invariant, infrastructure, emergence — against the timestamp that
  taught it. A protagonist/antagonist frame turns that vocabulary into a design starting point
  and picks the rung on a five-type solution ladder (MVP, scaled, optimized, optimal,
  specialized), closing on a removal test drawn from Saint-Exupéry and Rams. Six reference kits
  follow — data, compute, network, scale, reliability, security — each opening with a pair of
  two-panel diagrams that split its four usage patterns and closing with its invariants, and covering the
  practices a junior meets in year one: ordering and identity, changing a schema without an
  outage, deleting across every derived copy, dependency supply chain, and quotas. The deck then
  designs Instagram end to end around the follow graph's asymmetry: bounded out-degree, unbounded
  in-degree, and super nodes that force the hybrid fan-out rather than it being a preference.
  Capacity is worked from a daily average up to a peak page-fetch rate, and the design's own
  fixes are checked against the promises that motivated them. The method is framed as four movements — discover, design,
  develop, deliver — of which the deck teaches the first two and hands the last two to the
  reader as the only honest check on their own design. Sixteen ask-then-answer exercises: three at
  the ends of Parts one to three, ten across Part four's six kits — including a full
  discover-then-design pass on a course-registration spike — and one inside each design and in
  the closing review. A second design then runs the whole method again from
  nothing — a parking app where drivers scan a sticker on the bay and pay — climbing the ladder
  from a one-table MVP through a scaled rung to an optimized one, where the card fee turns out
  to be the bill and the servers never were. Its payment path is worked to the
  point a reader could implement it: two taps deduplicate on a unique key and two racing scans on a
  unique index over the bay while one is in flight, a webhook writes only while the row still
  waits so a redelivery cannot overwrite a refund, the row carries the amount at insert so a retry
  sends the same request and the minutes so an expiry can be computed, `started_at` is read
  off the charge rather than the handler's clock, and the key's lifetime — Stripe's
  twenty-four hours is the worked number — bounds a sweep that past that window refunds what
  it cannot deliver or writes the row off, rather than re-sending. The sweep itself gets a
  slide: it asks the provider rather than guessing, and each of the four answers it can get
  back writes a different status and either holds the bay or frees it. Choosing a store runs in three passes — shape and
  access, then a capability no shape provides (similarity, ranked text, proximity, live push,
  retention, traversal), then the operational properties that break a tie — so a capability adds
  a store beside the source rather than replacing it. Part seven maps the feed design back to the
  kits, runs the removal test on it, and hands over a nine-field worksheet. Thirty-two Mermaid diagrams, each carrying a key insight,
  `profile: teaching`, and a generated glossary appendix from the deck's own acronym registry.
  Every diagram was sized against the deck's own smallest type token: the six kit-pattern
  diagrams that held four panels each are now twelve two-panel diagrams, which took their node
  labels from 51% of `--fs-meta` to 106%, and no diagram now draws a label below 81% of it.

- Tavola has a demo page at `/tavola`: a host and a guest run in one tab over Tavola's in-memory network, so a visitor can knock, admit, edit from either side, make the guest view-only and remove them, without opening a second browser. The home page's Tavola card and the Libraries menu link to it.

- **New component: `team-profile`, the people slide.** A roster of named people,
  each under a portrait, with the role they own — meet-the-leaders, meet-the-team,
  and the QBR roll-call. Five compositions off one authoring shape: the default
  three-up cards, `lead` (one hero row above a rule, the rest ranked beneath),
  `bench` (six up, face and role only, for the long roster), `sides` (two labeled
  rosters facing each other), and `bio` (one person per row, the note on a line of
  its own). Write `- Name` and nest the portrait, the backticked role, and one
  line on what they own.
- **Anyone with no photo gets a monogram, not a hole.** The engine reads the
  initials off the name and draws them in the circle, so a half-photographed
  roster still reads as one wall — the customer side of a QBR is almost never
  photographed. The monogram is quiet beside real faces and takes the categorical
  palette when nobody has a photo, because it is standing in for something missing
  in the first case and carrying an identity in the second.
- **Each composition holds the roster it advertises, and reflows to keep it.**
  The counts are measured on real renders rather than inferred: `bench` and the
  default three-up hold twelve and eight, `lead` nine, `sides` six a side, `bio`
  six. `lead`'s ranked band widens by a column per extra person so it stays one
  row — a fixed four columns used to wrap the sixth person to a second row that
  landed off the slide, taking a name with it. A coda or footer takes 121px out
  of the stage, and every composition absorbs it: the default turns its cards on
  their side, portrait beside the words instead of above them; `lead` tightens
  its band; `sides` closes its column gap; `bio`, whose rows are already at their
  floor, drops to five and says so in its capacity note.

- **More acronyms and abbreviations are spoken.** Acronyms with one meaning across academic, corporate, team, government and nonprofit decks (GPA, AUC, CRM, QBR, VP, RFP, OIG, GIS, WCAG); the dotted abbreviations with one meaning (e.g., i.e., etc., vs., approx., a.m., p.m., Ph.D., Mr., Ms.); and capitals joined by periods (U.S., D.C.), spelled. An acronym with two meanings (AP, ERP, CFR, …) is never guessed: `lint:deck` names its meanings so the deck can say which (`narration-acronym-ambiguous`).
- **The Studio editor completes a term's fields** (`pronounce`, `expansion`, `definition`) inside `terms:`. On a phone, a completion's help text now sits below the whole list instead of covering the options under the selected one.
- **The Studio warns when the chosen Gemini voice misreads words by position.** Gemini Flash-Lite TTS was measured saying the same term differently depending on where it falls in a sentence; Workspace settings now says so under the Voice model card and names voices that read it the same every time.

- **One `terms:` map for how a deck's words are spoken.** A plain value is what the voice says (`Derby: Darby`); the long form keeps what a term stands for, how to say it and its glossary definition apart (`EBITDA: { expansion: …, pronounce: ee bit dah, definition: … }`). Every narration path reads it: Present, the narration bake, Share and Export, `--captions` and the tours. `acronyms:` and `lexicon:` still work as older names, and `lint:deck` offers to move them (`terms-key-renamed`).
- **A term now matches the forms a deck writes.** One entry covers plurals and possessives (`CROs`, `CRO's`), hyphen and slash compounds (`CRO-led`, `CRO/CFO`), the title-case and all-caps forms of a lower-case or Capitalized key (`Derby`, `DERBY`), and multi-word names (`"Twinkima G"`). Before, only the exact token matched, so each variant read as written.
- **Studio: one Terms list under Deck setup → Speech**, replacing the separate Lexicon and Acronyms lists. Each row has "Say it as", "Stands for" and "Definition", a silence toggle, and ▶ to hear the term in your current voice before a slide uses it.
- **The Studio assistant can fix pronunciation.** It adds or changes deck terms (`set_terms`) and shows how a slide or a line will be spoken (`preview_speech`), so you no longer paste YAML by hand.
- **`@laticent/cadenza` exports `houseTerms()`**: the built-in terms with what each stands for and how it is said, for a glossary or a term picker.

- Two more formats are written down as specs, each a draft for the owner's sign-off with shared test cases: the theme contract (`spec/THEME-1.0.md`: what a theme file holds, the 118 tokens it declares, its manifest, and what a reader refuses) and the `.lattice` project file (`spec/LATTICE-FILE-1.0.md`: the archive, the manifest, carried packages, and the checks a reader runs before trusting one). `node tools/theme-conformance.js` runs the theme cases against Lattice.

- `engineering/development.md` §Context cost now sizes the `MAX_THINKING_TOKENS` lever instead of only naming it: thinking is 37% of output tokens and about 6% of the bill, measured over 69 turns. §Re-measuring gains the script that produces it, with the five traps that each produced a wrong number first — the transcript stores no thinking text, one API message spans several records that repeat the same usage, a mid-stream record carries a partial `output_tokens`, the o200k-to-meter gap is proportional rather than constant, and some turns record an `output_tokens` below their own visible content.
- The script now self-checks: run over turns that did no thinking, it must find none. That line is what catches the proportional-gap trap, and the signature cross-check does not — a correlation is scale-invariant, so it validates the estimator's shape and never its level.
- Recorded the measurement, the priced cap options and a recommendation against a repo-wide default in `engineering/decisions/2026-09-22-thinking-is-a-third-of-output.md`.

- **New `topic` anchor** — marks a topic WITHIN a section, where `divider` marks the boundary
  BETWEEN sections. A horizontal cut: the topic's name and one-sentence claim above, the
  section's topics as a scale below with the current one lit on the seam.
- **The sibling track is DERIVED, not authored.** `lib/transformers/topic-track.js` reads the
  `## heading` of every `topic` slide in a section and builds each slide's track, the way
  `lib/forms/tile/progress` derives section position one level up. Renaming a topic is a
  one-slide edit, and the track cannot go stale or mark the wrong item. Authoring a `<ul>`
  on a `topic` slide overrides the derivation for that slide.
- **`topic fact` variant** — one flat canvas with the type hierarchy inverted: the claim takes
  the display tier and the name demotes to a label on a rule, with a mono provenance line at
  the foot. For when the room needs the finding rather than the label.
- On an overridden track the current item is marked by bolding the WHOLE label
  (`- **Payback**`); if nothing is marked, the item matching the slide's own heading is lit.
  Emphasis inside a label (`- Cost to **win**`) is styling, not a marker.
- `findTopLevelH2` moved from the masthead kernel to `lib/core/top-level-h2.js` so both callers
  share one depth-aware heading reader instead of cloning the depth-blind regex. That reader is
  now a tokenizer rather than a chain of regex masks: it skips a comment only where a comment can
  START, skips RAWTEXT content, and honors quoted attribute values — so `<div data-tip="a <!-- b">`
  and `<style>/* <!-- */</style>` no longer hide a slide's heading. It also matches `<H2>`
  case-insensitively, as `:scope > h2` always did on the runtime path. Rendered output is
  unchanged on all 184 committed `examples/*.md` (measured at 4999ea3).

- **A guided course in the Show me menu.** Four new narrated tours join the welcome tour, each ending on a "Go further" card for the next: **Read** (the quiet view and the article view), **Craft** (every panel: Coach, Chat, Live, Library, Views, Slide and Deck settings, Version history, Setup), **Present** (every control in the room) and **Share** (every way a deck leaves the Studio). The last offers the lessons.
- **Tours save and restore your screen.** Whichever tour you start, it sets up the layout it needs and puts back your stop, panels, folded pane and slide when it ends, however it ends.

- **New `tower` chart for reinsurance and insurance programs.** Write each layer as its limit in excess of its attachment (`$40M xs $50M`, also `x/s` or `excess of`) and list each reinsurer's share under it. The chart stacks the layers from the retention up, keeps one color per reinsurer across every layer, shows any unplaced share as `Open`, and prints each boundary figure on the right. Layers are drawn at equal height so small bottom layers stay readable; their sizes are printed beside them. Narration says the layers aloud ("forty million dollars excess of fifty million dollars") from the bottom up. Demo deck: `examples/tower.md`.

- **Trama, the graph-chart library (`@laticent/trama`).** The flowchart's layout engine and browser pipeline move into a workspace package: dagre places the boxes, one solver routes every line, and a pipeline measures a chart in its own fonts, fits it, lays it out in a worker while you type in the Studio, and paints it through a chart adapter. It has no dependencies (dagre is passed in) and knows nothing of Markdown or CSS. Flowcharts draw exactly as before.
- **The CLI warns when it cannot lay out a flowchart.** If the flowchart's layout code fails to load, the export says so (`⚠ flowchart layout unavailable … flowcharts export as their fallback tiles`) instead of exporting the tiles silently. The published CLI bundle carries Trama inline, so an install of the CLI needs nothing more.

- **Added: `lib/core/dom-provider`** — parse a rendered-HTML string into a DOM and
  serialize it back, using the parser the environment already has: the browser's
  native `DOMParser` (0.100 ms per slide, 0.9% of the Studio's edit→paint budget)
  and jsdom in Node. Groundwork for collapsing the fifteen transformers that carry
  two implementations of one restructure. Not yet wired into the render path.
- **Added: `npm run parity:transforms`** — runs both implementations of every
  registry transformer over the gallery corpus and classifies each difference.
  Currently a report, and explicitly **not yet trustworthy**: it calls
  `applyAllToDom` without the runtime's front-matter and form-class pre-steps, so
  most of what it flags is that gap rather than a real disagreement. The tool and
  its decision note both say so.

- Add the 2026-10-25 issue and follow-up triage note: what to close, what to fix before the 1.0.0 release, and eight agent workstreams.

- **Chrome is drawn, not typed — ten new `--shape-*` mask tokens.** Every arrow,
  chevron, spark, transport control and status mark the engine draws now comes from an
  SVG mask whose color is the element's, so it renders identically whatever fonts a
  machine has. Eighteen `content:` glyph occurrences across ten stylesheets were typed
  glyphs (`✓` `→` `❯` `✦` `●`); a typed glyph has no shape of its own — the deck's type
  family carries none of them, so each machine substitutes a different font, a color
  emoji, or a hollow box. Governed by HARD RULE #29. (They are `--shape-*`, not
  `--icon-*`: the docs site already owns 32 Lucide `--icon-*` on `:root`, and five of
  the names would have collided with different geometry.)
- **`lint:deck` now coaches typed glyphs instead of silently rendering them.** A `✓` in
  a deck gets a WARNING — never an error — naming what it will look like on another
  machine, the modifier that does it properly, and the concrete fix. Authors keep
  writing whatever they like; the linter offers the better option.
- **New `state-cells` modifier.** Puts the universal status markers (`[x]` `[-]` `[ ]`
  `[/]`) to work in ANY table's cells — previously only `obligation-matrix` decoded all
  four, and `matrix-grid` decodes a different, positional set of three. So a comparison
  table can now carry the color-blind-safe status disc rather than a typed check.
- **The a11y and print status glyphs are deliberately unchanged.** They are the
  grayscale-safe shape channel for color-blind and toner-only readers, and the
  measurements behind them (empty-alt `content` is the only thing that keeps them out
  of the accessibility tree; the doubled declaration is a cross-engine pair) are
  recorded in `engineering/decisions/2026-08-25-typed-glyphs.md`.
- **New demo deck `examples/drawn-not-typed.md`** — what a typed glyph actually does
  on a machine that is not yours, both new modifiers in use, and the three places the
  rule deliberately stops.

- A new library, **Veduta** (`@laticent/veduta`, `docs/src/lib/veduta`): a headless, dependency-free core that decides which units of a long list a view should mount, at what fidelity and in what order, for a stage and a map beside it. Three window policies (single, multi, picture-in-picture), a fidelity ladder, a page-global live budget priced per connector, and a capacity the host reports. It costs the same at 120 and at 100,000 units, and its window equals the Playground filmstrip's. Has a mark, a catalog entry, a guide page and a demo page on the docs site; not yet published to npm.

- **The Playground knows which authored slide each preview page belongs to.** `rendered-index.ts` joins the page stamps of the preview split to the deck outline and names slide clones (focus steps, pane slides) and split runs, with a test over all 292 example decks at three sizes. No rendered output changes.
- **A slide map in the Playground.** **Map** in the toolbar opens a rail of every slide beside the preview (under it on a phone or tablet), with first, previous, next and last (on a phone the strip folds into the walk bar beside a stacked Prev, position and Next). Tiles near the rail are live pictures, the rest are sketches read from the slide's source, and it follows the preview whether you scroll, step or type. Off by default and remembered per browser.
- **A slide map in the Studio.** The map button in the slide navigator bar opens the same rail beside the focused preview (under it on a narrow pane), numbered within a reader lens, with first, previous, next and last. Off by default and remembered.

- A one-block prose component (`big-number`, `redline`, `image`, `citation-card`, `collage`) now states the words its main slot holds at each venue (`venueCapacity.prose`, with a row per register where one differs), and `lint:deck` warns with the new `venue-prose` rule when a slide is past it. The numbers show in each component's docs "By venue" line and in the pick list.

- **Vetrina — `caption: 'cursor'`**, a fifth narration style: a speech balloon anchored where the cursor is resting, which steps aside while the cursor performs (typing, clicking, dragging, a deictic stroke) and comes back when it stops. It never follows the pointer — a caption that drifts during a fixation cannot be read — and Exit moves to a persistent corner chip, so a caption that can hide never takes the escape hatch with it.
- **Vetrina — `bounds: 'host'`**, which confines the tour's chrome to the `root` element it drives instead of the window. It is a clamping box, not a containing block: the overlay layer stays `position: fixed` and click-through, and no host CSS has to change. This also fixes the `bar` style's `width: calc(100vw - 24px)`, measured at 704px of caption inside a 642px app.
- **Vetrina — a narration port (`Narrator`, `SILENT_NARRATOR`, `findCueWord`)** plus a Cadenza-backed adapter at `docs/src/lib/vetrina-narration/`. Wiring one in gives every `say` beat the line's real duration instead of a reading estimate, and a word clock — both with no audio, since a timed track is text arithmetic.
- **Vetrina — `Step.at` / `scene().at(word)`**, the word cue: the beat's action lands on the word that names it. Whichever side is behind waits, so the cursor arrives exactly as the narration reaches the word (measured: 1 ms). Degrades to the beat's normal order with no narrator, or when the line does not contain the word.
- **Vetrina — `pacing.ts`**, one cited duration model behind the five hand-tuned literals: Fitts's law for cursor travel (target size finally matters), a caption reading budget matched to Cadenza's 150 wpm and pinned to it by a cross-library test, a register beat that costs nothing when the cursor is already on target, and a typing reveal above the ~40 ms threshold at which characters stop resolving as separate events. **It is opt-in** — `theme.pacing` defaults to `'legacy'`, which reproduces the old literals byte for byte, because adopting the grounded numbers re-times an existing tour by ~13% and that is a decision, not an upgrade side effect.
- **Vetrina narration — `voicedNarrator`**, the speaking rung of the same port. Hand it a `synthesize(text)` and it plays through Suono, drives the word clock off the real audio clock, and re-anchors to the clip's measured onset — Cadenza's hybrid align, where the estimate is the baseline and the measurement refines it. It owns no key, no model and no network, so the voice stays the caller's. A voice that fails does not take the tour down.
- **Vetrina narration — the voiced re-anchor scales EVERY sentence into the measured clip**, not just the first. Anchoring only cue 0 stretched sentence one across the whole clip and pushed every later sentence past the end of the audio, where it was never highlighted, on a timeline longer than the sound. `synthesizeTimeoutMs` (20s) stops a hung voice from hanging the beat, and an already-aborted run no longer reaches `synthesize` at all — with a real TTS behind it that was a billed request and audible speech after teardown.

- **Vetrina narration can lean left or right.** Suono's `play()` takes a `pan` (-1 left … 1 right) and a live clip glides with `setPan`; the storyboard sets it from where each beat's target sits on screen, so the voice follows the cursor. Narrators without `setPan` are unaffected.

- The video plugin has its own page on the docs site (a live demo with three examples and a Learn page), a refreshed mark that matches the other plugins, and a full reference: the four providers with every address form each accepts, the layouts, the Studio player, exports and migration. The Plugins hub counts nine.
- A demo deck, `examples/video-plugin.md`, shows all four providers (YouTube, Vimeo, TikTok, Instagram), the companion, gallery and code layouts, the accepted address forms and a slide with no poster. The plugin's conformance cases and the Studio's player check now cover every provider, not only YouTube.
- `lint:deck` warns when an `@video{…}` record is on a slide that is not a `video` slide (`video-slide-class`), where it used to draw an unstyled blue link and say nothing; the clip is now a quiet text link in the deck's accent, and when a `video` slide holds a second record (`video-extra-record`), which used to drop the second clip silently.
- In the `gallery` layout the provider's badge now sits on the matte's lower edge. With a portrait or square poster (the usual shape of a TikTok or Instagram thumbnail) it used to hang off the picture's corner.
- The Studio's video player now always shows "Not playing? Open on {provider}" under it. Some browsers (Firefox, Orion) block a third-party player frame and leave it blank with no error the page can see; the link opens the clip's own page.
- When a TikTok or Instagram player stays silent for 8 seconds, the Studio's video player says it didn't load and that a tracking blocker may be the cause, above the "Open on" link. The close button now sits on the backdrop's corner instead of over the player, so it no longer hides TikTok's logo.

- **Layout names as you type in VS Code.** The Marp kit ships `lattice-layouts.vsix`, a small extension: type `<!-- _class: ` and a menu lists every layout with its one-line summary, again after a space for a second class. It answers nowhere else, so typing prose never opens a menu. Install it with **Extensions → ⋯ → Install from VSIX…** or `code --install-extension lattice-layouts.vsix`. An Export-to-Marp bundle's README links to the kit's copy.

- **Waterfall `lower-is-better`.** `<!-- _class: waterfall lower-is-better -->` swaps the meaning colors for a walk where a rise is bad news, such as a loss ratio, claims, cost or churn: a rise is drawn in the fail color and a fall in the pass color, in every theme and finish. Direction is unchanged: the bars, the signs and the print textures still show up and down. It combines with `zoom`.

- `marks: tone ink` and `marks: tone accent` pick the one hue `tone` draws its charts in: the deck's heading ink, or the theme's accent, instead of chart color one. Per slide, `_class: marks-ink` / `marks-accent`. The names, edges and strongest step clear the slide on every built-in palette in both modes; a source under `pigment` or `etch` does nothing, and `lint:deck` says so (`marks-source-needs-tone`). Decks that name no source render exactly as before.
- **Etch on a dark slide changed look:** its chart bodies now clear 3:1 against the slide (they measured 1.14 to 1.57:1, so the outline carried the bar alone). The dark body is the category's lighter ink at 78% instead of its hue at 40%, so etch bars on dark read stronger and the doubled edge reads quieter. The bullet measure follows. Light slides do not change. This intentionally changes every etch chart on a dark slide (a `dark` slide, a `*-dark` theme or a dark color mode); the shipped example decks and goldens use etch only on light slides, so none of them moves as authored. Viewed in a dark color mode, their etch charts take the new dark body.

### Changed

- **Breaking:** `theme: carbone` now resolves **light**. Carbone was curated a real light
  face and takes the house two-file shape, so a deck that wants the graphite canvas asks
  for `theme: carbone-dark`. The dark surfaces and ink are the ones carbone shipped
  before (its categorical order changed later; see the carbone-curation entry). One
  rendering DOES change on the dark face, and for the better: a
  `<!-- _class: light -->` slide used to keep a graphite canvas while its inks flipped
  light (the #1527 seam), and now the canvas genuinely goes light.
- Carbone gained a curated light face. The electric lime `#7DE38A` measures 1.47:1 on an
  off-white canvas and cannot carry text, so `--accent`'s light arm is `#037829` — the same
  hue at 95% of the same chroma, 60% of the lightness, reading 5.24:1. The bright value
  stays the brand axis and the spectrum ribbon, and the code block keeps its graphite ground
  on both faces, so the terminal register survives the flip.
- The last `KNOWN_BELOW_AA` diagram-ink sanction (`errorTextColor`, 2.34:1) is **retired**.
  It was never a diagram defect: carbone's status trio declared light arms tuned for an
  off-white canvas the palette did not have. Giving it that canvas resolved the pair without
  the CVD trade the recorded alternative required.

- The `@visual` pixel baselines are taken against a fixed fixture deck (`docs/e2e/visual-fixture.ts`) instead of the Studio's seeded welcome deck. The old shot baked that deck's copy — including the live catalog count its own gate keeps current — into three committed PNGs, so adding a component turned them red in a PR that never touched the Studio's chrome. The fixture carries no number the repo tracks, and the spec now proves the seed loaded before it shoots.

- The docs site now builds on astro 7.2 with `@astrojs/starlight` 0.41, replacing astro 6.3 and
  Starlight 0.39. The two can only move together — Starlight 0.41 is the first release to peer
  astro 7 — which is why #1483 sat blocked for three weeks. Nothing the Lattice package ships
  changes; the built site is the docs site only.
- `astro.config.mjs` names its Markdown processor explicitly —
  `markdown: { processor: unified({ rehypePlugins: [rehypeScrollableTables] }) }` — instead of the
  `markdown.rehypePlugins` shorthand astro 7 deprecates, and `@astrojs/markdown-remark` is now a
  direct dependency. The shorthand still works and still builds this same processor, but it does so
  by importing a package astro 7 no longer installs, which reached the tree only as a transitive
  dependency of Starlight's `@astrojs/mdx`. The WCAG 2.1.1 table tab-stop should not rest on another
  package's dependency graph. The rendered site is byte-identical across the change, all 1,427 files.

- The e2e suite's 21 inherited fixed `waitForTimeout` sleeps are all dispositioned: six are
  replaced with the signal they were standing in for (an overflow-marker attribute, the
  filtered grid's height, the Present dialog, the exported page's boot stamp, and a shared
  `markersSettled` helper that waits for webfonts and then for the marker set to stop
  moving), and fifteen are kept with a written reason — absence assertions, poll intervals,
  measurement windows, and quiescence before a perf counter is zeroed. No behavior change
  for deck authors; this is nightly-suite reliability and wall clock.

- **Investigated (no behavior change, and the flip is still NOT shipped): the palette/base concat
  sign-off sweep, and it changes the recommendation.** Three things are now measured that were
  not. **The blast radius** — all 32 themes in both modes, before and after, 576 slides a side:
  every one of the 64 grid states changes at least one slide. Sixteen of the 32 theme files are
  `-dark` wrappers that render identically to their parent at a fixed `color-mode`, so the honest
  distinct figures are 36 of 36 states and 99 changed renderings rather than 64 and 202 — the
  conclusion is unchanged and the earlier four-themes-light-only sample was still a wide
  underestimate. **The preview already renders the
  flipped order** — `lib/engine`'s `composeCss` inlines the base at the theme's own
  `@import 'lattice'` position, so the Studio, the docs site and the browser playground show the
  palette's value; driven on the real engine, 932 of 932 disputed tokens resolve exactly as the
  flip would and none as the export does. Preview and export therefore disagree *today*, on every
  theme, and the flip makes them agree rather than swapping which one is wrong. **And the flip is
  not purely an activation of better values**: across 960 contrast pairs (the twelve `--hljs-*`
  against `--code-bg`, the status trio against `--bg`), 684 change, 411 get worse, 11 cross below
  their floor and 3 cross above. Looking at those 11 rather than trusting them corrected the
  reading twice — `a11y-achromatopsia`'s dark checklist genuinely loses its rails and icons
  (the palette declares flat grays with no `light-dark()` pair, authored for a light canvas), while
  `a11y-deuteranopia`'s apparent regression is its intended blue encoding finally rendering and
  staying perfectly legible, which says the reference surface was wrong for that use rather than
  the palette. The flip stays the right direction; two masked authoring defects must be repaired
  first, and an `--hljs-* × --code-bg` AA gate should land with it.
  (`engineering/decisions/2026-08-11-palette-concat-signoff.md`)

- **Changed: `check:family-tiers` now says whether a new overflow is a defect or
  baseline drift, and proves which.** The overflow oracle reported every new clip as
  `NEW CLIPS: … Fix the layout; do not bless it away`, at every `@size`. That is true
  only where no split is available: the sweep sets no `autosplit`, so a clip means
  "overflows when the author has not opted in", and a component that declares a split
  path may paginate instead. The verdict now separates `NEW CLIPS (ring)` — which
  keeps the fix-the-layout wording — from `NEW CLIPS (may paginate)`. A landscape
  `@size` short-circuits to `ring`, mirroring the engine's own `AUTOSPLIT_APPLIES`.
  Enrollment in `split-oracle.json` is treated as an INDICATION, not proof: it is a
  component-type opt-in from the manifest, and `lib/core/auto-split.js` still rings
  when no seam is available for the content at hand. So the verdict now names a
  falsifiable check — `--verify-paginates <component>@<size>,…` renders each with
  splitting ON and exits non-zero on any that still clips.
- **Changed: the family-overflow oracle is re-blessed after a month of drift.**
  `test/oracle/family-overflow.json` was last blessed on 2026-07-28 (#1236), and it
  records what overflows with pagination disabled, so ordinary spacing and typography
  work moves it. No layout changed: `hd` — the one row where a clip is what a reader
  sees — stays at 0, and all 18 newly-recorded (component, `@size`) pairs were
  rendered with splitting on and produced no overflow. Three entries left the record
  as genuine improvements: `policy-recommendation` (square, story) and `roadmap`
  (square, story, mobile). `matrix-grid` joins the roster because #1627 gave it an
  adaptive arm; it clips nowhere.

- **The preview sanitizes faster, and stops re-sanitizing bytes it has already
  sanitized.** `sanitizeSlideHtml` configures DOMPurify once instead of on every
  call, which is ~0.8ms off every slide at a 4x CPU throttle (26-40% of the call,
  measured in real Chromium) on every route — including typing, where the
  HTML is new by construction. On top of that, the single-slide preview keeps a
  bounded memo of what it has already sanitized, keyed on the whole HTML string,
  so revisiting a slide — rail navigation, the overview grid's second pass,
  Present walking back, or an edit to a slide you are not looking at — costs no
  DOMPurify pass at all. Output is byte-identical; nothing reaches a preview
  frame unsanitized.

- **Changed: a changelog entry is now its own file, `changelog.d/<slug>.<category>.md`.**
  Every PR used to append to one shared `## Unreleased` region, so two PRs in flight
  always edited the same lines — and under a merge queue that is not a conflict you
  resolve once but an **ejection**, which silently clears auto-merge so going green
  again merges nothing. Measured over one evening of five PRs: seven ejections, every
  one a `MERGE_CONFLICT` on `CHANGELOG.md`, every resolution the same mechanical "keep
  both entries"; one PR needed six cycles across about four hours for a change whose
  content stopped moving after the second. Two PRs never write the same fragment file.
  The category lives in the FILENAME rather than in front matter, so deriving the
  release bump is a directory listing that no prose can confuse and a typo is a loud
  gate failure instead of an entry silently dropped from the release. `--bump`,
  `--notes` and `--check` read `## Unreleased` and the pending fragments as one body;
  the release folds them in under their `### Category` headings and deletes them, in
  the commit it already cuts. **Nothing regenerates `CHANGELOG.md` per PR** — a
  build-time assembly would make it a generated-from-everything artifact byte-gated by
  `build:check`, trading a visible conflict for the silent ejection that hazard causes.
  Fragments are ordinary repo prose, so unlike the exempt `CHANGELOG.md` they are in
  scope for the US-English gate. (`engineering/decisions/2026-08-11-changelog-fragments.md`)

- **Investigated (no behavior change, nothing deleted): whether `engineering/decisions/` is an
  archive or a queue.** 232 of 391 notes are `shipped`, which the generated index calls "pending
  teardown", and none has ever been torn down — 166 notes landed in the last thirty days, about
  five and a half a day, so no per-merge ritual would approach the fill rate. One evening of work
  against the corpus says the framing is wrong rather than the execution: **four of the five cards
  worked in this batch were scoped entirely by a note's "what this does not fix" section, and
  three of those notes are in the pending-teardown group.** Absorbing them into canon and deleting
  them would have deleted the backlog — canon holds a conclusion, while what these carry is the
  measurement, the runnable harness, the corrections and the caveats. Re-running one such harness
  found a four-theme sample had missed an accessibility regression across 64 theme-modes. The real
  defect is narrower than 102,554 lines: the index heading asserts a process that has never once
  run, which is a stale claim in a generated file. Recommendation is the issue's option (4) —
  call the folder what it is — but it retires a convention the owner wrote, so it was asked rather
  than taken. **Answered: the archive.** See the entry above for what landed.
  (`engineering/decisions/2026-08-11-decision-note-teardown.md`)

- **`engineering/decisions/` is now officially a dated archive — notes are corrected in place and
  marked `superseded`, never deleted.** This reverses a convention that had stood since the folder
  was created ("absorb into canon, then delete — this folder is not an archive") and that had
  **never once been executed** across 391 notes. Measuring it is what settled it: four of five
  cards in one batch existed only because a `shipped` note wrote down what it had *not* finished,
  so running the delete rule would have deleted the work queue. Canon holds a conclusion; a note
  holds the measurement, the harness, the corrections, and the caveats — and those caveats are
  what scope the next session. The generated index heading stops claiming **"pending teardown"**,
  a stale assertion in a generated file being the narrower defect underneath the complaint. The
  corpus total is surfaced in the post-merge standup instead of the index, where it is spoken in
  chat rather than committed and so cannot become the line two concurrent PRs disagree about
  (#1547). CLAUDE.md's guidance to leave a durable note is unchanged and endorsed.
  (`engineering/decisions/2026-08-11-decision-note-teardown.md` §7)

- **Charts now sit at the frame inset — the same 64px margin as prose, code and diagrams.**
  #1598 removed one of the chart's three inline insets and left the second, on the belief that
  a chart's wider berth was a deliberate design choice. It was not: the retired width calc's own
  comment justified it as a *sizing* workaround, the padding line carried no comment at all, and
  the nearest thing to a defense was the opt-in glass panel adopting "its **existing** padding" — a
  value already there for an unrecorded reason. Two measurements retired it, cutting in opposite
  directions. A **height-bound** SVG chart letterboxes to its box, so the inset was dead space —
  a quadrant renders pixel-identical at 64 and at 128. A **width-bound** one was *losing drawing
  size* to it: gantt's SVG grows 1024×238.9 → 1152×268.8, and gantt, map and word-cloud each
  repaint 5–10% of the slide. And it was an **alignment defect**: the masthead's hairline spans
  the full frame, so a chart at 128 read visibly narrower than the rule directly above it — the
  same misalignment the diagram had. Bars, kanban lanes, table columns and status pills now share
  edges with the rule and the title, and the opt-in **canvas** glass panel follows the frame with
  them (landscape 1024→1152, portrait 864→972), its own internal berth unchanged. Three per-chart
  overrides were **deleted** rather than added: the family's tall/strip value pulled *in* from the
  landscape default; state-chart's held a specificity tie whose both sides are now zero;
  timeline-list-tall's pushed *out* to three times the family's tall/strip berth, which is
  precisely the extra room this retires.
- **`claim-bleed` on a card- or table-bodied chart now warns, and no longer runs content to the
  trim edge if you do it anyway.** The house rule is that prose-dense layouts opt out of bleed via
  their manifest `excludes`, which makes `lint:deck` warn you off to `claim-hero` — but only
  matrix-grid had ever declared it. **progress, kanban, timeline-list, roadmap and journey now
  declare it too**, so the warning finally fires for them. And because that is a warning rather
  than an error, the render is made safe as well: those six floor at the frame's safe inset, the
  same berth the header and footer bands use, while SVG charts and the self-scaling state-chart
  bleed as intended. Before this, a `kanban claim-bleed` sliced its first card's corner and shadow
  at x=0 and a `journey claim-bleed` put an actor badge 4px from the paper — invisible until now
  because the chart's own 64px inset had been silently flooring every bleed.
- **Fixed: a journey mood marker no longer hangs off its own track — and still lands on its own
  gridline.** The portrait variant plotted the face at `left: ((mood − 1) / 4) × 100%`, so a mood-5
  face was centered **on** the track's right edge with half of it outside; the old chart padding was
  simply wider than the overhang. The 1–5 scale now maps across the track less one face width, and
  the gridlines are inset by that same half-face, so a face still sits exactly on the line for its
  value — a mood chart's whole contract is that position *is* the value. `npm run check:chart-fit`
  is down to 3 clips (from 4, and 5 before this line of work); `overflow:check` is clean across all
  268 decks. `engineering/decisions/2026-08-11-stage-owns-the-outer-inset.md`. (#1598)

- **Every chart figure is 128px wider and every diagram now lines up with its own
  title.** The stage owns the outer inset — a body owns only the spacing between its own
  elements — is now a named Forms invariant (`design/forms.md` §6.1). Chart and diagram were
  both re-deriving the frame inset with the same `calc(100cqi - 2 * var(--sp-2xl))` expression,
  and the chart stacked its own padding on top: a chart's figure sat 192px from the slide edge
  and a diagram's 128, against prose's 64. Both calc copies retire, `.chart-body` and the
  mermaid box fill their container exactly, and the chart's five per-chart inset tunings move
  to `.cell-stage` verbatim — so a chart's **berth is unchanged** and the block axis is
  neutral to the pixel (the `cqh` basis is the same number, subtracted one box higher), while
  the inline duplicate is reclaimed. A diagram's body now shares one left edge with its title,
  dek and Key Insight for the first time. The opt-in `canvas` glass panel keeps its inset and
  owns it in the `.canvas` rule, where a box that paints a surface earns one. Kept by two gates: `checkStageInsetOwnership`
  (`tools/check-ownership.js`, via `build:check`) and a measured inset assertion in
  `check-chart-fit.js` at landscape/portrait/square.
  The change is **inline-only**: a body's BLOCK padding turned out to be a clip margin, not an
  inset (`overflow` cuts at the padding box), and removing it clipped nine decks that had never
  clipped — so it stays, renamed for its job. The adversarial trio caught four override paths
  that had to be re-checked against the new tie (`no-form`, `canvas`, `claim-hero`/`claim-bleed`,
  a tall/strip `state-chart`), each now measured byte-identical to its pre-change render; and
  the reclaim exposed two boxes that were bigger than their container by construction —
  **gantt**'s SVG (a `max-height: 100%` that never bound) and **matrix-grid**'s figure
  (`width: 100%` plus a `padding-left` under content-box sizing) — both fixed here.
  `npm run overflow:check` is clean: zero newly-clipping pages across 268 decks.
  `engineering/decisions/2026-08-11-stage-owns-the-outer-inset.md`. (#1598)

- `quadrant` now sizes its item labels **per slide** instead of from one constant shared by every quadrant in every deck. That constant had to be the largest size the most crowded slide in the corpus could carry, so a sparse chart printed at a size a fourteen-dot chart needed. The kernel takes the largest size the slide's own geometry can carry: measured across the 25 quadrant slides in the tree, 22 print larger than before and 5 reach the house's smallest type tier, where none did. A slide that cannot be lifted renders byte-identically to before.
- The size search will not buy type with attribution. Its first cut accepted any size at which every name still placed, and on the gallery's own headline slide that took the top rung and pushed seven of eight names off their dots — the worst by about 15% of the plot width — stacking three into a column that reads as a list, with one name parked on a neighboring quadrant's fill. Every name was present, so nothing objected; the render showed it. A rung is now accepted only while no more names travel, and none travels further, than at the size the slide already rendered at.
- `quadrant`'s label width budget scales with the chosen type size, so a bigger name keeps the same characters-per-line instead of wrapping to three lines and breaking mid-word.
- The `--quadrant-dot-size` custom property is new, and is the floor rather than the size — themes can retune it, and the kernel writes the per-slide choice onto the label group.

- **Changed: the Studio's posture dial reads Read · Write · Craft.** The full stop — every
  panel, the activity bar, every tool docked — was called **Build**; it is now **Craft**.
  Nothing about the surface changes: same three stops, same chrome at each, same one-click
  reversibility. The word does. "Build" was doing five jobs in this app at once — `npm run
  build`, "rendered at build time", the anima `motion-style: build` ("Build reveals in reading
  order"), tour builders — and the one place it named *a place you stand* was the one place it
  was ambiguous. **Your saved stop survives the upgrade**: a workspace that stored the old value boots
  into Craft and normalizes on the next save. (Not the *downgrade* — a browser still running a
  pre-rename bundle, after a revert or in a tab left open across the deploy, resets the stop to
  Write. One click on the dial puts it back.) The `motion-style: build` deck front matter is a
  different word and is untouched — no deck changes. `engineering/decisions/2026-08-11-studio-craft-stop-rename.md`

- The overflow / type-floor / Fix-Me markers are now measured **once per settled render** instead of on every animation frame in which anything in the document changed. A sweep is triggered by the things that can actually change a verdict — the debounced content pass, fonts settling, a resize, a scroll bringing new slides into view — and probes only the slides in the viewport band whose verdict is stale. On the filmstrip this is 9–26× cheaper per sweep (58-slide deck: 9.4ms → 0.4ms; a 40-slide all-overflowing deck: 20.7ms → 1.9ms), and it stops the watcher from forcing layout on slides the preview had deliberately virtualized away.
- The three marker tabs are now **part of the rendered slide** — the engine emits an empty, hidden `.overflow-tab`, `.illegible-tab` and `.fixme-tab` in every `<section>`, and the watchers only fill them. Nothing creates or destroys marker DOM any more, so the live preview and an exported artifact carry the same markup, and the browser runtime and the export's inline watcher write to the same element instead of each minting their own.
- The Fix-Me signal is drawn **inside the slide**: an `outline` on the culprit cell plus a corner label, replacing the floating overlay layer that was rebuilt on every pass and re-synced on scroll. It now tracks scrolling and the preview's own scale for free, and it cannot perturb the layout it is measuring.
- New on-demand bench tier, `npm run bench -- --sweep`, times the sweep in a real browser against a filmstrip-virtualized deck. Nothing measured this path before: it runs over laid-out DOM, so the in-process render tier could not see it and the whole-cycle export tier drowned it. `bench:check` gates the scoped-vs-whole-document ratio against a 3× floor.
- **Fixed:** the two `image`-layout marker berths (`.illegible-tab`, `.fixme-tab`) were being folded into the `.image-text` panel by the runtime, duplicating them and pointing `section.image .image-text > :last-child` at an empty marker div instead of the author's last block. Nothing moved on screen — a composition rule won the tie — but the panel-order invariant was being violated.
- **Fixed:** an auto-split cover page carried no marker berth, so its ring depended on the runtime minting one at watch time rather than on the markup. The export now re-berths after the split converges; verified on a 26-row deck split into 10 real pages, every page carrying exactly one of each berth.
- **Fixed:** the viewport band alone left slides silently unmeasured — a document nobody scrolls (a print, an Export-to-Marp bundle, which renders through this runtime) got only its first viewport measured, and a slide scrolled straight past could be skipped permanently. An idle **completeness backstop** now sweeps the whole document at the current generation, so every slide gets a verdict; it costs 0.1–0.4ms because the cache skips everything already measured. A max-wait on the interactive debounce fixes the second half — a trailing debounce never fired during a continuous scroll.
- **Fixed:** the Fix-Me signal would have baked into Studio raster exports (PNG/PPTX/PDF). The old overlay lived outside the capture's clone boundary by accident; moving it into the slide moved it inside. `.lattice-exporting` now suppresses it, restoring the previous property explicitly.
- `window.latticeSweep.complete()` gives every slide a verdict without re-opening a generation — what the backstop runs, exposed for a host that needs it now (before a print or an export).
- `window.latticeSweep` lets a host that knows when its render landed (the Studio, the Playground) drive the sweep directly rather than waiting on the observer's settle window.

- Slide layering is now a model instead of a habit. A slide is six named planes (`lib/base/base.tokens.css`): `--z-canvas` and `--z-atmosphere` sink below the words, content rests at the natural flow, and `--z-chrome`, `--z-mark` and `--z-alarm` rise above it. Every layering decision at slide scale names one. This executes the plane model the Form manifests have always declared: every Cell and Tile carries a `z`, and until now nothing read it.
- Every `section` is a stacking context unconditionally. It used to be gated on `.form`, so a sovereign frame such as `title`, `math` or `divider` formed none at all (`image` and `scene` declared one for themselves) and its `z-index` values escaped to the page root, where they were ordered against *other slides*.
- **Fixed:** the section-number watermark painted *under* a finish backdrop rather than above it — its manifest declares the atmosphere plane while its CSS said `z-index: -1`. On patterned finishes the texture ruled straight across the ghost numeral.
- Running chrome (header, footer, progress rail) shared one plane with body content under a `finish:`, so which covered which was decided by DOM order. Chrome now sits above content by definition, on `--z-chrome`, replacing the literal `z-index: 3` and its `section.finish > :is(header, footer)` companion — that companion existed only to undo the blanket rule this change removes.
- Status stamps and the authoring tabs are named planes — `--z-mark` (100) and `--z-alarm` (90) — preserving the order the engine has always shipped: a classification marking outranks an engine annotation on a delivered artifact.
- The deck logo names the content plane (`--z-content`). Its kind is chrome, but a plane says what may cover what, and the mark belongs with the content it sits among — on the chrome plane an off-corner brand logo covered a pull-quote. Nothing in the model is exempt.
- `image`'s `statement` composition no longer prints a page number. The glyph full-bleeds over the photo there and measures 1.72:1 where the image lightens; every other `image` composition and all of `scene` keep theirs.
- Two new gates. `checkZPlanes` (`npm run build:check`) rejects any `z-index` outside the local `0–9` band that does not name a plane token, plus plane tokens nothing reads and tokens nothing defines. `test/integration/invariants/slide-planes.test.js` renders a corpus and asserts every real direct child of every section is on a named plane or in the content flow, and that the canvas and atmosphere planes are the right way round. The Form manifest ↔ CSS check (§4.3) is now an equality test — the manifest plane and the CSS plane must be the same plane — where it was only a monotonicity test that the watermark defect passed.
- **Removed:** `base.finish.css`'s blanket `section.finish > *:not(.backdrop)` rules, their `:where(…)` frame-chrome exclusion list, and the `checkFinishChromeExclusions` gate that kept the list honest. With planes there is nothing to exclude.

- **The Studio's lint popup is a Lattice surface now, not library default chrome.** The
  hover card that reports an authoring problem is restyled as the Coach panel's finding
  card — a severity glyph and word beside the rule id, the message, then the fix as a
  filled accent pill on its own row — replacing `@codemirror/lint`'s stock interior (a
  5px `#d11`/`orange` rail and a `#444` button). Severity reads on three channels (glyph
  SHAPE, the word "Error"/"Warning"/"Note", and color) so it survives the `a11y-*`
  palettes, where the severity hues collapse toward one gray. On a touch device the card
  takes reading sizes and the fix becomes a full-width 44px target.
- **Both code editors now share ONE lint definition** (`docs/src/lib/lint-theme.js`). The
  Studio deck editor and the Playground each dressed the same `@codemirror/lint` DOM
  independently, so the two popups looked different and a fix to one skipped the other.
- **Fixed: the Playground's lint popup was an unthemed light box, dark mode included.**
  It never themed `.cm-tooltip`, so the popup fell through to CodeMirror's built-in
  `#f5f5f5` on every palette — body text on that fill measures 1.32:1 in dark mode, and
  the severity word 1.09:1. Both editors now share the shell as well as the interior.
- **Fixed: lint severity colors never tracked the palette.** The Playground painted the
  squiggle, the gutter marker and the panel with `--db-sev-error` / `--db-sev-warning` —
  tokens referenced in four places and **defined nowhere in the repo**, so their
  `#c0392b` / `#b8860b` fallbacks won on all 36 palette × mode combinations. They now use
