  dot grows about its own center. A small hold zone keeps the card from flickering at mark
  edges. The `ChartDetailLayer` prop `tilt` is renamed `lift`.
- **Fixed: a stacked-bar chart's hover details now open.** The chart never emitted the
  `stacked-bar-svg` class the reveal layer looks for, so authored per-bar detail was never
  shown on hover or tap. Its `<svg>` now carries `cart-svg stacked-bar-svg`, like every
  other chart's figure class.
- **Fixed: thin chart marks can be tapped.** A slope chart's marks are its lines, which
  draw under one screen pixel wide on a phone, so a tap almost never landed on one. When a
  tap or hover misses every mark, the reveal now takes the nearest mark whose outline is
  within reach: 22 screen px for touch, 6 for a mouse. A mark the pointer is actually on
  still wins.
- **Fixed: tapping a label that names a chart item opens that item's card.** On a slope
  chart, tapping "Northwind" or its "31%" now opens Northwind's detail, the same as its line.
  The same applies to a funnel stage's label and value, a waterfall's category and value
  labels, a quadrant dot's name, and every row of a pie or map legend. The labels carry a new
  `data-mark-for` attribute that only the reveal layer reads, so chart motion and the Present
  Guide are unchanged. The printed chart is unchanged.
- **Fixed: the detail card's color dot on gradient-filled marks.** Bars, waterfall steps and
  other gradient-filled marks showed an empty dot that pushed the title right. The dot now
  takes the mark's outline color.

- **A chart keeps every block written before its figure.** The chart wrap kept paragraphs only and dropped a code block, blockquote, table or raw HTML between the heading and the figure without a warning, on a chart slide and in a chart pane alike. Each now renders above the figure, whole and in the order written, in a `div.chart-lead-block`. It hides at `claim-hero` and `claim-bleed`, a split chart carries it on its first body page only, and the Read · Article view carries it ahead of the figure. A table before a table-data chart (`heatmap`, `matrix-grid`, `roadmap`) is still read as the chart's data. No shipped deck had such a block, so every committed deck renders byte-identical. `examples/chart-lead-blocks.md`.

- **A chart keeps every paragraph written before its figure.** The chart wrap lifted the first
  paragraph as the subtitle and dropped any later one without a warning, on a chart slide and in
  a chart pane alike. Each later paragraph now renders above the figure as a `.chart-lead`, in
  the order written, and the Read · Article view carries it ahead of the figure. At `claim-hero`
  and `claim-bleed` the leads hide with the subtitle. `examples/chart-lead-paragraphs.md`.

- **Fixed: a chart label that runs out of lines ends on a whole word.** "peaked afte…" now reads
  "peaked…". A label that is one word too long for its line still cuts by characters.
  (`lib/components/chart/_chart-family/svg-label.js` `measureLabel`.)

- A chart no longer reads a mistyped value as a different number. Before this, `--5` plotted as -5, `(-5)` as +5, `(5` and `5)` as 5, `$(1,234)` as +1,234, `1,2,3` as 1.2 and `1.2.3.4x` as 1,234, with no warning. Now none of them is a number:
  - A bar, line or other point chart draws no mark for the row.
  - A pie wedge or funnel stage reads as zero.
  - A bullet row keeps the value in its actual slot and prints it as typed, instead of promoting its target to the actual.
  - The narration says the value as typed and binds it to no mark.
  - The new lint warning `chart-value-malformed` names each one and why.
- A minus sign (U+2212) after a currency, as in `$−5`, now reads as negative; it read +5. A look-alike where a sign goes (an en dash `–5`, a fullwidth `－5` or `＋5`, the emoji minus `➖5`, the katakana `ー5` a Japanese IME types) is refused and named, instead of reading +5 or as an unsigned 5.
- Well-formed numbers in every spelling read as before. None of the 427 shipped decks renders or narrates differently.
- Segno's `@laticent/segno/values` adds `malformedNumber`, which says why a string shaped like a number is not one.

- The chart census now measures OCCLUSION — whether a member's marks overlap each other — with a shape-accurate same-class test, which is what tells `radar` apart from `quadrant`: both paint a `<radialGradient>`, but radar's polygons layer and quadrant's zones tile. `chart-mark-separation.js` also composites `stop-opacity` instead of reading `stop-color` alone, so an ALPHA ramp is measured as what the reader sees rather than forced to a self-range of zero.

- The chart detail card now closes when attention leaves the preview: a press or focus outside the preview, the page going to the background, or (in the editing preview) Escape. On a phone it no longer stays over the editor after you switch from Preview to Edit. Every surface that shows the card (Playground, Studio preview, Present) shares one `ChartDetailLayer`, so all three get the fix.

- Chart design language: a ramp's fill is SCALED by a finish, not replaced and not held. An earlier revision held it, on the reasoning that a choropleth's own steps already sit at the discrimination floor — but holding it made `map` render identically under all three finishes, which is the defect a finish exists to avoid. A finish now sets the band's floor and span; the datum keeps its position inside it, so neighboring steps keep their gap.

- Chart design language: a mark that carries text has its wash level CAPPED by the register, not exempted from the finish. An earlier revision pinned it outright, and measured, that made `gantt`, `progress` and `matrix-grid` render byte-identical under all three finishes. Each finish now picks a level inside the cap, measured against 4.5:1 for the mark's own text (worst case 4.98:1 across 8 theme × mode combinations).
- A state-keyed mark carries its own resolved ink on the element, so a finish needs no second status-to-slot mapping.

- Chart design language: the register pins a text-bearing mark's wash *level*, not which hue is mixed into it — so a correction that collapses a member to one hue reaches a BACKDROP mark, while a finish still may not move its depth.

- **Two chart labels that print on a tinted mark now use the body ink.**
  `state-chart`'s step ordinal and `kanban`'s size token were both set in
  `--text-muted`, which is calibrated against the slide — but neither sits on the
  slide. Measured on the rendered gallery they were **4.02:1** (light) /
  **4.48:1** (dark) and **4.69:1** / **3.38:1** against the surfaces they actually
  sit on. Three of those four are under the 4.5:1 floor; kanban's light arm was
  already passing, and the change makes it consistent rather than compliant.
- **`radar`'s scale rungs were painted UNDER the series polygons.** SVG has no
  `z-index` — later in the document is on top — and the 2.5 / 5 / 7.5 labels were
  emitted with the grid, so every polygon reaching that far dimmed the number the
  polygon is read against. They failed AA on **all twelve themes**, 2.60–4.36:1.
  They now paint last, and carry the family's canvas-coloured halo
  (`paint-order: stroke`, the idiom stacked-bar's total and waterfall's value
  already use) so a rung sits on `--bg` whatever runs behind it.
- **`concrete` flattens the chart fill wash.** `chart-family.css` states the
  contract the wash exists to keep — "the wash only tints, so `--text-heading`
  labels clear it on both canvases" — and concrete is the one theme where that was
  false, because its canvas is an unusually dark greige (`#B8B8B5`) and the same
  mix lands far closer to the heading ink than it does on a near-white page. It is
  not fixable from the ink side: concrete's `--text-heading` already resolves to
  `15,15,14` and pure black reaches only 4.20:1 on the old bottom stop. The wash
  is read through `var(--palette-fill-*, <engine default>)` so a palette can move
  it; every other theme is untouched.
- **Verified across 12 themes × 2 media — `screen` and `print` — on both sides of
  the change, with the same instrument: 196 text AA failures → 2, and the mark
  floor no worse (346 → 338, no mark class worse, two better).** The two that
  remain are the same defect in both media: a `state-chart` connector crosses one
  corner of a node label on `concrete` light, putting **0.1% of that label's
  pixels** at 4.25:1. That is a layout defect in the dagre edge layer, it
  pre-dates this branch (it measured 3.41:1 there), and it is not a colour choice.
- The instrument changed too, and the old numbers should not be trusted. The
  solver now SAMPLES the backdrop out of the render — two screenshots of the same
  slide, one with the glyph fill removed, and the pixels that differ are the
  pixels a glyph covers — instead of compositing a backdrop from computed style.
  The modeling version scored text over a gradient against the **more flattering**
  end of the ramp and discarded the ink's own alpha, and both defects hid real
  failures: it reported 0 where this reports 2, and 0 on `main` where this reports
  196. Each row now carries a `share`, the fraction of the glyph's pixels at the
  reported ratio, which is what tells a colour choice from a crossing connector.

- A video picked on the device whose file carries no type (some Android and desktop pickers do this) attaches as a video in the chat instead of being refused as "isn't an image", and the chat's picker now offers `.mp4`, `.mov`, `.webm` and `.m4v` files by name.
- Closing the chat with a clip from the device still waiting to be sent removes that clip from the Library, as switching decks already did.
- A Library clip that is too large is never told to trim to a length the 15-second limit then refuses, and a clip that is too short never reads as a length the chat accepts ("1.5 seconds" for 1.46 s).
- Regenerating a turn whose photo or video was deleted from the Library tells the model it could not be sent, so it says so instead of describing a clip it never saw.
- A video in the Library list that cannot be attached can be reached with the keyboard, and its reason is read with its name.
- A clip just under a minute shows as 1:00, not 0:00.
- A video on a sent chat message now plays when you tap it, in place and with the browser's controls. It showed a play mark that did nothing.

- The cost estimate beside the Studio chat now includes the Library: with photos in it, each turn carries a short list of them and three extra tool definitions, and the estimate rises by a few tenths of a cent to match (and falls back when the photos are removed). With no photos the estimate is unchanged.
- When the chat looks at several photos in one turn, the Library is now read once for the turn instead of once per photo.

- The chat's model menu no longer jumps when it finishes loading the model list. The "Ask a question" and "Make an edit" price rows now show a dash until the price arrives, instead of appearing late above the source buttons. Before, the buttons dropped 50 px as the prices landed, and a tap on "On-device" at that moment could miss and leave the source unchanged.

- **Fixed: on a busy machine the CLI no longer gives up starting Chrome after 30 seconds.** Puppeteer's own 30-second launch limit fired before the CLI's 90-second render watchdog, so a slow Chrome start failed with "Timed out after 30000 ms while waiting for the WS endpoint URL". Every browser `lattice` starts to render or export a deck now gets the watchdog's limit, which `LATTICE_RENDER_WATCHDOG_MS` still sets. A Chrome that never starts now fails after about twice that limit (180 seconds by default), because the render is retried once with hardening flags; it used to fail at 30 seconds. `lattice video` keeps Puppeteer's default.

- The CI-green beacon and the golden-diff sticky comment now read every page of a PR's comments, so a PR past 100 comments no longer piles up duplicate beacons.

- The iOS Simulator photo check no longer fails when a phone's parked preview misses a redraw: it opens the Preview pane to confirm the deck, as a person would. Four other tests that waited on a clock, or read a value once, now wait for the state they need: the narrated-player word highlight, the Playground back gesture, the Library rename across decks and the slide-strip shortcuts. On Windows, a confinement test that hangs now says where it stopped instead of failing with an empty `null !== 0`.

- `claim-hero` and `claim-bleed` now drop the deck's running `header:` along with the footer and meta bay, so it no longer prints over the slide heading. A slide that set `_header: ''` only to clear it can drop that line.

- `lattice video --help` names the Studio's export menu as **Share → Webpage**, the label the Studio shows, instead of "Share -> HTML".

- The CLI names its output page and the MP4 encoder pages with `pathToFileURL` instead of string concatenation, so the address is a valid `file:///C:/…` on Windows (and percent-encoded correctly for a path with a space or `#` everywhere).
- A host-qualified `file://host/share/x` address is refused before any file-system call, so on Windows it can no longer reach a network share.

- **A slide's closing quote holds a beat again.** The pause after it was removed a day earlier because deleting it left the `.vtt` sidecar byte-identical — but a `.vtt` is derived from the last cue's END and cannot represent silence after its own final line. The exported webpage player holds that gap deliberately ("so the slide boundary does not land on the final syllable"), so the beat was real all along, on the surface that carries a voice. Restored, and pinned on a real downloaded player rather than on the artifact that is blind to it.

- **Internal: a code package's load limit now bounds only the package.** `openPackageSandbox` gave
  the same time limit to the sandbox's own page load and to the package's top-level code, so a caller
  passing a limit under 5 seconds could see a browser navigation timeout instead of the package's own
  error. The page now keeps its own 5-second limit. The export's default path already used 5 seconds
  and is unchanged.

- **Collage:** a photo you can open now says so before you click. The pointer becomes the zoom cursor over it (in the Studio preview too, where the frame takes no pointer events), the photo gets the accent ring the keyboard focus already draws, and it rises a little more (3% instead of 2%) while its neighbors recede. Print and PDF output are unchanged.

- **Fixed: a collage photo under a still mouse in the Studio now shows the zoom cursor once the collage packs.**
  A live collage lays out its photos only after it has measured them. When the mouse stopped over the preview while
  the photos were still loading, the Studio checked what was under the pointer before the photos moved into place
  and never checked again, so the photo that then packed under the mouse showed no `zoom-in` cursor and did not pop.
  The Studio now checks again when the collage packs.

- `engineering/gotchas/export.md`: an embedder that hosts slides and offers its own light/dark control must pin `color-scheme` on the slide from that control — `light-dark()` reads `color-scheme`, not the engine's `.dark` class, so a host page set to `light dark` leaks the reader's device preference into the slides. Only the light direction fails, which is what makes it easy to miss.

- The package description, the agent kit's picker and catalog lines, and the design and engineering docs now give the catalog's real size: 80 components (52 layouts plus 28 chart kinds), not 61. The agent kit reads the count from the catalog at build time, so it cannot go stale again.

- Compose now reads a fenced code block's closing line the way CommonMark does. A line indented four spaces (or a tab) inside a ``` fence is code, not the fence's end — so the math or table after such a fence still locks the slide in Compose, instead of unlocking it and letting the next edit corrupt it. A fence nested in a list item still closes where markdown-it closes it.

- `dist/docs/grammar.json` now lists the `anima` fence (`body: "json"`, used by `scene`) beside `functionplot` and `mermaid`, and LFM 1.0 §3.3 documents it. The engine already rendered it; the registry and the spec now say so.
- Compose: the language chip's picker now stays on its code block when the editor scrolls, instead of staying where the chip was when you clicked it.
- Compose: a `~~~` fence keeps its tildes (and a four-backtick fence its four backticks) when you edit its slide. Before, Compose rewrote every fence it re-serialized with three backticks.

- Compose: a click into a slide now keeps its caret, so the words you type next go where you clicked. Two cases sent them elsewhere, mid-paragraph in another slide:
  - **After an undo or redo.** Clicking another slide and typing within about three seconds sent the typing back to the slide you came from. The undo's highlight cleared itself with a change that ignored a caret move the editor had not read yet, and put the old caret back. The highlight now reads the caret first. A Markdown paste that finishes after a click gets the same fix, so it lands where the caret is now.
  - **On the first click after Compose opens, on a busy page (seen in Safari's engine).** The editor library put its own caret back before the browser reported the click, so the first words landed where the caret was when Compose opened, often the top of the deck. A click that focuses Compose now has its caret read first.

- **Fixed: Compose no longer sets authoring comments as prose, and no longer corrupts the
  multi-line ones.** An HTML comment is a note to the author, never a thing on the slide, but the
  Compose parser did not model it — so every `<!-- … -->` landed in the writing surface as editable
  text. A comment spanning lines fared worse: markdown read its indented continuation as a CODE
  BLOCK, so re-serializing the slide put the closing `-->` inside a fence and the engine rendered an
  empty `pre` onto the slide. One keystroke on such a slide was enough, and 25 multi-line comments
  across 7 shipped decks were exposed. Comments are now a schema node carrying their source bytes
  verbatim. The COMMENT'S OWN BYTES survive whatever shape it is in — internal line breaks, hanging
  indent and all. Its surrounding blank line is normalized like any other block's, so a comment
  written tight against a paragraph gains one on the next edit to that slide; that changes the
  source, never the render, and it affects a handful of shipped decks.
- **Added: a run of comments reads as one control.** Adjacent comments — a `caption:`, a
  `describe:` and a note all belong to the same slide — show as pills on a single row, labeled by
  CHANNEL rather than all called "note", with exactly one open at a time and its words in a shared
  panel below. Clicking another pill moves the panel instead of opening a second. Previously each
  comment rendered its own box with its own Remove button, so three comments meant three identical
  stacked "NOTE" panels. `caption:` and `describe:` also drop their prefix in the panel — that is
  the syntax selecting the channel, not part of what the author wrote.
- **Fixed: removing a note on a locked slide no longer looks like it worked.** A slide Compose
  cannot round-trip takes no edits, and the delete was silently filtered. It is reachable by
  accident, because a note's own contents can lock its slide: `<!-- TODO: kill the ~~old~~ wording -->`
  made a slide read-only with no visible cause. The control now says to edit in Markdown.
- **Fixed: a comment no longer hides text the slide renders.** `<!-->` and `<!--->` carry their
  terminator inside the opener, and the scan skipped past it — so `<!--->` followed by a line of
  prose swallowed that prose into the comment. A `---` inside a comment could also be read as a
  setext underline and rewritten into a visible heading; the rule now sits where the engine's own
  HTML-block rule sits. A comment inside a list item stays prose, because lifting it out turns a
  tight list loose.
- **Fixed: a trailing note no longer mislabels the block above it in Compose.** Key-insight,
  below-note and eyebrow all survive a comment in the gap — the transform that decides them counts
  elements only — so Compose skips comments when looking forward. A SUBTITLE does not survive one:
  it is hoisted by a string match that an intervening comment defeats, so Compose no longer claims
  a subtitle the engine will not render.
- **Security: a pasted comment cannot carry a directive into the deck source.** Comment text is
  written back verbatim, so a crafted `div.cs-comment` from a page the author does not control
  could have landed `<!-- _backgroundImage: url(…) -->` in the source, where it becomes a real slide
  directive. Pasted comments now need this editor's own provenance token, are refused if they are
  directive-shaped, and must be one self-contained inert comment — the check refuses every way the
  HTML parser can end a comment early (`-->`, `--!>`, and the abrupt `<!-->` / `<!--->` forms).

- **A pasted image can no longer write a slide boundary or a background-image directive into the deck.** An `<img>` pasted into Compose with a line break in its alt text or title wrote the line break into the deck source, which started new slides and could carry an `_backgroundImage` directive the export would fetch. A pasted image now takes only a clean source, and the Markdown writer keeps an image's alt text, title and source on one line.

- Compose's clipboard now speaks Markdown. Pasting Markdown (from a text editor, a chat reply, VS Code or a `.md` file's text) turns slide breaks into slides, `<!-- _class: … -->` comments into layouts and inline syntax into formatting. Before, it saved the text escaped into the deck (`\- \*\*Revenue\*\*`, `\---`). Copying from Compose puts the selection's Markdown on the plain-text clipboard: a phrase as its inline Markdown, slides with their layouts and breaks, and the whole deck as the deck file. ⌘⇧V still pastes text literally.
- Pasted slides go after the slide the caret is in (before it at its very start, in place of an empty one), never splitting it. Pasted Markdown with headings or lists keeps them as blocks.
- A pasted deck's front matter (theme, size, pagination) is applied to the open deck key by key, and the Studio names the settings it applied; Undo takes them back with the slides. Markdown that would load anything from another site is refused with a message (the paste is rendered through the engine and checked the way Insert checks a sample slide); paste it in Source if you trust it.
- A deck file dropped on Compose opens as a new deck, as it does anywhere else in the Studio. Before, the editor swallowed the drop with no message.

- Compose: a list item whose text is `[x]: /u` keeps its escaped brackets when you edit it, so it still draws its text instead of an empty item (it read back as a link reference definition).
- Compose: an escaped `\[x\](/u)` or `\[x\][ref]` at the start of a list item or a table cell stays literal text when you edit it; it was turning into a live link.
- Compose: a list item that starts with a state marker (`- [x] text`) shows the checkbox chip only where the slide draws it: the top-level items of a checklist slide, and the nested items of a verdict-grid or pricing slide. On any other slide or depth it is plain text, as on the slide, and a tap no longer changes the source with nothing to see.

- **A pick in Compose's object editor edits the object it was opened on, never its neighbor.** The editor kept its
  object's position as of its last render; a change that shifted positions before the next render (an earlier code span
  turning into a pill, say) left it pointing at the next object, and a Size pick on a spark could write `lg` to the pill
  beside it. Every write now reads where the open object is at that moment, and refuses an object whose source is not
  the one opened.

- Compose: the slide settings gear on a slide's formatting bar opens the settings panel at Write. It only set state before, because the panel docks at Craft, so on desktop and tablet the click showed a first-use nudge and nothing else. It now reveals Craft the way the compact toolbar's button does.
- Studio: the first slide chip in the slide navigator is no longer clipped on load. The rail centered the active chip while it still had zero width, which scrolled it 39.5px; it now waits for a real width and centers once.
- Compose: inline code (pills, sparks, avatars) no longer gets spellcheck underlines. Prose keeps its spellcheck.
- Studio: the "N issue" chip in the editor bar is a button that opens the Coach and names the unknown layouts ("compare-table isn't a layout Lattice knows. Fix all swaps it for the closest match."); the Coach's issue card says the same.

- Compose keeps a line break inside a paragraph. Editing a paragraph used to join `line one` and `line two` into one line, though the slide draws each newline as a break; the newline now writes back as written.

- Compose writes a list inside a quote as a tight list, with no blank lines between its items, as the source had it. Before, saving from Compose turned it into a loose list. A list the paragraph above cannot hold (an ordered list that starts after 1) keeps its blank line, so it stays a list.
- On a chart slide, Compose saves the chart's rows as a tight list even when an older save left blank lines between them. A blank line between chart rows changes nothing on the chart, and those blank lines made every later save keep them. A slide you do not edit keeps its bytes.

- **Compose's slide toolbar no longer grows by itself after the Studio loads.** When a slide's toolbar was measured before it was laid out, its reserved width waited for the next editor update, so on a first visit the toolbar could show narrower and then widen with no caret move. It now takes its reserved width the moment it is laid out.

- **Fixed: an `inventory` row alone on a split page keeps its ordinal on its own
  title.** The ordinal hung off the row box, so when auto-split gave a row its own
  page — page-tall, prose centered — the numeral had to be centered too. Centering
  its box put it on the *body's* baseline instead, 199px (render px, 2x) below the
  title it indexes, reading as a label for the clause rather than an index for the
  row. It now hangs off the title itself and is carried by the same centering, 2px
  off at the same measurement. Rows that share a page render byte-identical; a row
  authored without a bold lead keeps the previous placement.

- **The two curated model decks now carry the Lattice mark.** `design/forms.gallery.md` taught the logo Tile in prose while rendering no logo at all — which is how it came to claim on two slides that the masthead bay holds it. It does not: the logo is frame-anchored to the slide box, which is why the mark rides the corner *above* the bay. With `logo:` set the render now contradicts a wrong sentence on the same slide. `examples/gallery-jargon.md` gains it for brand presence; it makes no claim the mark verifies.
- Adds `lib/base/_logo/lattice-mark-min.svg` — the repo's first non-fictional logo asset (`acme-logo.svg` stays the placeholder for feature demos). The **minimal** variant is deliberate: at watermark size (~6% of slide width) the full mark's nine circles congest into a blob, while the four-bond mark stays legible. It is also the smaller artifact, so there is no tradeoff.
- **Both committed PDFs grow**, and the cost is the mark repeated on every slide rather than its complexity: `forms.gallery` 455 KB → 563 KB, `gallery-jargon` 1.80 MB → 2.85 MB. `--keep-vector-images` was measured and is *larger* (3.13 MB), so rasterizing is not the cause.

- `cycle`: the chevron between stages is now a real inline SVG element (`span.cycle-link`, inserted by `cycle.transform.js`) that owns a slot in the stage row, not a `li::after` pseudo-element placed into a fixed gap. At the hall venue the old mark was `1em` of a type size that scales 1.5x, sitting in a gap that does not scale, so it painted over the next card. The slot is sized from the same type size, so the cards now give way to the chevron at every venue. The chevron draws in the accent color and turns to point down in the tall and strip layouts. Split pages (one stage each) get no connector, as before. Measured at `venue: hall`: the chevron clears both cards, and the 6-stage ring fits as it did before the change.

- **Dark mode no longer repaints a frame that paints its own canvas.** `section.dark` set the deck-wide canvas at the same `(0,1,1)` specificity as a frame's own rule, and component stylesheets are bundled before `base.modifiers.css` — so at equal specificity source order decided it and the deck ground won. Nine frames are now exempt: the four anchors (`title`, `divider`, `closing`, `topic`) and the five accent covers the splitter emits (`decision-cover`, `compare-code-cover`, `compare-split-cover`, `list-tabular-cover`, `split-panel-cover`). A tenth painter, `lat-split-cover`, needs no entry — it is declared after the rule and already wins.
- **The accent covers were an accessibility defect, not only a cosmetic one.** A cover keeps `color: var(--on-accent)` — the theme's inverse surface under dark — while losing its accent ground, so it rendered dark ink on a dark ground. Measured in Chromium on indaco: `decision-cover` and `split-panel-cover` both went from **1.52:1 to 6.10:1**.
- **`divider` gets its spectrum rail back** — `background-size` was collapsing from `6px 100%` at the default 16:9 export to the deck-wide `100% 1px` hairline, and it had been shipping that way in `divider.gallery.dark.pdf`.
- **A dark split cover now draws the spectrum bar above it.** The old rule carried `border-top: none` deck-wide; the four anchors set their own, the five covers did not. The same covers already draw that bar in light mode, so this brings dark into line rather than adding a treatment.
- A new gate, `test/unit/palette/dark-canvas-ownership.test.js`, parses the built bundle with css-tree — source order is a property of `dist/lattice.css`, so no source-tree walk can ask the question — and fails on a painter declared ahead of the rule without an exemption, on an entry that no longer paints, and on `lat-split-cover` moving ahead of the rule.
- **Not fixed: the `spectrum:` register repaints the same frames** through `section.dark.spectrum-off` and `section.dark:is(.spectrum-edge-*)`, which out-specify a frame's own canvas rather than merely outranking it on order. The *surface* is unchanged here and still flattens; the finish above is excluded across those registers so it follows whatever the slide really paints. Tracked as #2291.
- **A finish on a dark bookend or accent cover now composites against the surface that slide actually paints.** `--fin-canvas` (#1656) names the color every finish layer mixes toward, and it excluded `.dark` because `section.dark` used to repaint a bookend — so once the exemption above landed, a finish on a dark `title` mixed toward the deck ground while the slide painted `--surface-inverse`. The five accent covers were never named in that file at all. Both follow their own canvas now.
- **`topic` is named in that file for the first time.** It paints `--surface-inverse` in every mode and had never been listed, so a finish on a topic slide composited against the deck ground.
- The re-point applies **only where the frame keeps its canvas**, which is a per-frame question: `print` remaps the consumed tokens and `section.print` resets the surface, while `accent` / `spectrum-off` / `spectrum-edge-*` out-specify a frame's own rule — but each of those needs `.dark` to fire, so excluding them unconditionally would break light decks. `divider` keeps its canvas wherever its own `(0,3,1)` spectrum carve-outs beat the repainter, and `topic` takes three arms — `section.topic:not(:has(> ul.tile-track))` restates its canvas at `(0,2,2)`, so a topic carrying its track loses it as `title` does, except as `.fact`.
- Measured over 18 frames × 219 modifier classes × {plain, dark} plus every register pair, in both DOM shapes — 9,918 cells per palette, repeated on all 33 palettes in Chromium 131. Five representative palettes were re-run in Firefox 142 and WebKit 26, where all three engines agree cell for cell, computed `rgb()` values included. Outside the two families tracked as #2294, `main` leaves **26–759** rows per palette compositing against a color the slide does not paint, and this leaves **0** on every one.
- **A `fact` topic keeps its panel under print, and that took a third arm.** `section.topic.fact` `(0,2,1)` restates topic's canvas above `section.print` `(0,1,1)`, so a fact slide holds its inverse panel where a plain tracked topic correctly gives it up — and a blanket `:not(.print)` on the tracked arm sent `--fin-canvas` to white over a surface still painting `rgb(236,236,236)`. That is the same #1656 failure this change exists to remove, on a shape the engine really emits: `fact` hides the track with `display: none`, but the `<ul>` is still in the DOM, so `:has(> ul.tile-track)` matches. Present on `main` in both DOM shapes; the arm that shipped fixed the trackless half and left the half that ships. The exclusions on the new arm were measured across all seven registers rather than copied from the arm beside it.
- **The `topic` arms moved into their own rule block**, because Selectors-4 invalidates a whole selector list on one unparsable complex selector. While topic's `:has()` arms shared a list with `title`, `closing` and `divider`, a renderer that does not understand `:has()` dropped the declaration for those three too — frames that were immune before this file learned about topic. `dist/marp-kit/lattice.css` ships the rule to third-party Marp renderers, so the split bounds the loss to topic for one duplicated declaration.
- **The gate that is supposed to catch the next one can no longer be disarmed in silence.** Its shape derivation was a regex demanding `tag.class`, with no self-check — collapse the topic split AND neuter the derivation and it passed green. It now reads the bundle with css-tree, refuses to guess at a `:has()` form it cannot build into a probe element (and fails naming it), and asserts the tracked-topic shape is still there. A new `variant x register` axis covers the pairing that hid the `fact` defect from both gates, and the anti-vacuity check now names the DOM shape it inspects — it had been silently reading the trackless topic, never the shape that ships.
- **The probe the gate measures with now has to prove it matches.** The shape derivation's self-check tested the probe *string* — that some shape mentioned `tile-track` — which a probe can satisfy while not matching at all. Wrapping the built element in one classless `<div>` keeps every row's label reading `[tile-track]` while `:has(> ul.tile-track)` stops matching, so the tracked axis silently measures the trackless shape again; measured, that one token plus deleting the `topic.fact` arm shipped green through both gates. Each probe is now asserted in the browser against the selector it was derived from.
- **The rule-block split is gated, in both places it can be undone.** Nothing detected collapsing the two `--fin-canvas: var(--surface-inverse)` blocks back into one list — the mutant passed both gates. The contract now asserts the invariant rather than a rule count (no rule may mix a `:has()` arm with a non-`:has()` arm, which survives a legitimate third block where a count would not), and the bundle gate asserts the same thing over `dist/lattice.css`, because a merge introduced by a build step that folds rules sharing a declaration block is invisible to a source-level check.
- **A second demo deck, `examples/finish-canvas-print-face.md`**, shows the third arm. The dark deck could not: `print` is a deck-level color mode, and its `fact` slide resolves no track (the section's other topic slide declares `_track:`, so derivation yields too few labels and returns none), which left it matched by the arm that already shipped and rendering identically with and without the fix — while its own caption claimed otherwise. Measured on the new deck: page 4 differs, the other five pages are identical.

- **Fixed: the docs dev server (`npm run dev`) now runs the Studio's webpage export and the
  Compose view.** Both imported named exports from CommonJS files under `lib/`, which the dev
  server cannot serve. The export's diagram bake failed, so every Mermaid diagram shipped as raw
  source, and Compose failed to load at all. Each import is now a default import, and a docs unit
  test fails on the named shape. The built site was never affected.

- **Studio preview: a diagram slide no longer shows its Mermaid source before the diagram.** Typing on a diagram slide repainted the raw ```mermaid fence for ~160ms on every keystroke — 10 painted frames, on an idle machine — with the finished SVG already in the runtime's cache. Three fixes: an un-tagged fence now paints nothing in a document that is injecting Mermaid, so something will draw it (the slot it reserves is unchanged, so nothing on the slide moves; an export, whose runtime is stripped, still shows the source), the runtime hands back a cached diagram in the same task as the swap that brought the slide in rather than 150ms later, and the Studio — the editor preview and Present alike — keys its preview frame on whether the DECK has a diagram rather than the shown slide, so moving onto a diagram slide patches the preview instead of rebuilding it. Measured on the built Studio: raw-source frames 10 → **0**, and the diagram is back in **23ms** instead of 172ms (28ms instead of 368ms when navigating). A diagram nothing has rendered yet still takes its render time, now behind an empty slot rather than its source.
- Fixed a latent cache defect this exposed: `diagramScopeKey` keyed a rendered diagram on the section's raw inline `style`, which the runtime itself stamps (`--_sec-1cqi`, the deck-logo placement) — so the same slide produced two different keys either side of that stamp. The key now reads the CSSOM's own serialization (`style.cssText`) instead of the attribute — the browser rewrites values, not just whitespace, once anything calls `setProperty` — and drops what the runtime writes on BOTH halves of the key: the stamped properties, the FIT agent's `transform` (rewritten on every pane or window resize, so a resize used to re-render every diagram in the preview), and the overflow / clip / fit / illegible marker classes its watchers toggle while a slide settles.

- **Fixed: the `numbered` section stamp renders again — on every render path, and alongside `silent`.** It wrote the numeral onto `section::after`, the pseudo the engine reserves for the page number. Two owners took it back: the pagination mask (ours, and Marpit's own on the marp-vscode / marp-kit / export-to-Marp path) comments out any non-pagination `content` on that pseudo, so the counter was stripped from every browser surface while the emulator PDF kept it; and `silent` / `no-paginate` null the same pseudo at an equal specificity from a later file, so `divider silent numbered` — the sample shipped in the docs, the manifest and the gallery deck — rendered nothing anywhere. The numeral now rides the slide heading's `::after`, which neither can reach, and no longer suppresses the page number.
- **Changed: the stamp is one running count on dividers only, at the top-left edge, inked to be read.** Four changes to what it is, not just where it comes from:
  - **One counter.** `divider` and `divider light` share a single series, so a mid-deck light break reads 05 after 04 instead of restarting at 01. The `lat-divider-light` and `lat-closing` counters are gone.
  - **Breaking: `closing numbered` is removed.** A bookend is not a section, and a closing that announced itself as "01" was the clearest symptom of the three-counter design. `title` never took the modifier. Authors using `closing numbered` should drop the token; the class is inert, not an error.
  - **A masthead in the top band, set as display type** — a `--fs-hero` numeral in `--font-display` at weight 700 with no tracking, on the divider's own left margin, over a hairline that stops just past mid-canvas so the top-right corner stays free for a deck logo. It had been `--fs-h1` at `+0.04em` tracking, a heading size and a label idiom on a display mark. The two rungs follow the on-dark ramp's division of labour — `--on-dark-secondary` for the numeral, `--on-dark-ghost` for the rule, resetting to `--text-secondary` / `--border` on `divider light`. It is pinned to the SECTION rather than the heading, so it holds the same position on every divider however long the heading runs.
  - **A numbered divider suppresses its running header and footer.** The masthead owns the top band. The page number is untouched — it sits bottom-right. 
  - **The mark's band is reserved, so a long heading cannot climb into it.** Pinning the numeral was not enough: the headline block is flex-centered, so it grew in both directions and at four lines its top edge crossed the hairline while the numeral struck through the eyebrow. The slide now reserves the band with symmetric padding and centers the block with `safe center`, which falls back to `start` exactly when the block would overflow — the top edge stops at the band and the growth goes downward instead. Headings of one or two lines render byte-identically to before (the reservation is symmetric, so the midpoint does not move); a three-line heading shifts 6.14px down, and from there the block pins with a constant `2.5cqi` of clearance under the mark's painted edge. `divider light` and `divider qr` needed it too — measured without the band, a light divider carrying a lede sits at −15.2 and `divider numbered qr` at −85.3. And because the growth now runs toward the bottom, a heading long enough to fill the band eventually leaves the FRAME, which the engine already reports — `⚠ OVERFLOW` on export, a "Content clipped" tag on the slide, the runtime ring. The collision was silent before because an absolutely-positioned pseudo lying on the copy is an overlap, and the overflow probe measures spill past the frame.
  - **The value is an attribute now, not a CSS counter — because the counter was wrong on every Marp surface.** Marpit scopes a theme by prefixing its selectors, so `body { counter-reset }` became `section body { … }`, a `<body>` inside a section that matches nothing; and Marpit puts each slide in its own `<svg><foreignObject>`, so the sections are not siblings and each one implicitly started its own counter. The result, measured on real marp-cli 4.5.0: `01` on **every** divider in the deck. `lib/core/section-index.js` stamps `data-lat-section` from one kernel through two adapters — the engine's HTML and a live DOM — and the stylesheet reads `attr()`, which is the same mechanism Marpit's own pagination uses for the same reason. Where nothing stamps it the numeral does not draw at all: a blank mark is a gap an author can see, a wrong one is misinformation the room cannot check. Verified on real marp-cli 4.5.0 against a 13-slide deck with four dividers: `01/02/03/04` in **both** its HTML and its PDF output, the PDF's confirmed in the text layer, alongside the same series on our own export and packed browser path. The runtime stamps at boot as well as in the transform tail, which is what lets a consumer that captures the page early still get the number.
  - **Inked as content.** It was bound to `--on-dark-watermark`, the 12% decoration rung, under an `opacity` — 1.4:1, present but not readable. It now takes `--on-dark-secondary` (`--text-secondary` on `divider light`), the same rungs the eyebrow beside it uses, with no CSS opacity: measured 5.05:1 to 11.79:1 across the shipped palettes. It also moves from `--z-atmosphere` to `--z-content`.

- **Fixed: a stale `docs/node_modules` in a web session no longer breaks the docs
  build.** `.claude/hooks/session-start.sh` gated its docs install on the astro
  binary merely existing, and every astro version ships one — so on a warm
  container carrying a tree installed against an older `docs/package.json`, the
  gate read "already installed" and skipped the repair it was there to do. The
  next `cd docs && npm run build` then died at config load on
  `@astrojs/markdown-remark does not provide an export named 'unified'`, naming
  neither the staleness nor astro. The install now runs unconditionally
  (`--no-save`, so it reconciles the tree without rewriting
  `docs/package-lock.json`) and is bounded at 180s, since npm burns ~73s of
  fetch-retry backoff when it needs the network and cannot reach it. Measured:
  ~2.4s on a current tree, ~4s to heal a stale one. Web sessions only — the hook
  deliberately exits early on a local checkout.

- **A hand-written card can now reach `status:ready`.** The Definition of Ready gate reads
  two fields out of the issue body, and it recognized only the exact headings the work-item
  *form* renders. Most cards are not filed through the form — they are typed into the web
  UI or opened by an agent — so a card carrying a repro and a `## Definition of done`
  checklist met the bar in substance and failed it on form. Measured 2026-08-23: **6 of 167
  open cards were `status:ready`**, and the whole Ready column was months-old leftovers, so
  no session could pull work from the board without a human dispatching it. The parser now
  accepts the headings people actually write (`Definition of done`, `Acceptance criteria`,
  `Acceptance`, `Done when`; `Swimlane`, `Governing doc`, `Design doc`) in a **second pass
  that runs only for a field whose form heading is ABSENT** — so the alias pass never
  touches a form-filed card, including one that left a required field at `_No response_`,
  which the gate goes on rejecting. (Parsing is *not* byte-identical in every case: a body
  containing an unclosed fence or an HTML comment now parses the way GitHub renders it,
  which is the point of the masking below and can change what a malformed card yields.) An alias heading can neither truncate a
  canonical value nor hijack a field the form supplied. Headings inside **fenced code blocks**
  are also no longer treated as fields at all: a `# Done when` in a pasted shell snippet used
  to invent an acceptance check whose value ran past the closing fence into unrelated prose.
  Fence matching follows CommonMark in full — same character, at least as long, **and no info
  string on the closer** — so a card pasting a nested markdown example (outer ```, inner
  ```markdown) cannot leak the headings inside it as real fields. HTML comments are masked too,
  and because a comment renders as nothing while a fenced block is visible content, field values
  are sliced from a comment-only mask: an acceptance check written as a code block still counts,
  while one that is entirely commented out does not.
  (`.github/scripts/issue-form.js`)

- The Playground editor's matching-bracket highlight now tracks the palette. It painted CodeMirror's fixed teal (`#328c8252`) on all 36 palette-modes because the theme rule read `--cm-match` through a bare `.cm-matchingBracket` key, which compiles to two classes and loses to `@codemirror/language`'s three-class base rule — so the token resolved and nothing read it.
- A bracket with no partner is themed for the first time. It fell through to the base theme's fixed red, including on the four a11y palettes that exist to avoid that hue; it now seeds from each palette's own `--fail`, and is **dashed** where a matched pair is solid. The line style is load-bearing rather than decorative: the a11y palettes tune `--accent` and `--fail` for their own CVD, which leaves the two rings 1.40-1.52:1 apart there — the same color, to a reader.
- Both bracket marks now ring the cell instead of washing it. The bracket at the caret is always on the active line, so a fill stacks on the active-line band: swept over 18 palettes x 2 modes against the six inks these editors paint, that stack drops below AA from 10% alpha upward (4.42 for `--text-body` on cuoio/light), and 8% is too faint to be worth a token. A ring sits at the cell's edge rather than under the ink, so the ink keeps the active line's own 5.03.
- **The Playground's editor no longer draws its own text selection.** It installed CodeMirror's `drawSelection()`, which replaces the browser's native highlight with DOM it paints itself — so the Playground ringed a selection with a 1px accent hairline that the Studio's editor never drew, and needed a duplicate `--cm-selection` token because the drawn band cannot read `::selection`. Nothing on either editor used what that extension is for (no multiple selections, no rectangular selection, no search multi-cursor). Selection is now the native highlight everywhere, owned by one rule — `::selection` in `styles/native-widgets.css`.
- The editor caret now tracks `--text-body` on every code surface, not `--accent`. It marks the insertion point among the text you are typing, so it has to stay as legible as that text, and `--accent` carries no AA guarantee against the canvas.
- The two deck editors share one chrome definition (`docs/src/lib/editor-chrome.js`) instead of each declaring the canvas, ink, gutter, caret, focus reset and iOS zoom guard for itself. Genuine per-surface differences — type size, padding, line-height, the gutter divider — are now passed in rather than forked. Four dead rule groups were deleted from the Studio's theme, including a third, unreachable copy of the selection wash.
- The Playground's line numbers sit on their lines again. Sharing the chrome moved `line-height` onto `.cm-content`, and `.cm-gutters` is a sibling of that element rather than a child — so the gutter fell back to CodeMirror's base `1.4` and every number drifted about 1.35px above the line it labels, all the way down the file. The same fix closes a 3px version of the gap that the Studio's editor had already.
- Selecting text in the Playground no longer leaves the active-line band underneath it. `highlightActiveLine()` marks the line at the caret whether or not anything is selected, so a selection covering that line stacked two accent washes: body text over it measured 3.96:1 on cuoio/light, under AA, against 4.61 for the same selection anywhere else. The band's job is to show where the caret is, and a selection shows that more precisely, so it stands down while one is up.
- **Two behavior changes come with native selection, both matching what the Studio's editor has always done.** On WebKit and Safari a selection no longer stays visible after the editor loses focus — click a toolbar control and the highlight clears (Chromium keeps painting it). And the Playground no longer shows CodeMirror's default dotted focus ring; that ring was a fixed near-black which is nearly invisible on a dark palette, and the caret is a text field's conventional focus affordance.

- The Studio no longer re-reads every slide on each keystroke. The class editor parsed each slide from scratch about eight times per keystroke (59 full parses per keystroke on the 7-slide starter deck, a regression from the directive-editor change); it now remembers each slide, and a keystroke costs about one parse.
- The Studio and the Playground update the deck model they already hold on a keystroke instead of parsing the deck again for the outline, the slide split and the preview.

- **The Source editor keeps your selection when the deck changes elsewhere.** A slide-settings or note
  write the Studio made while you held a range (a select-all included) collapsed it to a caret, so the
  next Delete removed one character instead of the selection. The whole range now maps through the write,
  and a range the write replaced entirely becomes a caret instead of an inverted selection.
- **A navigation that was waiting for the editor's text no longer lands after you have moved.** A slide
  reveal parked until the editor caught up (a restore after reload, a slide added and gone to) now yields to
  a click, a select-all or typing made in the meantime, instead of moving the caret out from under you.

- `lint:deck --fix` rewrites a moved empty box (`[ ]` to `[!]`) on a deck whose body opens with a separator (`---`, `***` or `___`). The fix used to aim two lines off, fail, and stop every later fix in the deck from applying.

- A deck whose body quotes a section tag now renders every slide. A `<section` inside an HTML comment or inside `<style>` text used to derail the export, which shipped a multi-slide deck as a one-page PDF with exit code 0. It also derailed the per-slide passes, so every slide after the quoting one lost its masthead band and stage cell. Every section walker now uses the shared one, which reads comments and style text as text.
- An empty comment written `<!-->` or `<!--->` no longer hides the slides after it. The section walker read it as a comment running to the next `-->` in the deck, so every slide in between lost its masthead band and stage cell.

- A chart value written as a whole European number, dot-grouped thousands then one decimal comma (`1.234,5`, `€1.234.567,89M`), now plots at its own value: 1234.5, not 1.2345. `1,234.5` reads as before, and so does anything looser, so a list comma after a decimal in prose never moves a number. A lone `12.000` is still read US-first, as 12.
- The narration says a value the way the chart reads it: `1,5` is "one point five", not "fifteen", and `1.234,5` is "one thousand two hundred thirty-four point five". The change it reports between two points is the change the chart draws.
- A chart value written with ISO space grouping (`12 000`, `1 234,5`, `€12 000k`, also with a no-break or thin space) now plots at its own value. Before, it was not read as a value, and the fallback plotted its first group: `1 234` became 1. Only exact three-digit groups count, so `4 beds` and `Q1 2025` keep their reading.

- A JPEG saved with an EXIF Orientation of 5 to 8 (a phone photo held upright) is now measured at build time as the shape it is painted, not the shape of its stored pixels. Before, the `image` layout picked its treatment for a landscape shape while the browser drew the photo upright, so the PDF and the live preview disagreed. Decks with rotated phone JPEGs may pick a different `image` treatment on the next build. No JPEG committed to this repository carries a rotation, so no gallery slide changes.

- A Studio export of a photo-heavy deck was about twice as slow as before the shared slide camera, and could run a phone out of memory. A 52-slide 4K deck's PDF now exports in 52.7 s in Chromium, from 112 s (`main`: 51.9 s, with a 33 MB file; this one is 6 MB). What changed: the camera leaves out the `@font-face` rules for families a slide does not draw with, and the page's copy of a face the host already supplies (79 rules and 1.7 MB of base64 went into every slide's SVG); it swaps picture addresses in one pass; the shared PNG encoder reads and compresses 64 rows at a time instead of holding three whole-picture copies (its files are byte-identical); and the Studio's PDF writes PNGs in workers while the next slide is captured. Captures still take turns.
- The Studio's Share → PDF test for the 4K Resolution choice (`pdf-shared-writer.spec.ts`) now uses the dropdown that replaced the radio buttons.
- A picture's address written as text on a slide (a photo credit that quotes the URL) was overwritten by the picture's base64 in PowerPoint, LibreOffice and PNG exports; the camera now swaps addresses only in CSS and attributes. A face used only by `::marker`, `::first-line` or `::first-letter` is no longer pruned from a shot. A PNG worker that never answers is given up on after 45 s and the file is written on the main thread; the Studio's picture cache is capped at 24 MB and cleared at the start of each export.
- Every Studio picture export now writes its PNGs with the shared encoder in a worker pool that starts when the export begins and ends 10 s after the last picture. The PowerPoint fallback lane (no worker) and the PDF's page-picture lanes used the browser's own `toDataURL`, which made the same slide's PNG three times larger than the worker lane's.

- Studio exports keep the deck's name on iPhone and iPad. Firefox and other iOS browsers saved every export as an internal ID like `76f752a8-….pdf`, because Firefox for iOS names a page's download after its link and ignores the name the page asks for. On iOS every browser — Safari included, for one native behavior — now finishes an export with a single **Save** message that opens the share sheet with the named file; **Save to Files** keeps the name. The message goes away when you switch formats or close Share.
- Every Studio download on a computer now carries the deck's name on the download link itself, not only in the `download` hint, so desktop Firefox keeps it too when the hint is dropped, and the Print panel's 2-up / 4-up / Notes PDF tab shows and saves the deck's name instead of an ID and `document.pdf`.
- On a phone, the Share sheet and the other bottom sheets stay full height unless you are typing into one of their text fields. The Share sheet could come up half height over the Studio on an iPhone after a Webpage export.

- On an iPhone, iPad or Mac Safari, a Studio PowerPoint or LibreOffice export of a deck with phone photos came out with the wrong layout, a larger file, and sometimes the wrong pictures. Three WebKit-only causes, all fixed. (1) The `image` layout never read the size of a photo over about half a megabyte, because WebKit's regex engine returns no match on the pattern that found its address; the slide kept its fallback layout with a bigger photo box. Both address readers (`lib/core/image-aspect.js`, `lib/core/css-url.js`) are now plain scans that return what the old patterns did, at any length. (2) The export could take a slide's canvas before WebKit had drawn it, so a LibreOffice file repeated slide 2's picture on every slide after it and a PowerPoint title slide came out blank; the slide camera now makes WebKit finish the draw before the canvas leaves it, and the Studio sends its encode workers the canvas's pixels instead of an `ImageBitmap`, which WebKit delivered blank. (3) The browser shrank a 12-megapixel photo itself inside the slide, and WebKit left grain a JPEG cannot compress.
- The slide camera now shrinks a photo that has twice or more the pixels it covers on the slide, itself, with a Lanczos-3 resize, as lossless PNG, before the slide is drawn; a photo under twice is left to the browser as before. Measured against the original resized with Lanczos, in the real camera: a 12-megapixel photo at 3x its box went from 27.6 dB and SSIM 0.827 to 49.2 dB and 0.9985 on WebKit, and from 37.1 dB and 0.974 to 40.7 dB and 0.989 on Chromium. In the Studio's PowerPoint of a three-photo deck of 12-megapixel photos, Chromium went from 583 KB to 491 KB, and WebKit now writes 492 KB (on `main` it laid the slides out wrong). Vector pictures and the PDF's embedded originals are unchanged.
- The Studio export holds the shot until an `image` slide's photo size is known (capped at 4 s, as before), through the measure registry it already waits on.

- **Exports write their JPEGs with one encoder of our own, so a picture's size no longer depends on the browser.** The PDF photo layer, picture PowerPoint and LibreOffice files, image sets, cropped pictures in editable Office files and recompressed author photos all used the browser's own JPEG encoder, which differs by engine: on one 52-slide deck's pictures Firefox's wrote a third more than ours, and the deck's picture PowerPoint came out 43.3 MB from an iPhone where Chromium wrote 12.5 MB: at the same quality, Safari's own encoder writes 1.5 to 2.2 times the bytes (measured in an iOS Simulator). The PowerPoint export's main-thread fallback also wrote every slide as a lossless PNG; it now writes the same pictures as the worker. The encoder (now `@laticent/lastra` `createJpegEncoder`) writes the same bytes from the same pixels in Chromium, Firefox, WebKit and the command line, within about 1% of libjpeg's size, in the Studio's worker pool.

- **Documented: the eyebrow position takes plain inline code, and a pill or a mark there
  is not a kicker.** The eyebrow is a POSITION — a paragraph whose only child is a
  `<code>` element, before a heading or list — so the `{LABEL}` / `[x]` grammar replaces
  that element with a `<span>` and the promotion silently drops: `` `{DRAFT}:c2` `` above
  a heading renders as a pill alone on a line. Escaping it (`` `\{DRAFT}` ``) keeps the
  `<code>` and keeps the kicker. The same is true of the SUBTITLE position — a code-only
  paragraph immediately after a heading, promoted by the same rule. Measured across every
  shipped deck — well over a thousand spans across the two positions — **zero** affected,
  since a real one reads `Section 01` and starts with neither a brace nor a marker; so
  nothing rendered differently, and what was missing was anyone writing it down. A census
  test scans both positions on every run and fails if a deck ever writes one, naming the
  file, the line and the escape. (No exact count is quoted here on purpose: three were, and
  each was overtaken within days — by a scanner fix, then by a routine rebase that added
  decks. The test is where the number lives. The scanner fix is worth knowing about
  independently: it stopped at the first non-blank line after a span, so an HTML comment
  between a span and its heading hid the span entirely — markdown-it strips the comment and
  promotes the eyebrow anyway, so the census was certifying a deck it had not looked at.)
  The scan is line-based, so it misses a code-only paragraph written with DOUBLE backticks
  or WRAPPED across two source lines — 13 such spans exist, none of which dispatches, so the
  conclusion holds. A parser-based walk that sees them is built and lands with the
  corpus-wide census on its own branch.
- **Decided: the variable grammar will be BRACED — `` `{$now.date}` ``, not
  `` `$now.date` ``.** The render-time built-ins proposed for the engine
  (`$now.date` / `$now.time` / `$now.datetime` / `$now.year`, plus `$deck.*` and
  `$slide.*`) were specced bare, which would have made `$` a third opening character
  beside `{` and `[`. One brace pair dispatches everything and `$` becomes a namespace
  inside it, so the grammar is two characters with one rule each — **braces dispatch,
  brackets mark**. The sigil is kept rather than collapsing to `` `{now.date}` `` because
  dropping it would put built-ins in the same namespace as author pill labels and require
  reserved words inside it — the mechanism deliberately refused for `{x}`. Nothing ships
  yet; this fixes the spelling before decks are written against the other one.

- **Fixed: the Playground and Studio now color every language the CLI does.**
  The preview bundle carried highlight.js's 36-language `common` build while the
  CLI export carried all 192, so the same deck rendered differently in the two
  places with nothing logged — a `powershell` fence measured 11 highlight spans in
  an exported PDF and 0 in the Playground. The preview now fetches the grammars a
  deck's fences actually name, one small file each (median 1.9 KB), so coverage
  matches the export without putting the full build in front of first paint: a deck
  using only common languages fetches nothing at all, and the bundle grew 2.4 KB
  rather than the 259 KB (gzipped) the full build would have cost.
- **Added: `lint:deck` flags a shell script tagged with a terminal-session
  grammar.** In highlight.js, `bash` (aliases `sh`, `zsh`) parses shell scripts
  while `shell` (aliases `console`, `shellsession`) marks the `$` prompt in pasted
  output and leaves the rest plain — so a script fenced ```` ```shell ```` renders
  almost uncolored and reads as broken highlighting. The new `shell-fence-is-script`
  suggestion names the tag and the one-word fix. It stays silent on a genuine
  transcript: any prompt-prefixed line means the block is a session.
- **Added: the engine declares which fenced-code languages it can color.**
  `engine.languages` answers `has` / `list` / `needed(markdown)` / `missing(markdown)`
  and registers a grammar at runtime. Which languages a build supports used to be
  decided by an esbuild hook in a build script and observable nowhere, which is why
  the preview/export gap went unnoticed.

- **Fixed: "Save a version" no longer fails silently when the browser's storage is full.**
  Version history now lives in IndexedDB instead of localStorage, where 25 copies of a large
  deck could not fit in Safari at all and a full quota in any browser dropped the save
  without a word. Existing versions move over automatically on first load. If a save still
  fails, the Studio says so; the version stays in Version history until you reload.

- **Fixed: `lint:deck --fix` no longer deletes a deck's title slide.** When a fix removed the only front-matter key
  (for example a retired `logo-on: all`), it left an empty `---`/`---` block. Every front-matter reader takes that block
  as running on to the first slide break, so the title slide became front matter and disappeared from the render, and
  lint afterwards reported nothing. A fix that empties the front matter now removes the block. The fix is in the shared
  fixer (`applyFix`), so any other caller of it gets the same protection.

- **Fixed: Fix all no longer freezes the Studio on a large deck.** It ran every fix pass inside the click, so a deck
  that needs many passes (one card fixed per pass) froze the page for over 8 seconds. Each pass now runs on its own,
  so the page keeps responding while Fix all works. If you edit the deck before it finishes, nothing is replaced and
  Fix all asks you to press it again. The same holds in Compose and on the Playground.

- **Fixed: an offline Studio diagram draws instead of showing "Mermaid error".** When the preview's draw frame
  cannot load (offline, a stale deploy), the diagram on screen now falls back to the page's own Mermaid, which the
  warm-up caches, in the same preview rather than from the next one.
- **Fixed: the Studio editor's `@` kind menu and `@check{…}` answers open on the first span typed after load**,
  not only after one more keystroke.
- **Fixed: entering Explore on the Playground soon after load shows your draft**, not the first component's gallery.
- **Fixed: Escape closes Present the moment it is on screen.** Present attached its keyboard after paint, so a
  quick Escape on a second or later open could do nothing.

- The Playground's Explore tab keeps showing the deck you were editing. A walk that warmed up behind the editor and landed after you switched used to replace your deck with a component gallery, and a switch right after typing rewrote the whole preview instead of patching it.
- A dialog or sheet opened again just after it closed is no longer drawn under its own dimming, where a tap on its button closed it instead (adding photos to the Library one after another).
- Closing the Stage window by hand no longer announces "Stage disconnected" on a busy machine. The console now calls it a lost Stage only when the window shows someone else's page, rather than when the browser was slow to report the close.

- **Fixed: an approved code package or npm plugin no longer fails to draw at random when the CLI runs as root.**
  The sandbox browser's hand-built command line repeated `--disable-features`, and Chromium keeps only the last
  copy, so it dropped puppeteer's list and ran the package's frame in a process of its own. puppeteer then lost
  that frame on about half the renders under load, and the slide carried "it did not load" instead of the drawing.

- **Fixed: `test/unit/components` no longer sleeps or races the clock (HARD RULE #32).** All 19 counted hits in 6
  files are gone, and `tools/flaky-test-baseline.json` drops from 171 hits in 79 files to 152 in 73. `packCollage`
  (an opt-in `opts.work`) and the tiered hub-spoke layout (`meta.work`) now report how much their search did, so their tests bound
  arrangements and label passes instead of milliseconds. The flowchart live-layout tests drive the pipeline's 300 ms
  pause and 3 s worker deadline on a virtual clock (`virtualClock` gained `settle({ done })` and `advance(ms)`), and
  now check the pause at 1 ms short of it. Each rewrite was shown failing with its defect put back.
- **Fixed: a speaker note holding a long run of blank lines no longer stalls the linter and the deck model.**
  `readIsland` in `lib/core/directive-island.mjs` tested a regex whose two `\s*` split the blank lines every way:
  192 ms at 20,000 lines, about 19 s at 200,000. It reads the leading whitespace in one pass now, and gives the same
  answer as the old pattern on 20,000 seeded draws.
- **Fixed: `test/unit/trama` no longer sleeps (HARD RULE #32).** `pipeline-draw.test.js` slept 17 times, up to
  1.9 s, around the pipeline's font deadline, its re-check timer and the live settle's pause. Its windows now run on
  the virtual clock, so the 2 s deadline is checked 1 ms short of it and at it, and the baseline drops to 135 hits in
  72 files. Nine mutations of the built pipeline each fail a test.

- **Fixed: the Studio test "the strip's Undo is the editor's own undo" no longer fails under load.** It typed into
  the editor right after picking slide 2 on the strip, but the editor moves its caret to a picked slide one frame
  later. On a busy machine the text landed in slide 1, the focus followed it back there, and the ⋯ the test then
  clicked was gone before the click, so the slide menu never opened. The test now waits for the caret to reach
  slide 2. Slowing every frame to 200 ms reproduces the old failure every time; with the wait, all 74 cases in
  the file pass with slowed frames.
- **Fixed: renaming a picture no longer slows down sharply on a line with many picture references and backticks.**
  The Studio's rename (`renameAssetRefsOutsideCode`) checked each `asset:` reference against every code span from
  the start, so on such a line the work grew with the square of its length (1.28 MB took 16.5 s). It now walks the
  spans once, in order.
- **Fixed: 92 timing-dependent checks in the docs component tests now wait for what they are about.** Fixed sleeps
  became waits on a signal or fake-timer steps past the product's own timers, and stopwatch assertions became
  counts of work done (HARD RULE #32). `tools/flaky-test-baseline.json` drops from 469 to 377 hits. Two cold-import
  waits in `studio.controls` that ran past their limits under load now carry explicit budgets.

- **Fixed: the Studio library tests (`docs/src/lib`) no longer pass or fail on the machine's speed.** 96 places in
  39 test files slept for a fixed time, timed a window, or drew an unseeded random name. Each now waits on the
  signal the next check reads, runs on a virtual clock with exact values, or counts the work done instead of the
  milliseconds. Every rewrite was shown failing on a broken product line. Two stopwatches had read the suite's fake
  clock and could never fail; they are work counts now.
- **Fixed: the Studio's unit tests now run the library source, not a leftover build.** Every test that imported one
  of the 17 `docs/src/lib` packages (cadenza, segno, vetrina and the rest) by folder ran that package's built,
  gitignored `dist/`, so an edit to the source changed nothing until someone rebuilt it, and a stale build decided
  the result. `docs/vitest.config.ts` now sends each such import to the source file the package exports. With
  `recorder.ts` broken and its build left stale, `recorder.test.ts` passed before and fails now.

- **Fixed: the export integration tests (`test/integration/export`) no longer pass or fail on the machine's speed.**
  55 places in 24 files slept a fixed time before checking a real browser or a listener. Each now waits on the
  signal the check reads: the player's own state, the page's timer queue going empty, a beacon request that proves
  every earlier load was seen, or a listener drained of every connection a finished client opened. The security
  tests that assert nothing reached the network now run the same attempts against an unwalled witness right after the walled
  run, so their zero is proven, not assumed. Every rewrite was shown failing on a broken product line.

- **Fixed: a QR-card slide (`wifi`, `contact`, `gift-card`) with no card fields yet no longer keeps the browser
  runtime busy forever.** The runtime rewrote the slide's HTML on every pass even when nothing had changed, and that
  write triggered the next pass, so an open slide re-ran the whole deck's transforms about seven times a second. In
  Chromium, one such slide ran 21 passes in 3 seconds; it now runs 2, the same as a `content` slide. The three
  adapters now share one `rebuildCardsInDom` that writes only when the card changes.
- **Fixed: a `wifi` or `contact` slide with no card fields yet no longer loses its closing coda (Key Insight).** The
  card builder set the coda aside to re-attach under the card, then returned the slide without it when there was no
  card to build. It now returns the slide exactly as written, as `gift-card` already did.
- **Fixed: the runtime parity tests (`test/integration/parity`) no longer pass or fail on the machine's speed.** 34
  fixed sleeps are gone. The jsdom boots run on a virtual clock and read once the runtime has nothing queued; the
  real-Chromium checks wait for the page's timer queue to empty. Every rewrite was shown failing on a broken product
  line.

- **Fixed: the Playground voice tests (`test/unit/playground`) no longer pass or fail on the machine's speed.** 20
  fixed sleeps and one stopwatch assertion are gone: each test now waits for the request to reach the voice, owns the
  clock the latency record reads, or cancels inside the step it is about instead of racing two timers. Every rewrite
  was shown failing on a broken product line.

- On a phone, the `--fluid` viewer stacks a panes slide's panes, each at the full width, where it used to keep them side by side and leave a 30% pane about 92px wide. A text pane keeps its content height, a chart or picture takes the rest, and a narrow pane reads in its wide form while stacked. A tablet, a landscape phone and a desktop keep the panes side by side.

- **Fixed: a hint that keyboard focus opened no longer swallows the next tap.** Pressing Escape to close a
  sheet hands focus back to the button that opened it, and that button's hint opens. On a phone the Chat
  button's hint sat over Workspace settings in the header, so the next tap hit the hint and did nothing.
  The `Tip` component now lets the pointer pass through a hint that focus opened. A hint opened by
  hovering still keeps its own hit area, so the pointer can rest on it without closing it.

- `_focus: line N` now tags the lines of the code block instead of the first `<code>` in the slide, so a heading with inline code (`## \`_focus: line 8\` — …`) no longer takes the focus and leaves the block untouched.
- `_focusStyle: ring` on a chart mark shows again: the pigment finish set the mark's stroke `!important` and hid the ring behind a 1px hairline.

- `lint:deck` now checks `_focus`, `_focusStyle`, `_focusSteps` and `track:` on every slide, including a slide with no `_class`. A bare deck-wide `<!-- track: A | [B] -->` on such a slide used to pass silently.
- A mistyped `_focusStyle` now lists all five styles, including `blur` and `highlight`.

- **`lint:deck` names a slide that will clip at the deck's projection scale.** `scale-l`, `scale-xl` and `scale-2xl` grow the type but not the box, so a slide filled to its component's capacity spills past the frame: 25 of 64 slides on a real deck at `scale-xl`, and 133 slides across the component galleries. `capacity-scale` warns before you render (a warning under `venue:`, a note for a bare `scale-*`), and the export's `⚠ OVERFLOW` line names every clipped page. The scale is never reduced for you.
- **Code keeps scaling at a projection scale, and its line cap scales with it.** A `code` pane at a wide @size holds 15 / 13 / 11 / 10 lines at 1x / `scale-l` / `scale-xl` / `scale-2xl`, one or two fewer under an eyebrow, and `floor(102 / s)` columns.

- A page whose fonts were still loading no longer freezes in WebKit. Trama (flowchart and state chart) followed `document.fonts.ready` in a loop when WebKit returned an already-settled promise while a face was in flight, which starved every timer. It now looks again from a 100 ms timer. This fixes the Playground deep link to a flowchart or state-chart gallery slide on WebKit with the iPhone profile.

- The footer band gives its text back the room #3095 took on slides without a section rail. Empty rail and split-counter columns no longer reserve a gap, and the page-number column holds a fixed width only when a rail stands against it. Ten example decks whose footers ended in "…" now print them in full, and the rail still holds still.

- **An authored `form` token no longer changes a sovereign slide.** `<!-- _class: title form -->` used to keep the class, so a sovereign Frame picked up `section.form`'s chrome geometry and its ink moved 16px at 2560x1440. The Frame now decides alone — the token is stripped, which is what `lint:deck` always claimed it was.
- **`data-frame` is re-derived after an auto-split re-authors a page.** A `premise` cover becomes a `content lat-split-cover form` field page, and the attribute kept naming the Frame the AUTHOR wrote — measured across two shipped decks, eleven sections in all. Pinned by an invariant test over ten split-heavy decks, which asks the rendered DOM whether a slide claiming a sovereign Frame was in fact composed with chrome Cells.
- **`lint:deck` now sees every shape a deck used to leave Form by.** A deck-wide `class: no-form`, a Marpit directive split across lines, and `form: off  # a trailing comment` all warned incorrectly or not at all. Findings also name the slide they are on — they all reported slide 0, which put every editor squiggle on the deck's opening `---`.
- **A retired `form` token draws one warning instead of two.** The generic `unknown-class` rule had started telling authors to check the spelling of a token that is spelled correctly and is not coming back.
- **A `form` / `no-form` token quoted inside a code fence is no longer warned on** — a deck documenting the migration was warned about its own example.

- **A deck that merely MENTIONS a `<section>` tag no longer loses Form.** The shared section walker scanned for the literal string `<section`, so one HTML comment quoting `<section class="title">` opened a phantom section that never balanced — and every slide after it went unstamped: no `data-form`, no `data-frame`, no `form` class, no progress rail, no watermark (measured: 0 of 3 slides on a real render). The walker now runs on the same tokenizer the rest of the engine uses, so a comment, a closed `<style>`/`<script>` block and a quoted attribute are text, exactly as a browser reads them. This also removes a real split between the render paths — the DOM twin walks a parse and never had the bug, so the same deck used to get two different answers depending on which path built it.
- **An apostrophe in an unquoted HTML attribute no longer eats the rest of the deck.** The tag scanner treated every `'` and `"` inside a tag as a value delimiter, so `<div data-tip=it's>` — or any unbalanced quote, such as `<p title=5">` — opened a value that never closed, and everything after it became invisible to the scanner.
